For such offenses, the Director of Destinies, according to their gravity, takes away his years and allotted span; when the span is exhausted, he dies, and if there remain unexpiated worth, the calamity extends even to his descendants.

Moreover, those who unjustly seize the wealth of others are made to pay for it through their wives, children, and household, until death and bereavement come upon them; and if they do not suffer death and bereavement, then there befall them fire, water, and robbers...
Moreover, those who wrongfully kill others are but exchanging the sword for mutual slaughter.

Those who take wealth that is not rightfully theirs are like one who eats tainted dried meat to still his hunger, or drinks poisoned wine to quench his thirst; it is not that it does not satisfy for a moment, but death comes with it too.

When the mind gives rise to goodness, even though the good is not yet done, the auspicious spirit already follows; or when the mind gives rise to evil, even though the evil is not yet done, the inauspicious spirit already follows.

As for those who have formerly done evil and afterward repent and reform, doing no evil and practicing all good, in time they will surely obtain good fortune; this is what is meant by turning calamity into blessing.

Therefore the auspicious man speaks good, looks on good, and acts good; doing three good things a day, in three years heaven will surely send down blessing upon him. The inauspicious man speaks evil, looks on evil, and acts evil...

Explanation:
Obtaining goods by coercion, or demanding that others supply them; or being fond of encroaching on others' property, or being fond of seizing it by force.
Analysis:

Whatever goods are not rightfully mine by lot, yet which I insist upon obtaining, is called 'seizing by force.' To have others supply goods for my use is called 'extorting.' To obtain the goods of others by secret craft is called 'encroaching.' To take them openly by force is called 'plundering.' Goods gained by such means are naturally hard for one to enjoy; moreover, in the future they will surely cause one to lose even the goods that rightfully belonged to one's own lot in life!

Zheng Xuan said: 'From what I have observed, this thing called money is something everyone delights in; it is something men inevitably contend for. Among flesh and blood it stirs up disputes; among the well-known it ruins their good name; merchants lose their lives for it, and the common crowd beat and kill one another for it. Yet wealth comes suddenly and vanishes suddenly; rank rises swiftly and sinks swiftly to poverty. In sum, in governing the world money brings people but little blessing and much calamity. I have examined it closely: the shape of the word for money is a 'gold' beside two 'spears'; money is truly a thing that kills men, yet most are unable to awaken to it. Ah, money! Money! In my poverty I beg you to keep me alive but cannot obtain it; I am helpless against you and can do nothing about you. In my poverty you may wish to kill me, but that too you cannot do; you are helpless against me and likewise can do nothing to me.'
Story One:

There was a man of Zhao named Wei Gongxiong. In his youth he was extremely poor and could no longer support his mother in food and clothing; husband and wife wept together over it. The next day, while sweeping the ground, he found a silver ingot weighing twenty-five taels, and so his livelihood became somewhat better. Later Wei Gongxiong became a minister, with a salary of one hundred ingots of silver. When he received his salary, he found that one twenty-five-tael ingot was missing and was about to question the official in charge of funds the next day. That night he dreamed that a spirit told him: 'On such-and-such a day, month, and year, you had already borrowed one ingot!'
Further Analysis:

One must know that even if one's lot contains wealth, if the time and fortune have not yet come, one still cannot obtain it by human effort; how much less when one's lot has no wealth at all, yet one takes money by coercion?
Story Two:

In Kunshan there was an old man surnamed Yang. One day, sitting before his own gate, he saw a woman passing by who dropped a silver hairpin onto the stone-paved street; and when the hairpin fell to the ground it rang out with a clatter! Old Yang hurried forward to look, but to his surprise there was no hairpin; instead he saw an earthworm. Old Yang stood puzzled in place, pacing back and forth a long while without leaving. Suddenly a man came by and picked up the silver hairpin from the ground. Old Yang called out loudly, 'That is my hairpin that fell!' The gentleman knew old Yang was lying and, taking no notice of him, went on his way. Old Yang pursued him closely from behind, so the gentleman could only take out two fen of silver, telling old Yang to use half to buy fish and half to buy wine, and saying to him, 'Old sir, do not keep pestering me; use this silver to buy wine and cook fish and pass a merry night.' When old Yang returned home he told his daughter-in-law to cook the fish; as he was warming the wine, the neighbor's cat suddenly dashed in and carried off the fish, and the daughter-in-law struck the cat with a staff, thereby knocking over the wine; she also broke the dish that held the fish!

One should realize that when the silver hairpin turned into an earthworm, old Yang ought to have awakened. But old Yang was far too greedy and still persisted in demanding it by force; so he had not the good fortune to enjoy either the wine or the fish; how could he manage to eat them? Alas, old Yang truly was a man of thin fortune! A single small matter came to such a pass; as for other greater matters, one need not ask to know how it would go!
Story Three:

In Yin County, Zhejiang, there was a man surnamed Lu who was very wealthy but crafty and deceitful in nature. His neighbor, a Mr. Zheng, had some family property, and Lu secretly contrived to seize it; he tore down Zheng's house and made of it his own mansion and garden, leaving only one fine tree that Zheng's family had planted. Later Lu had a son who, at the age of five, still could not speak. Suddenly one day the son pointed at that tree and said, 'Tree! Tree! You are still here today!' The family was greatly startled, and after the child finished speaking he became mute once more. Lu exhausted every remedy to heal his son, but the son could never utter a single word. When the son grew up he was wild and lustful, giving himself to drink and pleasure, and spent all of Lu's fortune before he died. Everyone said, 'This child is the reappearance of Zheng, born into the world to demand repayment of the debt from Lu!'
Using violent force to plunder the goods of others so as to grow rich.

Officials who exploit the people and secretly plunder public funds, or rich tyrants and evil gentry who lend money at heavy interest; these are all acts of plunder and seizure. Wealth gained by such means is the karmic evil that breaks up families and scatters people, making wives weep and children cry. How can one enjoy such wealth with peace of mind? Has one not heard the principle of the piggy bank? In the Book of Han the piggy bank is called 'hou', which is what is now called a 'dumb gourd.' It is made of pottery with a single opening on top through which coins can be put in; once the coins go in, they cannot be taken out. People use it to save money, and when the money has filled it, they break the bank open to take the coins out, and so it is called a 'piggy bank.' While it is gathering money it only fears it is not full; when it is full, it must be broken before stopping. At that point the bank is broken and the money gone, and both become nothing. So the more one hoards, the more one loses; it is no different from the piggy bank!

In the Song dynasty, when Wen Yanbo, Duke of Lu, was serving as chief judge of Chang'an, he came one day to Benniu Yan, where there was an ox that suddenly spoke in human speech: 'I served in court alongside Wen Yanbo for twenty years; today how do I have the face to see him again!' The soldier in charge of Benniu Yan reported the matter to Wen Yanbo, who ordered the soldier to bring the ox; the ox lay prostrate on the ground with its head bowed, its tears flowing like rain. Wen Yanbo sighed deeply and said, 'My colleague, in life because he secretly plundered public funds, today has met this retribution!' Thereupon he ordered the household accountant to bring out twenty strings of cash to add fodder for the ox.

One must know that the money of the government is the tax paid by the people, and that Wen Yanbo's colleague, turning into an ox to build the dike, was repaying the debt he owed to the people. Seeing this case, one should reflect upon it carefully!

In Suzhou there was an oil seller who, one day while selling oil, passed a wealthy household and saw a five-year-old child wearing a red cap with a golden lock at the chest; he thereupon conceived an evil thought. He carried the child off to a secluded place and killed him, then took the gold ornaments, and suddenly became rich. Later he had a son whose appearance closely resembled the child he had killed, and he came to detest the child. When the child reached the age of five, it was the height of summer and very hot; the oil seller happened to doze off, and the child pulled out the silver hairpin stuck in his topknot and used it to stab playfully at the oil seller's chest. The oil seller thought it was a fly stinging him, raised his hand and slapped; and the silver hairpin pierced right through his chest, killing him on the spot.

Seeing this case, parents who delight in adorning their sons and daughters with gold ornaments and jewels should truly reform this habit; even if one is wealthy, one should not be ostentatious, lest one draw covetous eyes and invite the calamity of losing one's life!
Using crafty and deceitful means to procure one's own promotion.

A superior man, once he enters officialdom, should take loyalty, uprightness, fairness, and incorruptibility as his own proper duty. If, in order to seek promotion, he uses crafty and deceitful means, such a heart and mind is truly improper! Such a man in the court will surely not be loyal; as an official he will not be fair; and if he is sent out as a local official managing the affairs of the people, how can he remain incorrupt and self-possessed? Therefore the Most High here issues special warning. Moreover, a person's achievements, fame, rank, and emolument in a single lifetime are fixed by heaven at birth; even if he labors all his life to seek them, he cannot add the slightest bit. He will only make himself a laughingstock for the wise and be rebuked by ghosts and spirits!

In the time of Emperor Xiaowu of Liu-Song, the three men Dai Faxing, Dai Mingbao, and Chao Shangzhi held such power in the court that they could call the wind and summon the rain; none of those whom they recommended and brought in was ever rejected. People thought that through the recommendation of these three, one's official career would surely be smooth. Only Gu Kaizhi disagreed. He said, 'A person's official emolument is arranged by heaven long before; it is not something that stratagem and craft can transfer or change. One can only be respectful and cautious and strictly keep to one's lot; if one hopes for luck, one merely loses the lot one ought to keep; it has nothing at all to do with the gaining or losing of office.'

Someone, seeing this case, asked me, 'But nowadays it often happens that people who use strategy obtain office; what is the principle of this?' I replied, 'That too is his fate! If it were not that office and emolument lie in his lot, whatever means he used would be futile. Although one may capture birds and beasts by craft and deceit, a superior man would never do such a thing!'
Words of Praise:

Qian Bangqi of Dantu in the Qing dynasty once said, 'Even if a person has the ability to reach heaven, he cannot contend with the ordained fate. Yet only the practice of hidden virtue can surely turn back the ordained fate; and what is done yesterday has its effect today; what is done in the morning answers in the evening. The retribution in the unseen realm is swiftest, and the scrutiny of the spirits is most clear. This truly is the swiftest shortcut; anyone with a willing mind need only try and he will know!'
If reward and punishment are too light or too heavy, that is being unjust.

If, in rewarding the meritorious or punishing the guilty, one errs in the slightest, that is being unfair; and since public justice no longer exists, the people's hearts will not submit. Not only does this fail to reward merit and punish guilt, but it instead accumulates resentment and invites calamity!
Story:

Zhuge Kongming of Shu Han said, 'My heart is like a balance; I cannot lighten it for anyone or weight it against anyone.' Chen Shou praised him, saying, 'Kongming may be called a model of utmost loyalty and service to the age! Though a man were his enemy, if he had merit he was sure to be rewarded; and one who broke the law and was negligent in performing his duties, though a relative, was sure to be punished. One who confessed his guilt was worthy of forgiveness, and though his offense were grave, he was sure to be released; but one who with crafty words excused his offense, though his crime were light, was surely put to death without mercy. Hence all the generals of Shu at the time were able to lay down their lives for the state; even Wei Yan, that traitor to the state, had no complaint under Kongming's leadership; and the two generals Li Ping and Liao Li, though stripped of office by Kongming and sentenced to lifelong exile on the frontier, had not a word of resentment. Therefore those who hold the power of reward and punishment should take Kongming as their model!'
In ease and pleasure one should be moderate and not go to excess.

Ease and pleasure are what everyone delights in! The Book of Rites says, 'Pleasure must not be excessive, and desires must not be indulged.' The Discourses of the States says, 'When the people are toilsome they think of goodness; when they are at ease they think of indulgence.' The intent is simply to keep the people from wallowing in ease. Mencius also says, 'One thrives in anxiety and hardship, and perishes in ease and pleasure.' This too is to keep people from wallowing in ease and pleasure; how much more when ease and pleasure are excessive and utterly without restraint! But what the world calls ease and pleasure, the greatest of it is no more than wine, lust, wealth, and anger. People today who are addicted to wine disregard their bodies; lustful of beauty they disregard their illness; greedy for wealth they disregard their kin; and in quarrels they disregard their very lives. Before encountering these situations, they are able to understand such principles and to dissuade others; but when they encounter these realms themselves, they commit them in confusion. This is what is meant by being able to see through it but not able to endure it. If one can embody the four words 'ease and pleasure beyond measure,' then one's habits and nature will be changed, and these familiar realms of wine, lust, wealth, and anger will be forgotten; having cultivated to the point where desires are few and the mind pure, one can stand peerless between heaven and earth!

Once, when the monk Master Zhi Gong was conversing with Emperor Wu of Liang about music, Master Zhi Gong asked the emperor to have some prisoners brought out from the jail for a test. He ordered each prisoner to hold a cup filled with water and pace back and forth beneath the hall, warning them, 'If the water in your cup does not spill, I will commute your death sentence.' Then he had music played to divert the prisoners' attention and see whether they would be distracted. After a long while, not a drop of water had spilled from the prisoners' cups. Emperor Wu sighed and said, 'Did you not hear the music?' The prisoners all said, 'No.' National Master Zhi Gong said, 'They were afraid of being beheaded and fearful lest the water in their cups spill; how could they hear the music?'
If a person can, like those prisoners, constantly hold a heart of fear, then the mind of ease and pleasure will naturally not arise!

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, 'Diligent like one carrying bricks and tiles, cautious like one facing the deep abyss and treading on thin ice; the sages and heroes of old have all been thus diligent. Who am I, that I should dare to be so carefree and lead so idle and luxurious a life!' The Book of Changes says, 'The movement of heaven is vigorous; the superior man thereby strengthens himself without ceasing.' If a person is unwilling to strengthen himself, then before an urgent or personally vital matter arises he will want to pass his days in ease and wandering. But one who is determined to strengthen himself will find that the tasks he ought to do are endless. Only when one feels there are not enough hours in the day is there any spare time for amusement; thus naturally one does not dare to let go into indolence!

Fan Wenzheng of the Song dynasty said, 'Every night when I go to bed, I am certain to consider whether the salary the state gives me today is proportionate to what I did in the daytime. If they are proportionate, then I can sleep soundly in peace without shame or disgrace; if they are not, then I cannot sleep all night.'

In the Yuan dynasty there were two students of the Imperial College, born in the same year, month, day, and hour, who also passed the provincial examination at the same time and were appointed to office on the same day. One was given the post of professor of Ezhou, the other the post of professor of Huangzhou. Before long the professor of Huangzhou died. The professor of Ezhou was greatly frightened and made ready all his funeral affairs; but after several days he still did not die. So he prepared gifts and went to offer condolences to the professor of Huangzhou, weeping before the coffin, 'You and I were born in the same year, month, day, and hour, and our careers and positions have been the same; today you have gone before me. Even if I were to die now, I would be seven days later than you. If you have a spirit, you should appear to me in a dream and tell me!' That night he dreamed that the professor of Huangzhou told him, 'You, because you are frugal and thrifty in everything, will live long; whereas I, because I consumed to excess without restraint, died young!'

In the Liang dynasty there was a wealthy man surnamed Yu who built a high tower facing the main thoroughfare. From morning to night he and beautiful women sang, feasted, gambled, and played chess in the tower; the winners covered their mouths and laughed. It happened that three passersby were walking beneath the Yu's tower when a rotting rat fell from the beak of a hawk and landed right on their heads. The three passersby looked up and saw the people above covering their mouths and laughing. They were furious and said, 'The Yu family is wealthy and has enjoyed itself too long; we did not offend him, yet he has insulted us!' Thereupon they gathered a crowd and killed the entire Yu household.

Mr. Gu Xichou said, 'Even if the Yu's tower had not faced the thoroughfare, some strange calamity would still have befallen them. The proverb says that pride and excess bring many disasters, and the causes of disaster are not all the same; yet among the disasters of pride and excess, the disaster of lusting after women is the most severe and the swiftest. Hence guarding against lust for women is most important!' Wu Shi, the man of practical affairs, also said, 'Skin wrapping bone and flesh, all foulness, / Yet each strains to be alluring and deceives; / Heroes of a thousand ages meet their fall through this, / In a hundred years all share one grave of dust.' If a person can understand this principle and, together with the annotations in this book on 'Seeing a beauty and privately coveting her' and 'Lust to excess,' thoroughly understand them, and with reverence keep the teachings and prohibitions, maintaining the contemplation of emptiness, he will not sink into the enjoyment of ease and invite disaster.
Being harsh and cruel to one's subordinates or servants.

Officials who cruelly abuse their subordinates and the people, or masters who excessively punish and flog the household servants; these are acts of harsh cruelty. The matter of officials in high position abusing their subordinates and the common people has already been explained in detail earlier in this book; so now we will only explain the part about the master of a household treating his servants.

The Buddha told Sigala: 'In treating their servants, all people in the world should understand five things. First, they should first know their cold, heat, hunger, and thirst, and then have them work. Second, if they are ill, one should treat them. Third, if they commit offenses, one may not flog or punish them at will; one should first ask the reason and then administer discipline. Whom one can forgive, forgive; whom one cannot forgive, instruct and punish. Fourth, if they have a little personal wealth of their own, one may not seize it for oneself. Fifth, in distributing things to servants, one should be fair and not partial.'

Master Yuan's Model for the World says, 'The natural endowments of servants are mostly somewhat inferior to those of ordinary people, so they often make mistakes, and moreover are forgetful; sometimes they forget entirely what they were told. Most are also stubborn and often think themselves right. Some servants are also hot-tempered, speaking without regard for rank, not understanding the principle of superiority and inferiority. Therefore, when the head of a household sets them to work, he should treat them with a generous heart; use much instruction and do not be angry, so that the master's own heart may also be at ease. Even when servants commit offenses and should be punished and reproved, one should question them calmly and with equanimity; once they have been reproved, in employing them afterward one should keep a normal tone and expression, so that no other trouble arises. As for women, whose dispositions are narrow, stubborn, and willful, the head of the household should frequently instruct and teach them. The young people of the family also may not beat servants at will; if a matter arises, they should report it to the head of the household. If a servant is truly a vicious, coarse, and evil person, one should also send him away by a proper means, and not treat him with stern severity, lest such a person later bear a grudge and take revenge!'

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said, 'In treating inferiors, harsh cruelty is indeed improper; but to indulge them and let them act without restraint is even more improper! One often sees the servants of noble and high officials arrogant and unreasonable, and even exalted to the skies; when they go out they ride swift horses and wear bright clothing, and when they return home they gamble and drink; or when a guest comes to call they sit there without rising to receive him; or when a relative comes to visit they refuse and will not announce it. Thus distinguished guests and relatives leave in anger, while those of lower station or connection leave bitter and grieved; or even these fierce servants invent pretexts for trouble, rely on their master's power, and defraud others of money abroad, while the master turns a deaf ear. In the end it comes to all turning away and all kindred estranged, offending so many friends and drawing so much resentment! Therefore one must be extremely cautious!'

Tao Yuanming, the great poet of the Jin dynasty, admonished his son, 'Your daily work keeps you too busy to have spare time to look after yourself; now I am sending a servant to help you in gathering firewood and carrying water, to lighten your burden. But the servant is also another person's child, and you should treat him well!'

Dame Chengzhai, the wife of Yang Wanli of the Song dynasty, was already over seventy years of age. Every winter she would rise very early, go into the kitchen, and with her own hands cook a pot of gruel; only after every maidservant had eaten a bowl of warm gruel would she set them to their work. Her son Dongshan said to her: ‘Mother, the weather is so cold — why put yourself to such trouble?’ Dame Chengzhai answered: ‘These maids and servants are other people’s children too! The winter dawn is bitterly cold, so they must first have a little warmth in their bodies before they can be set to work.’

Wang Jianyi, the adjutant of Hongzhou, contracted an illness known as rebellious qi attacking the heart. After he had died and come back to life, he told his wife: ‘There was a young slave I used to command. Once I punished him far too severely, and he died of his injuries. Just now I was taken to the yin offices, and it was that young slave who had lodged the accusation against me; and it seems no settlement can be reached. This illness I now suffer is his doing!’ His wife said: ‘He was only a petty slave — how would he dare to be so bold?’ Wang Jianyi answered: ‘In the world of the living, men are divided into noble and base; but in the world below, all are looked upon alike!’ Not long after he had spoken, Wang Jianyi died.
Intimidating and threatening others.

Frightening others may be divided into two kinds. The first is when, meeting a person in urgent peril, one does not comfort him, but deliberately puts on a menacing show to terrify him and fill his heart with dread. The second is when, greedy for profit, one blusters and makes a false display of strength so that others will fear one, hoping thereby to gain one’s ends. I have heard that when living beings meet with terror and urgent peril, Bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara is able to bestow fearlessness upon them; and by this he realized perfect penetration, so that the Guanyin dharma-gate may be called the most excellent of dharma-gates. And all the beings of the Jambudvīpa world call Bodhisattva Guanyin the Fearless Giver who saves from suffering and rescues from distress. Yet those who frighten others — when they behold Bodhisattva Guanyin’s gift of fearlessness, one wonders what thoughts they can have. Therefore whenever a gentleman meets someone terrified and afraid, he never fails earnestly to comfort him, so that the other’s heart may be set at rest and he need fear no more. It is a pity that people do not know that one who delights in frightening others is reborn, immediately after death, as a roebuck or some such creature. In the daytime, when the roebuck sees other wild beasts, it flees in fear and panic; at night it hangs its head and horns upon the branch of a tree and sleeps with its body drawn up. No sooner does anything stir than it starts up and scatters in terror. Thus it is startled and then sleeps again, sleeps and then starts awake again; from dusk to dawn there is not a moment of peace. Such is its retribution!

In Huzhou there was a petty ginger-seller who went to Yongjia in Zhejiang to sell his ginger. In Yongjia there lived a rich man named Wang Sheng, who fell to haggling with him and quarreled. Wang Sheng flew into a rage and beat the seller cruelly on the back; the man was struck down to the ground and died on the spot. Wang Sheng at once applied first aid, and the seller was revived. Wang Sheng then apologized and gave him a bolt of silk as well. When the seller got back to his boat by the river, the boatman asked him: ‘Where did you get that bolt of silk?’ The seller told him all that had just happened. Thereupon the boatman took out money and bought from the seller both the bolt of silk and the ginger basket. After the seller had gone, the boatman happened to fish an unclaimed corpse out of the river, carried it to his own house, and then ran to Wang Sheng’s home and asked: ‘After noon today, a ginger-seller from Huzhou who was taking my boat home — because the injuries you gave him were so grave, when he was near death he begged me to tell his parents and wife that they must bring a charge against you before the authorities; and he left behind a bolt of silk and a ginger basket as evidence. Not long after he had spoken, he breathed his last. So I did not dare to come and not report it to you!’ When Wang Sheng heard this, the whole family wept and were greatly afraid. They bribed the boatman with two hundred strings of cash; at first the boatman pretended to refuse, and only then accepted with a show of reluctance, and together with Wang Sheng buried the corpse in the forest. Now Wang Sheng had a servant who went to the county office and laid an accusation, and Wang Sheng was thereupon sentenced and thrown into prison, where he died. The following year the ginger-seller came again to Yongjia and even called at Wang Sheng’s house. When Wang Sheng’s son saw the seller he took him for a ghost! The seller said: ‘I did not die! Today I have brought a few local products from Huzhou, and have come to thank your family!’ Wang Sheng’s son kept the seller there, and at once had the servant seized and haled before the authorities with his charge; the authorities then arrested the boatman. In the end both the boatman and the servant died in prison.
Resenting heaven and blaming others.

This Jambudvīpa world in which we dwell has always been known for its deficiencies; how then could anyone here have every matter go as he wishes? And the reason things do not go as one wishes must be that the merit accumulated in former lives was too thin, so that the blessings one enjoys in this life are thin as well. Therefore the only way is to keep carefully to one’s own lot, earnestly to reflect upon and repent of one’s faults, and so to mend and cultivate the blessings allotted to one by Heaven. This has been, through all the ages, the best method for one in straitened circumstances, and the best means of inviting good fortune and averting evil. Know that in blaming Heaven one only makes Heaven angrier, and in resenting others one only makes others hate one the more. Such conduct brings no benefit at all, and harm besides!

Jiao Junming won office through the examinations while still very young, yet a long time passed and he was never promoted. He often complained that his official career was beset with obstacles and grumbled against Heaven, and he even wrote out a petition and prayed to Heaven. At dusk on the day of his prayer, a plain white document suddenly fell down before the censer at which he was praying. Looking closely, he saw that the sixteen characters written upon it were in the script of the heavenly court, so that he could not make out their meaning. Hearing that the Immortal Maiden He possessed spiritual attainments, he went to question her. The Immortal Maiden would not tell him; only after he begged her bitterly did she say: ‘To accept a bribe of five ounces of gold cuts short ten years of life; to put a man to death unjustly brings certain punishment after death. Have you committed any of these faults?’ At this question from the Immortal Maiden, Jiao Junming was left without a word to say.

When Zhang Dun of the Song dynasty was chief minister, he banished to the Lingnan region all the great ministers who had served as chief councillors during the Yuanyou era. Fan Chunren was among them, and was already seventy years old. When he received the court’s order, he set out at once and gladly. Fan Chunren constantly admonished his sons: ‘Not the slightest resentment may be harbored in your hearts!’ Whenever he heard his children utter the least complaint against Zhang Dun, he would angrily put a stop to it. On the road to Lingnan the boat in which Fan Chunren was traveling capsized in the river, and he escaped with nothing worse than wet clothes. Turning then to his sons he said: ‘Was the capsizing of the boat, too, Zhang Dun’s doing?’

This case of Fan Chunren is altogether a lesson in the learning of rejoicing in Heaven and knowing one’s lot! If a man can understand this principle, he will be able to remain calm and unshaken in adversity, and naturally there will be no more blaming of Heaven or resentment of others.
Reviling the wind and cursing the rain.

Wind and rain both have the merit of helping Heaven and Earth to create and transform the myriad things, and each has its own deity in charge. When Confucius encountered a sudden thunderclap or a fierce wind, his countenance would always change, and he would face it with reverence. The Book of Rites, in the chapter Qu Li, says: ‘If a violent wind, a sudden thunderclap, or a heavy rain should come, one must change countenance; even if it happens in the night, one must rise, dress and cap oneself properly, and sit upright.’ Master Cheng of the Song, whenever he met with wind and rain, would always rise to his feet, because one must be reverent toward Heaven. Yet the ignorant common people, when it rains too much, complain that the excess rain will harm the crops; when fair weather lasts too long, they complain that Heaven has gone too long without rain; when the wind blows too fiercely, they complain that the wind is too violent — never reflecting on the principle that yin and yang each have their fixed measure. It may be that the government officials have governed with too great a harshness and fierceness, or that the people have created too much evil karma; all of these bring about wind and rain that come out of season and out of order. How then can one rail at the wind and curse the rain for being out of season? To do so only adds in vain to one’s guilt of defying Heaven!

In the district school of Xianning in Zhending there was a verger named Yang Kuan, whose duty was to attend to the sacrificial rites. Once, at a public banquet, he was serving as the wine steward; he noticed two whirlwinds beside the wall, and so sprinkled some wine for them to enjoy. Some time later, Yang Kuan went with a company of people to offer incense at Mount Tai. On the way he met two soldiers who invited him to drink; when the wine was finished, he had not yet had time to ask their names before they parted and went their separate ways. The next day, as Yang Kuan was climbing the mountain, he came to a shrine, and there beside the chief deity enshrined in it he saw two deities in the likeness of soldiers, just like the two who had invited him to drink the day before, and his heart was filled with fear. After he had returned to the inn, he saw those two soldiers again, and they said to him: ‘You need not doubt or be afraid. We two are subordinates of the Great Emperor of Mount Tai. Once we were sent on official business through your honored district, and were graciously favored by you with two cups of wine; so yesterday we invited you to a cup of wine in return.’ Having spoken, the two soldiers vanished.

In Ezhou of the Song dynasty there was a woman who one day took a clay basin down to the river to wash it. Suddenly it began to rain, and both the clothes on her back and the road were soaked through; whereupon the woman let out foul words and cursed Heaven. At that moment a strange gust of wind suddenly arose and swept the woman into the river. Her husband saw it and at once leaped into the river and pulled her ashore; but the clay basin had had a great hole broken through its middle, and it had settled exactly over the woman’s head, as though she had been fitted with a cangue. Whenever anyone tried to pull the basin off, the woman’s pain pierced to the marrow. The people who came crowding to her house to see were packed so tight that not a drop could have seeped through. A few days later, unable to bear the pain, the woman breathed her last.
Stirring up strife and contention.

When others have fallen into a dispute, one ought with kind words to urge them to settle it, so that a great matter may be made small and a small matter reduced to nothing; then both families will receive blessing. If instead one uses the occasion to egg them on to quarrel, or secretly stirs up trouble and instigates them, or steps forward to bear witness, or fabricates testimony on their behalf, or takes their lawsuit into one’s own hands in order to profit by it — such conduct is the making of sin! In the end it is sure to call down the wrath of men and gods alike; and when the karmic retribution comes before one, one will be unable to bear the suffering and will repent too late.

On the back of Liu Yuanzhi there grew a great poisonous sore. He consulted many physicians and tried every kind of remedy, all to no effect; and the doctors said to him: ‘We have done all that we can. I fear calamity is upon you!’ Liu Yuanzhi then engaged a Daoist priest to pray and make petition to the Lord of the Northern Dipper. That night he dreamed that a spirit told him: ‘You have offended against the law of the heavenly court; even if you pray and petition the Lord of the Northern Dipper, it will be hard to escape your punishment!’ Liu Yuanzhi said to the spirit: ‘But I have committed no crime!’ The spirit said: ‘You were engaged to teach in a certain man’s household, and there you wantonly incited them to go to law, so that two families were ruined.’ Yuanzhi said: ‘That was done by my younger brother Liu Yuanli, not by me!’ The King of the Underworld then ordered the judge to check the record once more, to see whether there had been a mistake; and indeed it was found that Liu Yuanli had done it. Thus Liu Yuanzhi’s calamity was lifted; and the following year Liu Yuanli died.

Thus the retribution for instigating others to litigation has always been exceedingly cruel; and such retribution may be seen and heard of everywhere, never missing by so much as a hair. Therefore I earnestly exhort the people of the world: a hundred trades can earn a man his living — why take up the trade of the litigation master? Recently I saw in the book The Netherworld Cases of Loudong the record of a litigation master who was dragged by ghost attendants into the underworld. The King of the Underworld said: ‘Though you practiced the trade of a litigation master, which creates evil karma, yet when you wrote out the plaints you constantly urged men to stop their disputes and by no means to bring false accusations; and again, in the plaints you always secretly set the charges down in a lighter form. Because you harbored such good thoughts, your guilt is for the time being remitted, and you are sentenced to return to the world of the living and have your life extended.’ Seeing this case, those who have long practiced the trade of litigation master and cannot change their calling should take it as a warning, so that they may at least create less evil karma.

In Xiuning there was a village schoolmaster. Though his family was very poor, he still applied himself diligently to learning, and above all he loved to study the law. In the village a rich man died, and his two sons quarreled over the property; the elder wished to bring suit against the younger, and so took generous gifts of money and begged the schoolmaster to write out the plaint for him. The schoolmaster said: ‘The only purpose of my studying the law was to be prepared beforehand, lest in some later year I be condemned and thrown into prison! How could I be willing to stir up a lawsuit for you?’ The schoolmaster then set before him many truths and many instances of the bond between brothers, and of how brothers who contend bring ruin upon both, to warn him. When the elder heard this, he was moved and awakened; and when the younger came to see the schoolmaster, he too was exhorted in the same way and was likewise moved and convinced. The two brothers thereupon were reconciled as before, and with one heart and united strength labored on, until at last they became rich. One day, when the two brothers were selling sapan-wood planks, they suddenly noticed the schoolmaster’s name carved upon the planks, and the two of them grasped what it meant, saying: ‘We two brothers, thanks to the schoolmaster’s exhortation, put an end to our dispute, and only today have we had the good fortune to establish our household and our calling; and the schoolmaster’s great kindness has not yet been repaid. Therefore Heaven has written the schoolmaster’s name upon the planks to remind us to know kindness and to repay it!’ So the two brothers agreed that when this lot of planks was sold, all the profit from it should be given to the schoolmaster. When they got home and settled the accounts, they had made three hundred taels of silver in all. At that time the schoolmaster, being advanced in years, had given up teaching, and was so poor that he and his son sat facing each other eating wheat gruel; when suddenly he saw the two brothers come forward with silver in their hands, bow to him, and explain why they had come to present the silver. At first the schoolmaster declined and would not accept it; then the two brothers said: ‘This is what Heaven has bestowed upon you!’ Only after hearing that did the schoolmaster accept the gift.

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: ‘Those who hold office should severely punish and suppress those who instigate others to litigation and those who are skilled at going to law; and when one has retired from office and dwells in the village, one should with tireless, heartfelt words persuade and stop both those already engaged in lawsuits and those not yet engaged in them. This is the foremost work of nurturing the nation’s vital strength; and such a man is a great servant of the state, and a great servant of Heaven and Earth!’
Foolishly pursuing factional partisanship.

Of the great sort: ministers at court forming factions and cliques, grasping the reins of government, openly excluding those who differ from them, or secretly undermining and entrapping others. Of the small sort: ordinary people in society joining societies or swearing brotherhood, calling to one another and drawing their own kind together, supporting one another. All of these belong to the reckless pursuit of faction, and are certain to bring great calamity down upon one’s head. Therefore officials and commoners alike should firmly and earnestly abstain from them!

In the Tang dynasty, Liu Zongyuan and Liu Yuxi were both men of towering talent and first-rate learning, their fame unsurpassed in their day. At that time Emperor Shunzong fell ill and could not speak, and the petty man Wang Shuwen abruptly seized the great affairs of the court. Liu Zongyuan and Liu Yuxi threw themselves in to attach themselves to Wang Shuwen; and moreover they recklessly clung to one another and drew one another along, thinking Wang Shuwen a second Yi Yin or Duke of Zhou, and sought advancement with frantic eagerness, as though possessed. Both were promoted by Wang Shuwen beyond all precedent to the post of attendant censor, and the whole court of civil and military officials looked at them askance. Not long afterward, Emperor Shunzong passed the throne to the crown prince, and Wang Shuwen’s schemes came to ruin; the remonstrating officials attacked him one after another, and both Liu Yuxi and Liu Zongyuan were demoted to the office of adjutant of a prefecture, and ended their days in misery in poor and remote places.

Alas! Had Liu and Liu not fallen in with Wang Shuwen’s faction, then by their literary talent and their character they would have been famous ministers of their age! Thus a single misstep may bring lifelong ruin; how can a man be anything but careful? And yet this was only the lesser harm! The disasters of faction in the Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties all began in this way. Therefore for one who is a great minister of the court to plant his own party and scheme for private ends — his guilt is all too great!

There was a young man of a poor family who was not only poor but of poor conduct as well. He was constantly in the company of an actor, who often gave him clothes to wear, so that the two became close friends. He knew that the actor was in fact a thief, yet he still went about the streets wearing the clothes the actor had given him. Once he was caught red-handed in the street by the man who had been robbed, and haled before the authorities to answer for the crime; but by that time the actor had long since fled far away. He was therefore unable to clear himself of the charge, and in the end he died in prison.

Again, there was the son of a rich man who loved to practice boxing and brandish staves, and in the course of it struck up sworn brotherhood with ten companions. When the rich man learned of it he even said: ‘In this way he can command respect in the district, and no one will dare bully my son hereafter.’ He did not forbid his son to form a faction. Later one of those ten sworn brothers actually turned robber; and when the affair came to light, the rich man’s son was implicated in the statement given to the authorities. Because the rich man’s family was wealthy, the authorities actually charged his son with being the leader of the bandits, and the rich man’s household was ruined by it. Alas! Those who delight in following factions and making friends would do well to take this as a warning!

Duke Yu Zhongxuan of the Yuan dynasty, whose name was Que, once said: ‘If a man draws near the worthy and good, / He is like a sheet of paper, understood: / Wrap orchids and musk within the sheet, / And it grows fragrant, sweet and meet. // If a man draws near a friend depraved, / He is like a willow wand, ill-behaved: / Thread fish and turtles on the bough, / And it grows foul and stinking now.’ In taking our stand in the world and conducting ourselves, we should repeat these words three times.
Heeding the words of wives and concubines, and defying the instruction of parents.

The words of wives and concubines are sweet, and so they easily find entry; the instructions of parents, though right, are hard to obey. And yet there is no word of a wife or concubine that does not run counter to the instructions of parents! This is why filial piety has declined in the world. Know that parents, having seen more of life, are sure to judge a matter aptly; and since their love for their son is earnest, the plans they make for him are sure to be thorough. How could the little that a young girl has seen and heard ever surpass that of parents mature in years and seasoned in affairs? This holds true in fact and in principle alike — it is not said merely to urge men to filial piety.

Mr. Zhang Gongchen said: ‘Though a son obey his parents’ instructions ten thousandfold, when all is said he has still not truly obeyed them! Everyone says that the words of wives and concubines must never be heeded, and yet in the end everyone exhausts every word of his wives and concubines! This is because principle cannot overcome desire: the bond is too close, and so the mind is clouded and one finds it hard to perceive. Therefore I hope that those who fancy they would never heed the words of wives and concubines will not take this for an easy matter! One who has not done fine and subtle work upon his own mind will not only be unable to practice it, but will also be unable to understand such a principle.’

A wife or concubine is her husband’s helpmeet within the household, and if she has good counsel to offer, it is not necessarily wrong for the husband to follow it. But among women the wise are few and the foolish many; and by nature most are narrow of heart, unwilling to listen to the views of others, and impatient of affairs; and they are moreover skilled at covering over their faults, and their speech is pleasing to the ear, so that the husband is the most easily deluded of all. And once deluded by the words of a wife or concubine, he is certain to defy the instructions of his parents; therefore the Supreme Old Lord laid down so strict a prohibition. As for estranging flesh and blood, alienating kin, bullying the neighbors, showing partiality among one’s children, and tyrannizing over servants — the source of these evil deeds lies for the most part with the women of the house as well. Therefore the husband should at all times reflect and take heed, and should also tell them plainly why such things may not be done. As for a husband who heeds the words of a beloved concubine and so ill-treats or casts off his wife — this above all is where human feeling most easily goes astray and is most easily deluded. How can one fail to be careful and circumspect?

A son ought to serve his parents with his whole heart and all his strength, and whether it be east, west, south, or north, he should follow their commands alone. If he agrees outwardly while opposing inwardly, and so defies his parents’ instructions, this is a capital offense at the root, an evil that admits of no pardon! As for those who defy their parents out of doting on a wife or concubine, the world has no lack of such men; but such guilt is one degree graver still.

Cheng Yanzun served his mother with the utmost filial piety, but his mother was of a fiercely severe temper and detested his wife, and drove her out of the household. Cheng Yanzun was then in the prime of manhood, but to comply with his mother’s wish he never took another wife as long as he lived; and his wife was a woman of great virtue, and though driven from her husband’s home by her mother-in-law, she never uttered a word of complaint. Whenever a festival or the New Year came round, she would always return to her husband’s house to inquire after her mother-in-law’s health; she herself lived alone, keeping her chastity for her husband and refusing to marry again. When the scholars of the time saw this, they all agreed that Cheng Yanzun’s wife was a rare and precious worthy wife, and they wrote a biography of her as a faithful and upright woman, to commend her filial conduct.
[Conclusion]

Alas! Cheng Yanzun and his wife may truly be called a filial son and a worthy wife, rare and praiseworthy! And those unfilial sons and shrewish daughters-in-law — when they see the filial conduct of Cheng Yanzun and his wife, can they fail to die of shame?

In Wen’an County there was a householder who married a beautiful wife; but this wife was of a fierce and headstrong temper and was unwilling to serve her mother-in-law. Whenever her husband came home she would complain to him that she was being cruelly treated by her mother-in-law; and the husband, hearing it, never answered a word. One evening the husband brought out a sharp knife and showed it to his wife. The wife said: ‘What do you mean to do with that knife?’ The husband said: ‘Did you not say that my mother ill-treats you? Let us take the knife together and go kill my mother — how would that be?’ The wife said: ‘Very well!’ The husband said: ‘Let it be thus: for the present, serve my mother well for one month, so that all the neighbors know how filial you are while my mother ill-treats you; then we will secretly carry out the killing of my mother.’ The wife did as her husband said, showing a cheerful countenance to her mother-in-law every day and serving her with the greatest diligence. When nearly a month of this had passed, the husband again brought out the sharp knife, toyed with it in the lamplight, and asked his wife: ‘How has my mother been treating you lately?’ The wife said: ‘Not as she used to!’ When another month had passed, the husband again took up the knife and asked his wife, and she said with great joy: ‘My mother-in-law is now on the best of terms with me; what we spoke of before must on no account be done!’ The husband slowly gripped the knife, glared at her in anger, and said: ‘Have you ever seen a husband kill his wife?’ The wife said: ‘I have.’ The husband said again: ‘Have you ever heard of a son killing his mother?’ The wife said: ‘I have never heard of such a thing.’ The husband said: ‘In a man’s life the greatest matter of all is to support his parents with filial piety; the kindness of one’s parents cannot be repaid even with the sacrifice of one’s own body! When a son grows up and takes a wife, the purpose is that she may serve his parents and continue the family line. I have been watching you all along: you could not be filial to my mother, and you would even have had me commit this monstrous crime. This knife of mine is in truth meant to cut off your head and give my mother joy; the reason I granted you a stay of two months was to give you the chance to reform and make yourself new, to be filial to your mother-in-law and fulfill your duty as a daughter-in-law; and it was also to show that my mother’s heart bears with you, so that you might know the fault is not my mother’s, and go to your death willingly with your eyes closed!’ When the wife heard her husband’s words she shook from head to foot with terror and burst into tears, and bowing to the ground she begged him: ‘If you will pardon me and let me live, I will be filial to my mother-in-law to the end of my days, and will never dare to be the least bit slack!’ Only after a long while did the husband consent. After this affair, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law became wholly harmonious; and before long the story spread throughout the district.

Alas! This householder of Wen’an County was no more than an ordinary husband, yet he was able to train and transform a headstrong wife and turn her from wickedness to goodness; even a gentleman learned in the books might have been unable to do as much, and would fall short of him! The proverb says: ‘In the world there are no parents who are in the wrong.’ And again: ‘In the world there are no parents who cannot be transformed.’ These are true words!

Liu Jiande’s wife was wicked and overbearing, and Liu Jiande could not master her, so he simply gave way to her. Once, when Liu Jiande’s mother fell ill, the wife ordered him to send his mother to live in a nunnery; the mother was unwilling to go, but Liu Jiande did not dare disobey his wife, and merely sent a maidservant to the nunnery to attend his mother and give her her broth and medicine. Therefore Liu Jiande’s mother, before she died, cried out loudly: ‘When I am dead and come to the underworld, I will surely lodge a charge of unfiliality against you before King Yama!’ A few days after the mother died, Liu Jiande’s wife fell ill and went mad, crying out at the top of her voice: ‘I ought not to have driven my mother-in-law out to the nunnery — the yin offices are now drawing out my intestines and flaying my skin!’ Thereupon her whole body turned a livid purple, and she died shrieking with pain. Two days later Liu Jiande too went mad and cried aloud: ‘I, Liu Jiande, was ruled by my wife and so defied my own mother; my wife has now had her intestines drawn out and her skin flayed by the yin offices, and is suffering torment in the incessant hell; and today the yin offices are urgent to arrest me. Let the people of the world take me as a warning! Never be deluded by a wife or concubine into defying your parents.’ Having spoken, he died. A few days after the husband and wife had been laid in their coffins, a thunderclap suddenly sounded from the sky, both coffins burst open, and the stench of the corpses drifted out; for miles around, the stink of the corpses of Liu Jiande and his wife could be smelled.

Know that ‘there is no crime greater than unfiliality’ — this is a truth that everyone knows. As for their being struck down by Heaven’s thunder after death, this shows that they were a rebellious son and a rebellious wife; and lest there be any who do not know it, it is written out here to proclaim it to all the world.
Forgetting the old upon gaining the new.

Whether it be the clothes one wears, the utensils one uses, the affection of friends, the ties of kin, wives and concubines, or young servants and maids — all of them, so to speak, admit of the distinction between old and new. And one who forgets the old because he has gotten the new belongs to the sort of men who are cold of heart and scant of kindness. A worthy of old said: ‘Rather than form a new acquaintance, it is better to deepen an old friendship.’ The principle in these words is profound! In ancient times the king of Chu issued an edict, hoping to recover a shoe he had lost, and said: ‘My shoe and I went out together, and yet it cannot return together with me; for this I am grieved without end!’ From that time on, none of the people of Chu dared to cast away anything old. So the king of Chu was truly a man of feeling through the ages, and truly a man who understood the great Way through the ages!

In the Eastern Han, Princess Huyang, the wife of Emperor Guangwu’s younger brother, had just lost her husband and was in mourning widowhood, and wished to marry Song Hong. Emperor Guangwu said to Song Hong: ‘A rich man has money, and so easily makes friends; a noble person has rank, and so easily marries a wife — is this not, too, the common feeling of mankind?’ Song Hong answered: ‘The friends made in poverty and low estate must not be forgotten; the wife of the chaff and husks must not be put out of the hall.’ When Emperor Guangwu heard Song Hong’s answer, he turned to the princess and said: ‘If you wish to marry Song Hong, I fear it cannot be done!’

To delight in the new and weary of the old is the common failing of the world, and among wives and concubines men are especially quick to change; often a distaste or a friction bred upon the pillow will plant the seed of calamity within the bedchamber, and the harm it does is more than words can tell. Therefore the people of the world must be exceedingly careful and circumspect in this.

There was a rich man who had no son, and so adopted his elder brother’s son and raised him for ten years. Suddenly the rich man’s concubine bore him a son, and the rich man thereupon disowned his brother’s son, and all his property went to the concubine’s son. In time the brother’s son made a household for himself by diligence and thrift, and was exceedingly filial, humble, and compassionate, so that the whole clan praised him. But the concubine’s son, when he grew up, was dissolute and unbridled, given over to wine, women, and gambling of every kind, and he squandered the rich man’s whole fortune; the rich man was filled with bitter chagrin, and died of grief and regret.

Jing Yang of Yizheng, when he was poor, was a close friend of Shi Cheng of Yangzhou. After Jing Yang died, his children lived in still greater poverty; the kinsmen and friends of former days no longer came or went, but Shi Cheng did not forget his old friend’s children, and often went to comfort them and bring them gifts, more diligently even than when Jing Yang was alive. Jing Yang had left behind several tens of scrolls of his writings, and Shi Cheng contributed a thousand taels of gold to have his friend’s writings printed as a book and circulated in the world. He said: ‘I truly cannot bear to see the fine writings of my departed friend buried in the dust along with him!’ Later Shi Cheng rose to a very high office.
Saying yes with the mouth while the heart says no.

One whose heart and mouth are both true is a gentleman; one whose heart and mouth are both false is a petty man. The petty man everyone still knows enough to guard against; but it is the man whose words speak of Yao and Shun while his heart is that of Jie and Zhou, who swears by mountains and seas while a trap lies hidden in his breast, that is hardest of all to fathom. Such a hypocrite, true in neither mouth nor heart, will surely be disloyal in serving his ruler and unfilial in serving his parents; in making friends he will surely be faithless, and in dealing with his subordinates he will surely be unrighteous. Such a man is a petty man among petty men! And if others are led by mistake to trust his words and so fall into his schemes, then the guilt of such a crime will bring retribution in the yin world several times greater than the same offense committed in the world of the living! The Buddhist scriptures say: ‘One who speaks falsely and with an evil tongue will after death fall into the hells where the tongue is torn out, where molten copper is poured, and where the iron plow is driven; and after suffering torment for many long kalpas, he can be reborn again only as a beast, feeding ever upon thorns and brambles. If he is again reborn as a man, he will be born without a tongue, and his breath will always be foul and stinking; even if he speaks good words, others will not believe him. Such is the retribution that comes from the karma of a mouth that is not true to the heart!’ How can one dare not to abstain from it?

Xue Wenqing of the Ming dynasty said: ‘The Book of Changes says: in ordinary speech one must be sincere. People generally suppose that the words of everyday talk do not matter, and so they fall into the bad habit of speaking rashly and carelessly; they do not realize that to speak one false word is already a fault in one’s speech. So one who can be sincere in ordinary speech must be a man of very lofty moral cultivation!’

Sima Wengong of the Song dynasty (that is, Sima Guang), speaking of how Liu Qi (Liu the Attendant) was able to achieve the cultivation of ‘exhausting his heart and governing his conduct,’ said: ‘His secret lay simply in having attained to sincerity — nothing more! And to accomplish the work of sincerity, one must begin by never speaking falsely.’ Sima Wengong also said: ‘Liu Qi’s whole life was simply the one word sincerity; he was able to bring the word sincerity to a point where it could not be overthrown!’ And the townsfolk and old farmers of the time said: ‘To pass through Nanjing and not see Liu the Attendant is as great a regret as to pass through Sizhou (Qufu in Shandong) and not see the Great Sage Confucius!’ Why were they able to move men’s hearts so? The answer is likewise simply sincerity!
Seeing this fact, we should know how the word sincerity could ever mislead anyone — and why then do people refuse to strive with all their might at the word sincerity?

Ren Guozuo once fell ill and for a long time did not recover, so he engaged Daoist priests to set up an altar of offering and pray to Heaven for safety and health. That night, as he slept, he dreamed that a spirit said to him: ‘Ren Guozuo, all your life you have been one thing in mouth and another in heart; from childhood to manhood you have not done a single good deed. The King of the Underworld has already fixed the record of the sins you have accumulated in this life, and the day of your death is at hand!’ And indeed, before long, Ren Guozuo died.

Know that among the five elements earth has no fixed position, and yet the five elements (metal, wood, water, fire, and earth) take earth as their master; the four seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter likewise depend upon it to run their course, and the myriad things must rely upon earth in order to grow. And when we come to the five constant virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and good faith, it is good faith that is the master. If the four beginnings of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom lose good faith as their root, they cannot be brought to completion as benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom either! Therefore the Doctrine of the Mean says: ‘Sincerity is the beginning and the end, the root and the branch, of all things; without sincerity there is nothing but emptiness and unreality.’ When people today speak, they have no sincere heart toward the other — how then can they accomplish themselves as human beings? If one can from this point reform and awaken, making word and deed accord and the within and the without correspond, then whatever comes one may face it with composure and constantly keep a margin in hand, so that looking up one is not ashamed before Heaven and looking down one is not ashamed before men. Would this not be a great joy? And yet this is the fault to which we are most prone! And when we guard against it and examine ourselves, we find it very hard to accomplish; therefore one must not relax in the slightest, so as to cut oneself off from light and uprightness and walk into a dark and perilous realm thick with thorns!
Greedily coveting wealth and deceiving one’s superiors.

To be disloyal and unfilial toward others, and to dare to deceive one’s sovereign, one’s parents, and one’s superiors — even if by this one gains wealth and rank for a time, in most cases before long one meets with ruin, and one’s sons and grandsons are left in wretched straits! Far better to be loyal and honest and to keep one’s integrity; then one may naturally preserve one’s person, one’s household, and one’s good name! As for the many abuses by which officials embezzle the government’s money and grain, and servants conceal their master’s taxes and rents, they are too numerous to count; all of them amount to taking one’s superior’s wealth from below, and in the end are nothing but a foolish waste of scheming. And yet the wealth so obtained was in fact one’s own by destiny to begin with; but because it came by an improper road, one ends by losing both the man and the wealth. Far better to take not a hair of such improperly gained wealth; then the wealth and emolument that are one’s own by destiny will certainly come to one by proper means from other quarters. From my own standpoint the money is the same money either way; but whether it is taken safely or taken perilously makes a world of difference in the outcome! This is a true principle, and people ought to understand it!

In the Chenghua reign of the Ming dynasty, Qin Hong was appointed by imperial order as grand coordinator of Shaanxi. The guardsmen and officers of the Qin Princely Establishment in Shaanxi had long run riot among the people, and the common folk suffered bitterly, daring to be angry but not to speak. After Qin Hong took up his post, he arrested and brought to justice every guardsman and officer of the Qin Princely Establishment who had broken the law, disordered the discipline, and oppressed the people, sparing not one. The Prince of Qin then memorialized the emperor, saying: ‘Qin Hong is so audacious that he dares to bully and trample upon the imperial kin!’ The emperor was exceedingly angry and issued an edict for Qin Hong’s arrest, imprisoning him in the prison of the Embroidered-Uniform Guard; and he commanded his trusted eunuch Shang Heng to confiscate Qin Hong’s property, but only a single bolt of yellow silk and a few old garments were found. Shang Heng reported to the emperor the poverty of Qin Hong’s household; and the emperor thereupon inspected Qin Hong’s property with his own eyes, and sighed again and again in praise of his integrity. He at once issued an edict releasing Qin Hong and bestowed upon him ten thousand ingots of silver in commendation of his integrity, and transferred him to be grand coordinator of Henan. After Qin Hong had taken up that post, the eunuch Wang Zhi came to Henan on business; at that time Wang Zhi’s power and prestige were at their zenith, and the other grand coordinators all lowered themselves and went humbly to pay their respects to Wang Zhi; only Qin Hong refused to bow and would not go to pay his respects. Wang Zhi, knowing that Qin Hong was loyal, upright, and honest in office, respected him all the more. Qin Hong then secretly memorialized the emperor, saying: ‘Wang Zhi, in going out from the palace to handle affairs in the provinces, violated the regulations and brought with him an excessive number of guardsmen and officers, harassing the locality.’ Later, after Wang Zhi had returned to the capital, the emperor asked him: ‘Are the grand coordinators of the various provinces worthy men or not?’ Wang Zhi praised Qin Hong alone as both honest and capable; whereupon the emperor showed him Qin Hong’s secret memorial, and Wang Zhi at once knocked his head on the ground before the emperor and confessed his fault, praising Qin Hong’s worth without cease. The emperor therefore pardoned Wang Zhi; and in the end Qin Hong rose to the office of minister.

In Shaoxing prefecture there was a provincial administrator who was much given to embezzlement and had amassed a family fortune of several hundred thousand. Later, after losing office, he returned to his native place and bought a hundred thousand mu of fine farmland, so that he was reckoned the richest man in the commandery. He often dreamed that his grandfather told him: ‘You are about to receive retribution!’ The administrator did not believe what his grandfather said in the dream. He had but one son and one grandson, and sure enough these thought of nothing all day but whoring and gambling, and both died young. Not long after the son and grandson died, the administrator was struck down by apoplexy and paralyzed; and his son’s wife and grandson’s wife both failed in the virtue of their sex, so that it was known far and near. Many men, seeing that they had money, sought to take advantage of them, and the administrator saw it with his own eyes but was powerless to do anything. By the time he was near death, all the property of his household had been squandered. As he lay dying, the administrator opened his eyes wide and cried aloud: ‘My office as provincial administrator was not small, and a hundred thousand mu of fields is not a little; I acquired it all with my own hands, and I have lost it all from my own hands — I cannot understand what principle this is!’ Having spoken, he died.

Alas! This was only the flowering retribution in this present life; the administrator’s karmic retribution lies in the hells! Who knows what further suffering he must endure! Yang Boqi put it well: ‘Though I leave my descendants no abundant property, yet if I can make later generations praise my descendants as the descendants of an honest official — is not the property I leave my descendants in this way the greater?’
Fabricating evil words to slander the innocent.

Even when another has indeed committed a fault, one ought to find some way to shield him; how much more so when a man is wholly innocent, and one fabricates rumors and invents wicked deeds in order to slander him! Such malice is fiercer than sword or axe, than tiger or wolf! For a man who has done no wrong is attacked by the slanderous words of a petty man, and others who cannot see the truth of the matter follow along in defaming him; and those who hear the slander find it truly hard to tell who is right and who is wrong. Thus the worthy and the petty are confounded together, and demotions and promotions of office are turned upside down by it — this is what the gentleman hates and detests with all his heart! The Buddha said: ‘The karma of an evil tongue will bring one after death into the hells of swords and weapons and of the torn-out tongue; and while alive, one easily suffers murder or the retribution of a maimed and crippled body.’

An old poem says: ‘Be careful never to give ear / To slander — hearing brings disaster near. / The ruler hears: his minister dies. / The father hears: against his son he cries. / Husband and wife who hear it separate; / Brothers who hear it grow estranged in hate. / Friends who hear it drift apart; / Flesh and blood who hear it break the heart. / A man of stately seven-foot frame, / Let not a three-inch tongue put him to shame! / Upon that tongue a Longquan blade is worn, / That kills a man and leaves no blood to mourn.’ Such is the harm wrought by slander; can one who hears slanderous words fail to be careful in discerning them?

Mr. Chen Liangmo of the Ming dynasty said: ‘Formerly, when I was on official business inspecting Gong’an County, there was an instructor named Bai who had gone to the capital to sit the metropolitan examination. His wife loved to do good; she had written his name on a petition, and had also given a tael of silver to a Daoist nun as alms; and with a fathom of hemp thread she had embroidered the petition upon a banner. It happened that the wife of one of Instructor Bai’s colleagues came to visit, and when she saw the banner and the petition she was greatly alarmed, and said: “For a Confucian official who teaches to have dealings with a Daoist nun — I fear it will damage his official career considerably!” When Instructor Bai’s wife heard this, she believed it to be true and thought that her husband’s career was finished from that moment, and her heart was heavy with gloom. When Instructor Bai returned after failing the metropolitan examination, he took this piece of hemp cloth to make clothing and also cut up the banner; and his wife was all the more grieved, and so hanged herself. I happened to hear of the matter and went to ask the county magistrate, who told me all the details; and I pitied Instructor Bai for what had befallen him, and grieved all the more for his wife. Later, when the provincial governor Lin Ershan was deliberating over the register of the worthiness or unworthiness of Confucian officials, he said to me: “It was because Instructor Bai had improper relations with a colleague’s wife, so that his wife was greatly displeased and often spoke to him in dissatisfaction, that Instructor Bai in a rage forced his wife to hang herself; a crime like this is simply intolerable to Heaven and Earth!” Thereupon I told the governor all that I knew about Instructor Bai. When Mr. Lin heard it he was filled with doubt, and as he sat pondering and hesitating, undecided, I said to him further: “I wonder from whom you heard the matter of Instructor Bai? If that person is a true gentleman, then what he says may perhaps be believed; but if he is not a true gentleman, then I beg you to inquire into it more carefully.” At this Mr. Lin was suddenly enlightened, and striking the table he said: “You are right! You are right!” and at once took up his brush and crossed out what he had just written about Instructor Bai. Later Instructor Bai was promoted to be an assistant instructor in the Directorate of Education, and I was transferred to Fujian as surveillance commissioner, in charge of judicial affairs there. In Putian I met Mr. Lin, and he pointed to the neighboring house and said to me: “The head of this household is surnamed Wu; he once served as assistant instructor of Gong’an County, and it was he who slandered Instructor Bai. He was always a man of crooked heart, and it was because I heard your words that I suddenly awoke. Later Instructor Wu was promoted to be instructor of Pingxiang in Jiangxi, and was likewise slandered by his colleagues there and dismissed from office; and as he was returning to his native place and passing over Lake Poyang, his boat capsized and he nearly drowned in the lake, and today he is utterly down and out!”’

The proverb says: ‘Those who love to talk of the affairs of the women’s quarters and of the various shortcomings of others are sure to anger the ghosts and spirits; if they do not meet with some strange calamity, they will certainly be reduced to utter poverty!’ How much more so when what Instructor Wu slandered and defiled was an innocent man? Then his retribution ought to have been more than this! Yet the way to judge what another tells one lies chiefly in observing what sort of man the speaker is; then one will not be misled by him!
Slandering others while claiming to be upright.

In taking his stand in the world and conducting himself, a gentleman and scholar must make himself upright, without a trace of the crooked or perverse; only then can he be called upright! As for one who has not himself attained uprightness, yet slanders others and calls himself upright — his conscience has long since been lost! How can he be called upright? Moreover, the man who is truly upright is sure to be loyal and generous at heart, and will speak only when speech is proper, so that others may know their faults and reform. But those who slander others blacken another’s name and give vent to their own anger, and then think themselves upright besides — are such men not both pitiable and hateful? Laozi said: ‘One whose cleverness is supreme and whose insight is profound, yet who is without human feeling, is simply driving himself into a blind alley’ — this refers precisely to those who delight in mocking and discussing others! Master Cheng Yichuan said: ‘Toward others, a gentleman should seek the faultless within the faulty, and should not seek a fault within the faultless; toward himself, it is just the opposite.’ Alas! The people of the world create endless karma of the mouth; this is why the Supreme Old Lord warned against it so sternly again and again!

In the reign of Emperor Jingdi of the Ming dynasty, the vice minister Wang Wei had been promoted through the recommendation of the junior guardian Yu Qian; yet Wang Wei, seizing the occasion of a fault Yu Qian had once committed, sent a secret memorial to the emperor slandering Yu Qian, hoping thereby to display his own uprightness. At that time Yu Qian enjoyed the deep trust of Emperor Jingdi, and the emperor summoned Yu Qian and handed him Wang Wei’s secret memorial. Yu Qian knocked his head on the ground and admitted his fault; and the emperor said: ‘I know well what manner of man you are; you need not feel any regret on this account!’ After Yu Qian had had his audience and came out, Wang Wei went up to meet him and asked: ‘What did His Majesty say to you?’ Yu Qian said nothing; and when Wang Wei asked again, Yu Qian laughed and said: ‘If this old fellow has done anything amiss, just tell me to my face — it is not certain that I would refuse to listen! Why must you be so hardhearted as to send the emperor a secret memorial exposing my faults?’ And with that he brought out the memorial and showed it to Wang Wei. Wang Wei was so terrified and ashamed that he wished the ground would open and swallow him; and Yu Qian, far from reproaching him, only laughed and comforted him!

Yang Tieya of the Yuan dynasty enjoyed a fame that bore weight throughout the land. At Linjiang there was a shrine commemorating the Lady Wang, who had preserved her chastity, and Yang Tieya inscribed a poem upon it, saying: ‘With armored horsemen laden, laden, a hundred li of road; / The green maples, in the dead of night, were written red with blood. / It should be that the peach-blossom waters of Liu and Ruan / Are not so clear as the Han River at Baling.’ Afterwards Yang Tieya never had a son. One day he dreamed that a woman said to him: ‘Though the poem you wrote on the Lady Wang cannot harm the lady’s good name, yet your heart was hard and cutting, and Heaven will punish you with the cutting off of your posterity!’ Yang Tieya felt deep remorse and composed another poem, saying: ‘Heaven grows old with the earth; thy handmaid goes with the soldiers; / Heaven and earth are without feeling, but thy handmaid has a heart. / Biting open her finger, the blood reddens the rosy peaks; / The traces of moss turn to the green of the snow-cold river. / She would die to the sound of the Xiang’s zither; / She will not live to the beat of the nomad’s reed. / In the third month the cuckoo cries out its blood; / In the autumn wind, tearless, she writes her mournful epitaph.’ Later he dreamed again that the woman said to him: ‘Since you have repented and reformed, you ought to have a son!’ And indeed Madam Yang bore a son; and from that time on Yang Tieya earnestly cultivated the Way, and attained the fruit of an immortal.
Cursing the spirits while claiming to be righteous.
