The ancient worthies said: ‘The wise and the upright are what we call gods.’ Toward the gods and spirits a gentleman always keeps a heart of reverence and awe; but the petty man dares to be utterly unbridled, supposing himself upright and without guile and able to make the ghosts and spirits submit to him — never knowing that his every stirring thought, his selfish heart, and his crafty schemes have long since been seen through by the ghosts and spirits, and that he is merely drawing guilt upon himself in vain.

In Zhenjiang there was a pastry-shop owner surnamed Yu whose youngest son died young of smallpox. Yu actually wrote out a plaint intending to accuse the Smallpox God before the City God; but his wife snatched the plaint away and burned it under the stove. That night Yu dreamed that he was dragged by ghost attendants to the yin offices. The City God said to him: ‘The hearth god of your household has reported to me that you have written a plaint to accuse the Smallpox God — what crime, after all, has the Smallpox God committed?’ Yu said: ‘The Smallpox God demanded sacrifices of me, and when I did not consent, the Smallpox God therefore destroyed my child!’ Before long the Smallpox God came into the hall and reported to the City God: ‘His son’s fate was to die young; it has nothing to do with this petty deity.’ The City God then gave judgment, saying: ‘In consideration of this petty commoner’s ignorance, let him be handed over to Magistrate Yang for punishment: twenty strokes of the staff and a month’s illness, as a warning!’ At that time Yang Shuting was magistrate of Dantu County. The next day, as Yu was hanging up the door panel at the entrance of his house, Magistrate Yang happened to be passing by and accidentally broke the great umbrella borne by his attendants; and for this Yu was punished by Magistrate Yang with twenty strokes of the staff. After the beating, Yu lay on a sickbed for a month until his injuries healed.
Know that the ghosts and spirits and the king’s law walk hand in hand; therefore one who offends the ghosts and spirits will often find himself transgressing the king’s law as well!
Abandoning the obedient and imitating the rebellious.

Mr. Shi Que of Wei in the Zhou dynasty said: ‘That the ruler be righteous and the minister loyal, the father kind and the son filial, the elder brother loving and the younger respectful — these are what are called the six obediences. That the base should encroach upon the noble, the young insult their elders, the distant estrange the close, the new come between the old, the small be added to the great, and wantonness destroy righteousness — these are what are called the six rebelliousnesses. If a man abandons the six obediences and instead learns to practice the six rebelliousnesses, he is himself hastening calamity upon himself!’ The Book of History says: ‘Following the Way brings good fortune; following the contrary brings misfortune’ — meaning that one who accords with this Way obtains auspiciousness, and one who defies it produces disaster. It also says: ‘Those who accord with Heaven flourish; those who defy Heaven perish.’ Now those who learn obedience will be wholly loyal and wholly filial, becoming sages and worthies; those who learn rebellion will be wild and violent, becoming rebels and bandits. The thought of abandoning obedience and imitating rebellion lasts but a single instant, yet the dividing of fortune from misfortune is as far apart as heaven from earth! How then can one fail to be careful?

Zhao Fengzi, a commoner of Wen’an County in Bazhou, was by nature strong and brave. He gathered robbers together with Liu Liu, Liu Qi, and others, and plundered wherever they went; and they also mustered their followers in separate columns to attack and ravage Henan. When he had fought his way into Biyang, he dug up all the graves of the ancestors of Jiao Fang, and said: ‘If I could kill that old villain Jiao Fang with my own hand, then I could answer for it before the world!’ Before long Zhao Fengzi’s followers were defeated by the government troops, and he turned toward Liu’an to plunder and seize; the government troops pursued him again, and Zhao Fengzi, at his wits’ end, snatched the ordination certificate of a monk, shaved his head, and disguised himself as a monk; but he was caught by the subordinate general Zhao Cheng, who hacked him to pieces inch by inch. And when Liu Liu and Liu Qi fled to Wolf Mountain in Tongzhou, a hurricane suddenly came upon them, and all the bandits they led were wiped out.

Know that there are two kinds of rebellion: the one is when a minister or a son betrays and defies his ruler or his father; the other is when robbers and bandits run amok and bring trouble to the villages. The rebellion of ministers and sons — disloyalty and unfiliality — has already been explained in detail above, and so here the discussion is devoted wholly to the rebels and bandits. The purpose is to make people understand how to rest content in their lot and follow principle, so as to preserve their own persons and households!
Turning from one’s kin toward strangers.

Turning from one’s kin toward strangers is not confined to a single kind of act. For example, to deceive and conceal matters from one’s parents while secretly entrusting them to one’s wife’s family; to treat one’s own parents in a commonplace way while lavishing affection upon one’s wife’s relatives; to haggle over every trifle with one’s own brothers while being especially generous to friends and outsiders; to disregard the poverty of one’s own clansmen while falsely claiming others as one’s kin — to keep at a distance those whom one ought to hold close, and to draw close those whom one ought to keep at a distance: all of these are turning from kin toward strangers! Confucius said: ‘To love others while not loving one’s own kin is called perversity of virtue; to respect others while not respecting one’s own kin is called perversity of propriety.’ When men today turn from kin toward strangers, it is either because they are swayed by private grudges and favors, or because they make distinctions according to the warmth or coldness of human feeling; and such perversity of virtue and propriety is exceedingly grave! Moreover it is a capital offense at the root, and its retribution is certain to be bitter!

Zhou Cong, having sat the examinations many times without success, went to Qiao Commandery and acknowledged the commandery clerk Zhou Ji as his father. Day and night he kept company with Zhou Ji’s children, and for the names of his three generations of ancestors he used those of Zhou Ji throughout. The next year, by this means, Zhou Cong passed the provincial examination, and from then on he never went back to his old home again. His own father wrote a poem reproaching him, and Zhou Cong died of shame.

Bai Xi of the Ming dynasty, having no son of his own, adopted the son of a butcher instead of letting his own nephew inherit the family estate. After Bai Xi died, a certain guest was lodging overnight in his house when he heard the sound of people running about; he rose and looked through a crack in the door, and saw men and women of many generations of the family pacing and peering about, as though they had gone long without food. Then he saw a man with a butcher’s knife thrust in his belt come staggering in; and before long this man went out again, belly thrust forward as though he had eaten his fill. And all those men and women of several generations stamped their feet and said: ‘It is over! We have no food to eat again — alas, how bitter it is!’ Having spoken, each with a mournful look went out of the house. When day broke the next morning, the guest asked a servant: ‘What was going on in the house last night?’ The servant answered: ‘Last night our master was sacrificing to the ancestors.’ The guest therefore understood that the one with the butcher’s knife was the master’s own father, and that the men and women of several generations were the ancestors of the Bai family and Bai Xi and his wife! The guest gave a sigh and left the Bai household.
Pointing to heaven and earth to attest one’s base intentions, invoking the gods and spirits to witness one’s wicked deeds.

Heaven and Earth are without selfishness and the gods and spirits are upright; all the responses of good fortune to compliance and misfortune to defiance are like an echo answering a sound. Even one who is careful and reverent may still fear to incur guilt — how much more so when a man dares to point to Heaven and Earth and invoke the gods and spirits to attest and witness his base intentions and his wicked deeds! This is nothing less than blasphemy against Heaven and Earth and the gods and spirits! And how could Heaven and Earth and the gods and spirits ever help a man to do evil? In acting thus such a man is only hastening calamity upon himself in vain!

The household of Zhang Zhong was utterly without harmony: between father and son, brothers, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, and the wives of brothers, the slightest dispute or clash would bring cries to heaven and appeals to the gods, each seeking to prove his own innocence. When the day came to divide the family property, the contention grew even fiercer, and they sacrificed to the gods and cursed one another. From that time on, Zhang Zhong’s household was constantly plagued by goblins and demons, and the family was constantly ill; within a few years nearly all of Zhang Zhong’s household had died.

The eminent Ming monk Master Lianchi said: ‘When worldly people make vows — praying, for instance, for a son, for long life, for deliverance from danger, for official rank, or for wealth and emolument — they may not, in praying to the gods and spirits, vow to slaughter animals and offer them in sacrifice to the gods. A vow of that kind is called an evil vow: it has guilt in it and no merit. As for vowing to give robes or banners, to build halls and shrines, or to provide vessels for offerings, such vows are fitting only when used to adorn the holy images and the place of practice. I would have all living beings gather in their thoughts, give rise to reverence and awe, and not harbor the least intent of deliberately seeking blessings for themselves; for great compassion and impartiality is what is called Buddha, and uprightness without partiality is what is called god. If a man seeks blessings for himself out of mere selfishness, how could Heaven and Earth and the gods and spirits ever send down auspiciousness and bestow blessing because a man has bribed them? By principle, the only way is to exhaust one’s own heart and broadly to practice all good — to be loyal and filial, friendly and brotherly, to pity the poor and cherish the aged, to relieve calamity and succor the distressed, to abstain from killing and to release living creatures, to perform every kind of hidden good deed, and to practice every kind of skillful means — doing all this to the utmost according to one’s own station and capacity. Then the merit of the good one has done will of itself move Heaven and Earth and the gods and spirits to send down blessings. But if one refuses to do good and merely gives rise to a presumptuous desire in making vows, then this is a base intention and a wicked deed, and a blasphemy against the gods and spirits! Here I make it known to all the world that they ought firmly to believe this truth.’
Regretting after giving.

Of all things, giving is the quickest way to establish merit; yet one must delight in goodness without wearying if one is to make progress. Even when one’s means are insufficient, one must always keep this mind; only so can one turn about the greed and stinginess in one’s own heart and keep one’s initial resolve from being lost. To regret before one has even given makes giving impossible; and to regret after giving means one will give no more. Such a mind steals benevolence and injures righteousness — this is the very root of the sickness of the heart! The reason the Supreme Old Lord does not single out the good deed of giving, but points instead to the sin of regretting after giving, is that what the sages most commend is reforming one’s faults and moving toward good, and what they most detest is a good deed not carried through to the end.

To regret after giving — if we trace it back to the first thought, one’s original mind was after all not a true delight in doing good, but only a passing impulse, a seeking after a good name, a hope of gaining blessing; so one was mistaken from the very start, and how could one fail to regret it? But if one gives with a true heart, having attained to the emptiness of both self and others — that is, within, not seeing the self that gives; without, not seeing the person who receives; and in between, not seeing the goods given — then there will certainly be no such thing as regret after giving. Therefore those who do good cannot but be attentive, earnestly observing the very thought with which they set about their good deeds!

Fu Ya took delight in goodness and loved to give; the gateway of his house was thronged with beggars. He often said to people: ‘The wealth of the world is not fixed! A man may be rich today and poor the day after tomorrow, like a turning ring! If I go a single day without giving, then for a single day I am not happy!’ The people of his time praised Fu Ya, saying: ‘Better not to be rich like Quan Xing — better to be poor like Fu Ya.’ (Quan Xing was a rich man of the day who was stingy about giving alms.) Later Fu Ya rose to the office of director of the imperial secretariat, and his sons and grandsons were even wealthier.

Xi Baisan was extremely poor. By chance he saw a Daoist begging for alms before the gate of a shop, and the shopkeeper would not give. Xi Baisan felt in the purse at his waist and found only a single coin left, and he gave it to the Daoist. That night Xi Baisan dreamed of the Daoist, who removed the growth from his cheek for him; and when he woke, he found that the fleshy wen on his face had indeed fallen away.

Xi Baisan’s single coin of alms delivered him from the suffering of his illness; from this one may see that giving does not depend on the amount of one’s wealth, but on whether the heart that gives is true! The people of the world ought to strive with all their hearts to practice giving and do good, and to urge others to join them — and even then they would be late; how much less should one regret after giving!
Borrowing and not returning.

Borrowing is a good thing: it makes up for what one lacks from what another has, and relieves another in his straits. The one who lends has already done one no small kindness — how can one rely on force or power and try to cheat him out of repayment? Know the principle that an old debt not settled in this life must still be repaid after death: for the lighter cases one must become his slave or maidservant; and for the graver, one must become an ass, horse, ox, or dog in his household, to repay the debt one owes.

Whatever one borrows from others must be taken care of. Unless it is absolutely unavoidable, one should not borrow from others; and having borrowed a thing, one should return it at once when one has done with it. In this way others will not be vexed, and one will have no shame in one’s own heart. As for borrowing money from others, one must repay it with even greater clarity; yet people today often borrow money and never repay it. They never consider that the money is not theirs: even if they keep it for themselves, in the end the money will vanish all the same, leaving them with nothing but a mounting debt — what good, after all, does that do them? Let everyone think it over carefully!

In the autumn of the wuwu year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, a resident of Beijing named Zhang Yuan kept a donkey that could travel two hundred li in a day; but this donkey loved to kick with its hooves and would bite as well. Only when Zhang Yuan and his two sons rode it was the donkey perfectly docile; but as for anyone else, there was no way for any man to ride the beast. Yet once, a certain man surnamed Yang ventured to borrow the donkey for a ride; and strange to tell, the donkey let Yang mount and ride it with perfect docility. After he had ridden it back, that night Yang dreamed that a man in black told him: ‘I am the donkey in Zhang Yuan’s household. In a former life I borrowed three hundred cash from you and did not repay it, and in this life I ought to make it up to you. Yesterday you rode me two hundred and eighty li; I beg you to ride me another twenty li, and then the debt I owe you will be fully repaid!’ Yang asked: ‘Then how much do you owe the Zhang family?’ The man in black, his face covered with gloom, said: ‘Much, much, much — it cannot be told.’ When Yang woke, he indeed went again to Zhang Yuan’s house to borrow the donkey for a ride; and when they had gone a little farther, the donkey suddenly leaped up and threw Yang to the ground. Yang calculated the distance traveled and found it was exactly twenty li, and he marveled at the donkey all the more; so he said to it most earnestly: ‘I understand now why you will not let me ride you any farther! But my home is still ten li away, and if I do not ride you, how am I to get back? Let it be thus: after I ride you home, I will buy ten cash worth of fodder and give it to you to eat, all right?’ The donkey stood there looking at Yang for a long while before it would let him ride it home in docility. Afterwards, whenever Yang purposely tried to ride it again, as soon as he came near the saddle on its back, the donkey would kick him with its hooves, bite him with its mouth, and bray without cease!

Mr. Zhu Zaian said: ‘Some men fall into debt because they are poor, others because though rich they borrow. To be poor and in debt is due to insufficient means to repay; but if, as the Scripture of the Middle Admonition says, one constantly and earnestly wishes to repay the debt, then naturally there is no fault. As for being rich and yet unwilling to repay, such a man either trades upon his own power and position, or else has darkened the principles of Heaven and lost his conscience! Know that a debt unpaid must be repaid life after life, and only when the debt is settled is the matter finished!’

In Anhui there was a merchant surnamed Wu who in all his dealings had always held to good faith and righteousness. When he was near death he told his two sons: ‘All the thousand taels of gold I possess were borrowed from Mr. Fu. You must repay every one of them for me; rather endure hunger and cold than be a man who betrays another’s trust!’ When the sons heard this, they obeyed their father’s dying command and repaid the debt, and the two brothers lived on in poverty and want. One day they suddenly found in a dry well in their courtyard two thousand taels of silver, bearing an inscription of a Tang dynasty reign title; they shut their gates tight and secretly hid the silver, and no one knew of the matter. The next day a man who lived in a neighboring county suddenly came to their house and said: ‘Are you not the sons of Wu?’ The brothers answered: ‘We are.’ The man then said: ‘Great wealth has come to you! A few days ago, being ill, I went in a dream to the mansion of Mount Tai, and there in the Treasury Office of the Mount Tai mansion I saw a man escorting money arrive, who called himself the god of wells and springs; and the Great Emperor of Mount Tai said: “This is silver from the inner treasury of the Tang palace. Because Wu handled wealth and goods with scrupulous integrity, and his sons have bitterly held to their father’s purpose, God bestows this silver upon Wu’s sons. The descendants of the Wu family, generation after generation, shall enjoy great wealth.” When I woke I felt this very strange, and so I came specially to your house to tell you of it.’ When the two brothers heard this they were greatly astonished, and they told him truthfully of the two thousand taels of silver found in the dry well. Today there are many wealthy people of the Wu surname, and all of them are their descendants!
Not resting in one's proper lot, but pushing and scheming to obtain beyond it.

The reason men are unwilling to rest in their proper lot, and think only that by pushing and scheming they will gain some benefit, is that they have never reflected that the poverty or wealth, the honor or lowliness of a lifetime are all fixed by fate — how can one scheme after what lies beyond one's portion? And as for the deluded mind that covets and hopes for advantage by chance, not only does it bring no benefit at all, but I fear it may even shave away one's blessings! Why not earnestly ponder the meaning of Mencius's words, 'To seek it there is a Way; to attain it there is a decree,' and of the Sixth Patriarch Master Huineng's saying, 'Every field of blessing does not leave the square inch of this mind'?

In the early Changqing era of the Tang dynasty, after the death of Pei Pu, the official in charge of the prison administration of Xinping county, his cousin Hua Yuan — who was then on a sojourn in Longyou — met on the road a military officer followed by a great retinue. Looking at him more closely, he found the officer was none other than Pei Pu himself! Startled and overjoyed, Hua Yuan said, 'Were you not already deceased? How is it that you now hold a military post?' Pei Pu replied, 'My present office is that of the Brush-Stripper of Western Sichuan, and I am in charge of the waxing and waning, the increase and decrease, of wealth in the world. You must know that every drink and every morsel of a person in this life is fixed by fate, much less his money! All of it is recorded in the yin offices. Therefore the wealth a man obtains all has its definite limit; if it exceeds that limit, it will be brushed and stripped away — either consumed and wasted by himself, or lost to a sudden calamity, or lost in business and investment, or scattered by illness — all of which is governed by me, this Brush-Stripper. The farmer who diligently plows and sows to gain food, the merchant who diligently manages to gain profit, the scholar who studies hard to gain office — all merely obtain the wealth that lies within their own portion; they add not a whit of wealth that was not within their portion. If one is not diligent, then even what lies within one's portion will be lost! That you have met me is also predetermined; you ought to receive two catties of white silver. If I gave you more than two catties, the excess would still be brushed and stripped away, and so I dare not give you more.' Having spoken, Pei Pu disappeared.

Liu Hang wrote quite well, and thought he might gain fame and office at an early age. At the time, the Perfected Lord Xusheng was delivering oracles at Mount Zhongnan, and Liu Hang thereupon asked the Lord about the matter of his own advancement. The Perfected Lord said, 'Your writing is fine, but your fate is too thin. If you can keep to your portion and withdraw without scheming, you may yet live out your remaining years; but if you scheme excessively, you will surely cut short your life!' Liu Hang would not heed the Lord's counsel, and in the end, unable to pass the examinations and scheming excessively, he died.

You must understand that the matter of gaining fame and office — this thing that can glorify one's ancestors and bless one's descendants — how can it be obtained by cunning and contrivance? Only by earnestly accumulating hidden merit can one gain fame and office in the unseen realm; and that is not overreaching scheming! The same principle holds for wealth.

After Zhang Yue retired, he returned to his native place and from then on shut his gate and would not go out. Moreover, he concerned himself no further with either public or private affairs. He practiced thrift and frugality with his whole body, to be a model for his descendants. He once quoted what Mr. Jie Ping of the screen had said: 'When a guest calls and one invites him to eat, though the fare be simple it should still be in accord with human feeling; set out the dishes according to what the household already has, and bring out the fruit afterward. Even for a newly formed kinship, one need not entertain with lavish dishes; even for an honored guest, one need not slaughter a beast or fowl. In this way one not only remedies the fault of extravagance, but also makes one's blessings the more enduring and frees oneself from worry, settling body and mind.'

Mr. Zhang Gongchen said, 'Being content in poverty and keeping to one's portion, being frugal in expenditure, one can spare oneself the need to ask favors of others; one can also save trouble and keep the mind pure. As for scheming beyond one's portion, it only brings hardship upon oneself; for the blessings a person enjoys in life have already been arranged by Heaven, and wealth and poverty, success and failure, are likewise fixed by fate. Even if a man can obtain something by using his wits, it is only because his fortune has come and he ought to receive it. If one can see through and understand this principle, the heart will feel entirely at ease. But if one waits until one is fully satisfied, who could ever reach that point? How much better to accept whatever comes, and be at ease with fate!'
To use one's strength to the utmost, and to exhaust one's will in wielding power and laying plans.

To wield power and lay plans to the full, without leaving oneself the slightest bit of room — and not to stop until one's power is utterly spent. This is what the proverb means by 'Having hoisted a full sail, one adds eight more oars.'

For example, a man in office uses his position to wield power and lay plans to the full against the common people; the wealthy use their influence to wield power and lay plans to the full against the poor and lowly. These are of course all violations of the Most High's prohibitions. As for using the strength of human beings to wield power and lay plans over animals — this too is impermissible. For example, the oxen and donkeys that plow the fields, the horses and mules one rides — if they are not what I cultivated in a former life to obtain, then they are creatures who owe me a debt. I ought to care for them and have compassion upon them. In using them, not only should I not exhaust their strength, but how can I say, 'Animals are of another kind, so I may do as I please with them'?

In the Liu-Song era, Xi Xiandu held the post of Cavalier Attendant in the Imperial Office. Emperor Xiaowu once ordered him to oversee and direct the corvee laborers, and he was cruel, harsh, and unreasonable toward them, beating and flogging the workers at the slightest excuse. Whether the weather was bitterly cold or scorchingly hot, in rain or snow, he would not allow the workers a moment of rest. Many of the laborers, unable to bear the suffering, took their own lives; and when Xi Xiandu's crimes came to light, he too was executed by order of the court.

When the Hanlin scholar Qian Hetan of Huating built a residence in the countryside, the laborers were all vexed and in pain, and the villagers were worn down into illness. One worker was unwilling to bear the labor any longer, and Qian the scholar angrily reproached him. The worker said, 'In the past, when the Judicial Commissioner Huang built his mansion, I took on this corvee labor and fell ill from exhaustion. Today Huang's house has already collapsed, the walls fallen down, and yet my illness has still not recovered. So I cannot take on this labor.' Before the scholar heard the worker's words, he had already awakened, and at once stopped the work.
For a husband and wife to engage in conjugal relations too frequently, exceeding the proper limit.

The crime of adulterous lust has already been explained clearly by the Most High earlier. As for conjugal relations between husband and wife, these in particular must be moderated. If one says that conjugal relations are not lust, then how can one escape the calamity of indulging the passions and destroying one's own life? For the seminal essence of the human body is scattered throughout the three burners and courses through a hundred vessels; and when the fire of desire stirs, it gathers and flows together, all issuing forth from the gate of life. So if conjugal relations are not restrained, even waters as vast as the ocean will run dry — how very fearful this is! Whenever a person's essence is full, then spirit is born; when spirit is full, then thought and wisdom are born; and the person becomes bright and strong, and whatever he undertakes succeeds. But if in youth one injures and wastes the primordial essence until all the brilliance of one's vital spirit is gone, then the enterprise of a lifetime is finished!

The lifelong illnesses of a person all begin at the time of the new marriage; for being young and ignorant, one often indulges the passions without restraint, and in consequence most fall into consumption, or become gaunt and weak, and some even die young. This drags one's wife into widowhood, to bear alone the misery of an empty chamber — never thinking that the wife with whom one will share a hundred years of happiness should accompany one's whole life. Why, in the very first month of the marriage, lay the root of a lifetime of illness and early death? Therefore, fathers and elder brothers, when their sons and younger brothers are about to marry, ought earnestly to instruct them and caution them against this.

The proverb says, 'When joy reaches its extreme, sorrow is born; when the passions are indulged, disaster follows.' Again it is said, 'He who is sparing in desire surely has many sons; he who is greedy in lust often has no heir.' Confucius said, 'While the blood and qi are not yet settled, guard against lust.' Lao Peng said, 'The superior man uses a separate bed; the middling man a separate cover; a hundred pills of medicine are not as good as sleeping alone.' The Buddha said, 'Female beauty is the root of all suffering, the root of all obstruction, the root of all killing, the root of all sorrow.' The Yellow Court Scripture says, 'Earnestly guard the chamber of essence and do not let it leak; close it and guard it, and you may live long.' Truly it is because lust causes a man to lose his nature and to forfeit his life. Some are harmed in secret and do not themselves perceive it; some clearly know the harm of lust yet are unwilling to turn back. This is precisely why the ancient sages and worthies admonished so earnestly and warned again and again! But ordinary people, not knowing the profit and harm, indulge their passions without the least restraint, and so the foul and licentious vapor angers the ghosts and spirits, and all manner of inauspicious calamities are thereby summoned. I pray that everyone in the world will resolutely overcome himself in time and gain the benefit of long life and health; otherwise, to sacrifice body and life for the sake of lust — such a person is beyond saving!

In his old age, Ren Huigong appeared still more hale and strong. Someone asked him the art of preserving his health. Master Ren said, 'It is only because I read the Wenxuan and had some realization! The Wenxuan says: If a stone stores beautiful jade, it makes the mountain more radiant; if water contains a precious pearl, it makes the stream more alluring — that is the principle.' Master Cheng Yichuan held that for a man to indulge his passions without regard for his bodily health was a thing most shameful; and so when he reached seventy, his spirit and strength were about the same as in his prime. When Mr. Li Juenian was a hundred, the color of his face was like that of an infant. Someone asked him his secret, and he said, 'I only gave up lust early!' By the time Mr. Liu Yuancheng was eighty, his body was still exceedingly hale; he said he had been sparing in desire for thirty years, so that his blood, qi, and spirit were as they had been before. The monk Zhou of Luling, over ninety, could still walk far distances with swift steps, and his hair and beard had not whitened; he said there was no other method than to moderate desire in one's prime. Zhang Cui of Taicang, over ninety, was still clear of ear and bright of eye and could still paint. When asked the reason, he said, 'All my life I have only had the mind of desire comparatively faint, and simply moderated the affairs of desire!' You must know that being old yet strong is the first happiness of a lifetime; and that the cause of such strength is nothing more than moderating lust and sparing desire — and it is by no means difficult for ordinary people to learn! Peng Zu said, 'To release twice in a month, twenty-four times in a year — this principle is the method of cautious moderation of desire.' Su Nu said, 'When a person reaches sixty, he ought to close and guard the chamber of essence and not let it leak — this is the method of upholding what is perilous and guarding against what is wrong.' But I hold that the people of the age of Peng Zu and Su Nu had thicker latent endowment, and so they could speak thus; but in this present age the customs are so thin and shallow that one cannot take the words of Peng Zu and Su Nu as an absolute standard — much less for those whose primordial qi is weak, who should doubly moderate and be extremely cautious!

In the Ming dynasty, in Quzhou there was a young man surnamed Xu, handsome, elegant, and of outstanding talent, and moreover quite renowned. Before he was twenty he passed the jinshi examination, and was selected by the court to serve as judicial assistant to Songjiang Prefecture. His relatives and friends all greatly envied him. Yet he was extremely lustful; he took over ten concubines, all lovely and beautiful, and spent each day in indulgent excess. He had been in office at Songjiang less than a month when he grew weak and died prematurely. All of his ten-odd beautiful concubines remarried others.

One named Yin Yusheng was exceedingly handsome, but given to lust. One night he dreamed that the city god reproached him, reckoned up the number of his transgressions of lust, and flogged him several tens of times. When Yin Yusheng woke, he found both his legs had turned black and blue, and the two legs then began to ulcerate and rot, and he died after being ill for over a month.

'Of all evils, lust is the chief; of all good deeds, filial piety is first.' This is said to be the iron, unchanging rule of Senluo Hall for all ages. From this one may know how strong is the ghosts' and spirits' love of filial piety and hatred of lust! The net of the law in the world of light has its loopholes, but it is hard to escape the punishment of the law of the yin offices. How can a man commit crimes that the ghosts and spirits detest? Therefore, from ancient times, those who have abandoned themselves to licentiousness and wallowed in the beauty of women have never failed to ruin their families and destroy their persons. As for the elderly, it is all the more improper to take a young concubine. For since I cannot govern her, she will resent me all the more deeply — and this accumulated rancor will damage virtue and deplete blessings! Moreover, the youthful disposition is hard to tame; and there are things even worse than this — how could one not take heed? Besides, when one is old, one is like the shadow of the sun at the mountaintop; one's own old life is in peril morning and evening, and yet one rushes to summon the ghost messenger to come sooner and escort one before King Yama — how foolish is that!
[Supplementary Note]

After a husband and wife have conjugal relations, or after a nocturnal emission, within three to five days one must not go into cold water, such as taking a cold bath; nor may one eat cold food, cool drinks, or cooling medicines. If one is ill and must take a cooling medicine, one should also state the reason plainly to the physician. In summer one must not crave the cool; in cold weather one must not brave wind and rain. If one violates these taboos and then engages in conjugal relations, the man is apt to contract impotence, and the woman is apt to contract wasting of the breasts, with the four limbs turning ice-cold, and death from abdominal pain. Moreover, if husband and wife do not carefully guard against these, observing the prohibitions, a pregnant woman will easily miscarry; so it often happens that conception occurs in the first half of the month, and then a miscarriage occurs in the latter half, and one does not know why. If a woman miscarries repeatedly, the liver meridian will be injuredive and she will be unable to conceive for life. The way to avoid it is that after a woman conceives, husband and wife must separate in bed or in rooms, and not engage in conjugal relations, so that there will be no miscarriage. If, after conception, one still engages in conjugal relations, even if one is fortunate enough to bear a son, he will surely be sickly and weak, hard to raise to adulthood; for he was already injured while in the mother's womb. So husband and wife cannot but be careful, lest they bring on future grief and pain. Again, some, in order to beget a son, put pills and powders into the womb, or take lewd quack aphrodisiacs. This heterodox magic not only fails to help one gain a son, but needlessly creates guilt — harming both virtue and body! The above principles should by rights be what parents must teach their sons and daughters-in-law; but most parents in the world find it inconvenient to speak plainly to them, and so I have set it out here for everyone; I only hope that everyone will cherish his own body, and also cherish the health of his children.

The Perfected Sun said: The human body is formed by the conjunction of blood and qi; it is not forged of gold, silver, copper, or iron. Therefore if one does not moderate the desire for sex, at first one does not feel the harm; but as day follows day and month follows month the injury accumulates, and inevitably the marrow and essence will be depleted, the blood and qi corrupted, and in the end death will follow. For the blood and qi of a person require six days to pass through the six meridians of the body; only after seven days are all the meridians opened (the sun, yang brightness, lesser yang, greater yin, lesser yin, and terminating yin, these six meridians), and, gaining release, does the blood and qi complete one full circuit. Therefore, with each act of conjugal relations, the blood and qi of one meridian are injured, and one must wait another seven days until the circuit reaches that meridian again before it can recover. Hence the Book of Changes says, 'In seven days cometh return' — this is to make men rest for seven days. But many people, before seven days have passed, engage in conjugal relations again, inflicting injury upon injury, and so a hundred diseases arise. For this reason, a limit is here laid down as the foundation for moderating desire and preserving the body. At twenty, the standard is once every seven days. At thirty, once every fourteen days. At forty, once every twenty-eight days. At fifty, once every forty-five days. By sixty, the marrow and essence and blood are no longer produced; at this point one should early cut off lust and forbid conjugal relations, and may no longer engage in them. The above limits refer only to spring and autumn. As for winter and summer, since summer's fire-qi is extremely hot, and the discharge is without reserve, and winter's water-qi is extremely cold, and the closure is extremely tight, both in winter and summer it is best to make cutting off desire the chief concern. If one can comply with the above limits, one can banish illness and extend life. If one violates them without moderation, then one will surely be diseased and have life shortened.

As for the taboos for preserving body and establishing life between husband and wife, together with the taboos of Heaven, the taboos of Earth, and the taboos of man — they are enumerated in detail in the book 'Precious Mirror of Longevity and Health.' If one does not refrain and does not know the taboos, then the sons born will not be raised, the body will be hard to perfect, and misfortune will surely come. Moreover, the circulation of the blood and qi of the human body is originally in correspondence with the seasonal nodes of heaven and earth; if one emits in inappropriate times, it easily makes the blood and qi discordant, and damages the essence and qi, a hundred times more severe than emission at other times. As for the days when the gods and spirits descend to inspect, or the holy birthdays of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, if husband and wife do not observe the prohibitions and defile or offend, they will incur rebuke and damage their hidden virtue. This is why some people in the world, though they are well-behaved, honest, and sincere, often suffer the calamities of much illness and short life, and the ill retribution of having their fame stripped and their years reduced; these are often due to not observing the taboos of the conjugal chamber!
To have a heart that is viciously cruel, yet a countenance that is kind.

A heart that is vicious and cruel is already hard to guard against; yet to add a countenance that is kind is all the more unfathomable! No one avoids tigers and wolves and dreads vipers and scorpions except that they are so venomous. If a person has a venomous heart and a kind face, so that outwardly he seems one to be trusted and befriended, but is often one who takes advantage of another's unpreparedness to vent his venom, then his sinister cruelty is more severe than that of tigers, wolves, vipers, and scorpions! When such a man dies, he will surely fall into the three paths, as swift as an arrow! And the retribution he draws upon himself in life after life will surely be endless suffering!

Cai Yuandu treated his guests with a beaming face. Though some of them were guests he disliked, yet the attitude he showed them was uniformly the same; and so his heart was hard to fathom, and people could only regard him as a smiling yaksha. Later Cai Yuandu was demoted and banished to a distant place, where he died.

People like Cai Yuandu are to be found everywhere in the world. We ought to deal with them by holding to what is right and treating them with propriety; and we should associate with them in an impartial, equal attitude. Then, though they be sinister and venomous, they will have no way to harm me!

Mr. Yu Tieqiao said: 'Whenever a person's eyes gaze downward and he utters not a word, and between his brows and eyes there is not the slightest trace of virtue's repose or kindly serenity, then he is certain to be a man of venomous heart. Such a man is one with whom one must never make friends, but should keep far away! In the past there was a monk who, sleeping by day, had his spirit issue forth from his nostrils and become a black venomous serpent crawling about on the ground; many people saw this incident. Later, when the monk died, his whole body split apart and turned into a serpent skin. Therefore, the sort of person we should keep far away in making friends is this kind of man! If he could but know that his own heart is venomous, and wash it clean with bitter remorse, as a good physician treats a venomous sore and must pluck out all the venom before it is healed, then such a man might not fail to enter the Way. But he will certainly never bring himself to do it! How helpless! Truly it is a sorrow!'
To sell to others, or give others to eat, filthy and unclean food.

Filthy and unclean food — whether because it was not prepared cleanly, or has been eaten by insects or bitten by rats, or has stood overnight in hot weather so that its color and flavor have changed, or has been stored too long and gone stale, moldy, and rotten — eating it is enough to cause illness and harm people. If one uses filthy food to sell to people or give to people, others will surely become resentful, and the spirits will also loathe it. As for the maidservants and servants in a household, who waste water and gruel, cooking more food than is needed and, when they cannot finish it, casting it into the latrine or the ditch — this is especially a great sin! For the most part the blame for such guilt falls upon the master of the household, who has not taught and managed his maids and servants well; therefore each should caution the other against this.

In the market of Hangzhou there was a wine shop selling roasted goose. One day, one of the roasted geese in the shop was encircled by a venomous serpent, and it happened that a village teacher from the private school saw it. The teacher thought, 'If this roasted goose is sold to someone and eaten, the eater will surely be poisoned!' So he wished to buy the goose. He agreed with the shopkeeper on a price of two hundred wen, but he had only a hundred wen on him, so he borrowed another hundred wen from a neighbor whom he knew, and bought the goose. The three then went together to an empty place nearby and buried the goose. Just as they were digging the earth, a large ingot of purple gold came up from the ground. The neighbor said, 'This purple gold is what I hid!' The shopkeeper said, 'This purple gold is what I dropped!' It happened that the county magistrate was passing by, and when he learned the circumstances he sighed and said, 'This is clearly the response to the teacher's kind thought! And yet you two would both contend to seize the teacher's benefit — this is to defy Heaven!' Thereupon the magistrate ordered the shopkeeper and the neighbor beaten with the staff, and gave the purple gold to the teacher.

In Qianzhou there was an official named Li Ji who, wanting to collect usury widely, sent a servant out to collect the debts owed to him. One time, when the servant could not collect the money, he bound the debtor to a tree and poured filth-water down his throat, and only then the debtor was willing to produce a thousand wen to repay the debt. Suddenly the servant, in front of Puan Temple, was struck dead by lightning. Because the servant's money was hidden at his waist, the money had entered into the flesh of the servant, and the skin was stretched over the top of the money.

This case does not merely warn against using filthy things to feed people; it also warns against wicked servants who rely on their masters' power to oppress others. For there are certain wicked servants who, leaning on their master's influence, press for debts, and some even go straight into the bedchamber of another's daughter, directly violating the woman's person, and often bring about great calamity. This is why the thunder-axe so often smites above the heads of wicked servants!
To use heterodox paths and perverse arts to delude the crowd.

Mr. Yu Yubi said: 'The Way is the straight road that all men travel together! The three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism are all the Way of the sages. Though the three teachings manifest outwardly in ways that are not the same, their supreme goal is to make people understand their own minds and see their own natures; their secondary goal is to make people reform their evil and move toward the good. Therefore the words of the sages of the three teachings are as if from one mouth; there has never been a case of delighting in the deceptive and mysterious to bewilder the world. However, there are some of perverse minds who take certain principles of the three teachings and distort them, using them to delude the world; these are all what are called heterodox paths and perverse arts, not the right Way! For example, Zhang Jiao of the Han dynasty, Sun En and Lu Xun of the Jin dynasty, the Red Turbans and Liu Futong at the end of the Yuan dynasty, the recent Wuwei Huangtian, and the White Lotus sect — these are all such heterodox teachings! Those who advocate these, with minds not upright and motives not good, use heterodox paths to bewitch the foolish people, to defy the sovereign and betray the kindness of parents, bringing down calamities that fill the heavens and planting the evil causes of the three paths. These are all the conduct of rebellious ministers and traitorous sons. The laws of the state will surely exterminate them; and the retribution of the yin offices is especially severe, with no rebirth for all eternity!'

In the Sui dynasty, there was one Song Zixian, skilled in many illusions. He made light radiate from the upper story of his dwelling, and transformed into the image of a Buddha to delude the crowd, and moreover claimed to be the reincarnation of Maitreya Bodhisattva come to save the world. He also hung a mirror in his hall; whenever a guest came to call, he used his magic to reflect in the mirror the guest's next life, showing it to be a serpent or beast, and then bade the guest bow before it, only then would it show the human form. By these means Song Zixian gathered several thousand people and began a rebellion. When the government troops came to arrest him, they circled the side of his dwelling and everywhere saw only pits of fire, so that no one dared advance. The commander said, 'This place has never had pits of fire; this is merely sorcery to deceive people!' Only then did the troops dare to advance, and indeed found there were no pits of fire. So they seized Song Zixian and cut him to pieces inch by inch.

Mr. Yan Maoyou of the Ming dynasty said, 'One who gains an art of sorcery by which he might deceive the world, yet does not transmit it, has exceedingly great blessings!' The ancients said, 'One who obtains the art of invisibility and does not test it for three years will surely become an immortal.' Again it is said, 'One who possesses the alchemy of the Daoists and yet does not use it — this man's mind is quite pure and honest, and he will surely enter the Way!' For the true cultivator takes as his chief concern the concealment of his light and the nurturing of his virtue, and the delivering of beings and saving of the world. If relying on a little art one comes to delude the world, then the root of gain and fame is not yet cut off, and to wish to enter the Way, one is still very far off! Not to mention those who use heterodox paths and perverse arts to commit lawlessness — they need not even be spoken of!

The Three Refuges of Buddhism say: 'I take refuge in the Buddha; I take refuge in the Dharma; I take refuge in the Sangha; and the one of supreme importance among these is the middle one, the Dharma! When the Buddha was in the world, he used this Dharma to teach and deliver beings; after the Buddha's extinction, he left this Dharma revealed to deliver beings. The Buddha expounded the Dharma, and the Sangha transmits the Dharma. If one does not take refuge in the Sangha, from whence would one hear the Dharma? If one does not obtain the Dharma, on what would one rely to cultivate? Yet it is the monk who, cultivating himself according to the Dharma and teaching others according to the Dharma, and taking as his heart the ending of birth-and-death and the realization of bodhi — it is he who is the Sangha. As for one who does not himself cultivate according to the Dharma, but traffics in the Tathagata's teaching to gain fame, profit, and support, and misleads people — though outwardly he wears the square robe and round shaven head, very like a monk, in truth he is a demon's child and graticule! But human life is hard to obtain, and the Buddhist Dharma is hard to encounter. Having obtained a human body, one must take refuge in the Buddha. In ancient times one could seek the Dharma from the Sangha; but in the present age one must first use the Dharma to test the Sangha. Having found a true monk, one should then settle the mind and receive instruction and cultivate with all one's heart. Then where is the Dharma? The Dharma is in the scriptures. Pray begin with the Collected Works of Yunqi composed by Master Lianchi.'
To privately and unlawfully use short rulers and narrow measures, light scales and small pints, in order to delight in profit and take advantage.

This speaks of the matter of cunning merchants and petty men delighting in profit. Rulers, measures, pints, scales, and the like are the instruments used to fix prices and unify human feelings. Some in this world may possess two sets, and actually use, in buying and selling, short rulers and narrow measures to take in much and give out little, or light scales and small pints to take in heavy and give out light. Consider their intention — they only wish to take advantage! How could they know that in taking half a measure of advantage from others, they injure a measure of their own virtue and blessings! Moreover, to injure others and benefit oneself surely brings retribution such as calamity from Heaven or the burning of the thunder-fire. Perhaps the master of the household does not know, while the sons, younger brothers, and servants in charge of the goods go out and in secretly practice this, and the guilt in the end falls upon the master of the household. So the master cannot but be clear-sighted in this!

In the Yuan dynasty, Duke Rongmin was frugal and upright, fond of doing good and given to giving alms; the measures of the household were all of one standard. He once carved an inscription on each measure saying, 'In giving out, thus; in taking in, thus; so may it be with my descendants forever!' And indeed his descendants were all able to revere and observe the laws of the world, and generation after generation they were greatly honored.

In Guangling there was a certain Old Madam Wang who used a short ruler to sell cloth. After her death she appeared in a dream to her son, saying, 'In all my life I deceived people with a short ruler, and the yin office punished me by causing me to be reborn as an ox in the family of the Hao of Xixi. Under the belly of this ox is the character Wang.' Her son then found the Hao family, and the dam there present had indeed given birth to a calf; the calf's belly had white hair forming the shape of the character Wang. When the son saw it, he bought the calf and took it home. If he fed it fine food, it would not eat; if he gave it fodder, it would eat. When it bore heavy loads and toiled in the fields, the ox seemed content; but if it was kept idle, it would leap and dash about a hundred ways, showing great unease. Do those who darken their consciences in delighting in profit know of such retribution?

In the Wanli era of the Ming dynasty, in Yangzhou there was a large grocery shop. When the owner was on the verge of death, he bade his son, saying, 'All my life I built up my fortune relying solely on this scale. This scale is made of blackwood, and the hollow in its middle contains quicksilver. When weighing out, I pour the quicksilver to the head of the balance-beam; when weighing in, I pour the quicksilver to the tail of the balance-beam; and in this way, taking in heavy and giving out light, was how I became wealthy!' When the son heard this, he resented his father's unfairness in his heart, but did not dare to speak of it. After his father's death, the son burned the blackwood scale; and in the smoke of the burning scale a dragon transformed and ascended to Heaven. Later, for no reason, his two children both died, and so he complained, saying, 'My father's heart was not impartial, and yet he has peace; today I am impartial in weighing, and dare not deceive others, and yet my two sons have died — is the Way of Heaven like this?' When he had spoken he went to sleep. Suddenly, it seemed he arrived at a government office, and the chief official within said to him, 'Your father, in doing business all his life, gave out light and took in heavy, deceiving others to fatten himself. The profits he gained, though many, were all part of the wealth and emolument allotted to him by fate. But because he deceived his heart and created karma, he offended Heaven. The High Lord sent down the two stars of Loss and Dissipation to be your sons; when they grew to adulthood, they would have spent your property, and then your household would have been burned, so that your wealth would be scattered and your sons dead, leaving no posterity — to manifest the retribution of your father's sins. Today you have reformed your father's evil practices, covering over the faults he committed; and you are fair in everything and kind to others. The High Lord has therefore recalled the two stars of Loss and Dissipation, and before long will replace them with two good sons to glorify your household. So you should the more strive to do good, and do not recklessly complain!' The son, waking, remembered one by one the words the heavenly official had spoken to him in the dream, and the more earnestly practiced doing good. In three years he had two sons in succession, and when they grew up both passed the jinshi examination; and moreover he had many sons and grandsons, and was very prosperous.

Mr. Zhang Gongchen said, 'When I was at Hanguan, I was on good terms with the descendants of this gentleman, and so I was able to know this matter in great detail. The reason I do not speak his name is in order to spare his relatives and friends from having to mention the faults committed by their elders of old!'
Mixing counterfeit goods in among the genuine.

Of late the markets offer any number of fakes — so many that the imitations nearly outnumber the real goods! This too shows how the world and men’s hearts are changing. In food and drink, in medicines, in gold and silk and other wares, the slightest deception or slip brings a heart so darkened that it harms others as nothing else can! And as for passing false silver and counterfeit notes, the offense is graver still; so Heaven’s condemnation falls on such men with especial swiftness.

In the Gengxu year of the Kangxi reign of the Qing dynasty, a certain Gu of Fujian, living in Jiangyin county, secretly sold false silver. He carried his false silver to the market, and no one, astonishingly, could tell it from the true; but false silver cannot last beyond ten days — once ten days are past, it betrays its own nature. A certain man, knowing how matters stood, took six ounces of gold and exchanged them with Gu for twenty ounces of false silver; then with that false silver he went to Changmen to buy gauze and satin. His purchases made, he took a boat home; passing Huadang by night, a great wind suddenly rose and capsized the boat, and all the gauze and satin he had bought, together with the baggage he carried, sank into the water. He was fortunate enough to be a strong swimmer, and so did not drown, but had to go home with nothing on his body. Gu, meanwhile, was struck dead by thunder that very day, and the forge-hammer with which he made his false silver was shattered to pieces by the same bolt.

Alas, how foolish men are! That Gu, who cheated the world with cunning arts, should suffer Heaven’s execution and be killed by lightning is no more than he deserved. But this other man, for a single greedy thought, straightway lost the six ounces of gold he had; and his clothes and baggage were worth, who can say, how many more ounces. To carry on business to such a pass may be called losing one’s capital with a vengeance! And he came within a hair of losing his old life too, drowning in the waves — it was perilous indeed! So pitiable are the ignorant and petty-minded.

The aim of doing business is to make a living. But if I must make a living, is my neighbor not to make one too? If I must feed a family, is my neighbor not to feed his? Moreover, the man who cheats his own heart and defies Heaven meets a retribution plain to see — never yet has one escaped death for himself and ruin for his house. So this is not the true heart of a man of business at all.

The grandfather of Minister Sun Shenchuan once found two ounces of silver in the course of selling goods. Afterward he noticed that the silver was somehow amiss and showed it to others, who proved it to be false. The grandfather thought: “Since this silver cannot be used, how can I keep it and let it ruin others?” So he walked to the bank of the East River, waded some tens of paces into the water, and cast the false silver into the deepest part. In later years his son gained an official degree and rose to the post of Vice Commissioner; and his grandson was none other than Sun Shenchuan.

When Shenchuan’s grandfather got hold of false silver, he threw it into the river; his heart was in accord with the heart of Lü Dongbin, and so his sons and grandsons rose to honor. Yet this was only the smallest part of his recompense.

In the Song dynasty there lived on Mount Lu a man named Lu Chang, who made his living selling oil and candles; in secret he mixed fish fat into his candles and sold them. And Huang Yu of the Jianlong Monastery mixed beef tallow into his oil and made candles to sell; in the end both men were struck dead by thunder.
Alas! Those who sell salt doctored with sand and wine doctored with water should take the end of Lu Chang and Huang Yu as a mirror for themselves.

In the Ming dynasty, when Zhang Anguo was prefect of Fuzhou, he found that the people of that place sold much false medicine, and so he posted a proclamation warning them all: “Tao the Hermit and Master Sun, because they wrote the materia medica and the Prescriptions Worth a Thousand in Gold, were able to succor creatures and benefit the living; they piled up so much hidden merit that their names are enrolled among the immortals. From that time to this, those who practice medicine and sell drugs, healing men in sincerity of heart and reaping blessings thereby, have been very many indeed! To say nothing of those recorded in the books — even in our own recent days such proofs are especially common. Some, merely by selling true medicine, come to possess ten thousand strings of cash; some enjoy peace and honor in their own persons and live out a ripe old age; some see their sons and grandsons win degrees, bring glory to the family gate, and raise the household to a new estate. So the recompense of good and evil follows a man as shadow follows form, without the least error. And I have myself seen men who sold false medicine: at first they piled up a little property and thought themselves clever and full of schemes, never knowing that in the secret accounts their allotted wealth and emoluments were being docked and diminished; some met with calamity after calamity in their own persons, some saw sons and grandsons drink and whore and gamble until the family was broken and the estate scattered, and some were struck down by heavenly fire and killed by thunder. For those who buy medicine are mostly men whose families lie sick, their hearts full of urgency, who bring their money to seek a physician’s help; these filial sons and worthy grandchildren only hope that the medicine they buy, once taken by their kin, will work a cure at a single dose — and instead they are ruined by false medicine! Not only does it do no good when taken; it harms the body besides. To kill one bird or beast in ordinary times still brings its karmic consequence; how much more so when, among all living things, man’s life is the most honored? If a man suffers such a calamity, the pain of it is without end, and the karma of it is harder still to expiate. How can one fail to abstain from selling false medicine?”
Seizing wicked profits by cunning fraud.

When a man seeks inordinate gain, there is no device he will not stoop to. What are nowadays called “going aboard the boat” and “striking the wooden bell” — talking up a matter and skimming a commission — and all such artful extortion and deceit, come under the head of seizing wicked profit; so one need not single out the private coining of money or the private boiling of salt as the only instances of it! And among the white-collar class there are many who commit this great evil; how then can one lay the blame only at the door of the common folk in the marketplace?

An old poem says: “The more cunning and the more clever, the poorer a man grows; / Cunning and cleverness — Heaven will not bear them long. / If wealth and honor came by cunning and by craft, / The world’s fools would feed upon the west wind.”

Zhang Feng was a man of excellent speech and of fine penmanship besides, and he knew the tax rolls and household registers of his district as he knew his own palm. He could reduce men who owned broad acres to poverty in a moment, with not a foot of ground left to stand on; and thus Zhang Feng came to hold lands beyond number, while the common people within his jurisdiction suffered bitterly and yet dared not speak of it — for if they spoke in the morning, by evening the men who came to press the tax would be at their doors. Zhang Feng was above all skilled in the arts of fleecing the people; whenever a superior came on inspection tour, he was constantly summoned to be questioned, and before long that superior would be clasping hands and laughing with him, until in the end he did nothing but at Zhang Feng’s bidding. Day after day he taught his superiors how to get at the people’s money; and when the money was got, the superior took only two shares while seven went to Zhang Feng. At that time the grand coordinator, Lord Tang, was a man of incorruptible integrity; learning how matters stood, he sent a strong man of great martial skill who bound Zhang Feng and dragged him to the yamen for trial. On the road Zhang Feng tried to bribe the strong man with heavy gold, but the strong man would not consent; thereupon he contrived to escape, and the strong man could not overtake him. The open country lay all about them and for ten thousand li there was not a cloud in the sky; when suddenly a dreadful peal of thunder sounded in the east, and Zhang Feng was struck dead there in the west — his belly burst open, his entrails spilled out over the ground. Those who saw it would not even gather his corpse and bury it; and even the wild dogs and wild boars found his flesh too foul to eat.
Using one’s power to oppress the sons and daughters of good families, making bondservants, concubines, and slaves of them.

Those who are born bondservants in this life are all men who in former lives created karma and piled up evil beyond one thousand eight hundred transgressions. Yet some are not bondservants at all, but were sons and daughters of good families; and if I use my power to force them into that station, then I am pressing the good into base service. As for selling the good into prostitution, that is a mortal sin beyond the ten unpardonable offenses, and of that I need not speak at all.

Zhou Xiang and Xue Chun of Zhangzhou were the best of friends. Xue Chun was very poor and had only one son; when he died, his son passed into Zhou Xiang’s keeping. But Zhou Xiang made Xue Chun’s son serve him as a slave, and for the least displeasure he would flog him cruelly. One day Zhou Xiang met Xue Chun on the road and asked in astonishment: “Are you not already dead? How is it that you have come back into the world of men?” Xue Chun answered: “I have come to see my son, and by the way to press my claim against you!” When Zhou Xiang heard this, the cold sweat ran down him like rain; and when he got home he suddenly dropped dead.

One constantly sees kinsmen and clansmen of rich and noble houses, reduced to poverty and with nowhere to turn, come seeking their patronage; and these houses are forever setting such kinsmen to do the work of servants, and even berating them in loud voices — this too is what the Supreme One forbids. Yet at the outset most of these people began with the heart of one who would relieve and pity his kinsmen, and afterward came to bully and oppress them instead. In doing so they not only gain no merit but lose their own virtue besides — and is that not a great pity?

Every year the Guangji Treasury of Zhejiang province conscripted the wealthy households of Hangzhou to serve as treasury clerks, charged specifically with the receiving and paying out of funds. One man who had been conscripted as a clerk embezzled so much of the government silver that he could not repay it; whereupon the prefectural judge, a certain Wang, had his wives, concubines, and children seized and brought to the yamen, and still he could not make the money good. Wang then ordered a small boat to carry his wives, concubines, and children out to West Lake, there to be used as attendants by those who came to tour the lake, with all their wages paid over to the government. In after years some of Wang’s own sons and grandsons sank so low as to become prostitutes.

There are parents of a certain sort who, driven past endurance, do a thing that is heartless and shameless, and sell their children away to be bondservants — but can our hearts bear it? Those who have both means and a ready love of right should help such people in their need and preserve the sons and daughters of good families: that is a work of abundant virtue. And even if I cannot manage so much, I should at least not insult and degrade them; for though in the end they may be sold to another, I shall not have failed to do what my heart would have me do.

Noble and base were never fixed by nature. It is merely that the children of the poor are sold to the rich, and so they are called base — but in truth they are all of good family. People nowadays treasure their own children like pearls in the palm; they give them fine food and fine clothes. Yet toward bondservants and concubines they flog them cruelly for the least trifle, give them coarse food and coarse clothes, and let them hunger and freeze — and these too are children born of fathers and mothers! Why is such injustice shown them? And they never reflect that the rich may become poor and the poor may become rich, and that the way of Heaven is past all knowing: who can guarantee that the good will not turn into the base, or the base into the good?

In dealing with others below one, a man should, when placed in wealth and honor, know in full the aches and pains of poverty and low estate; in the days of his youth and vigor, remember the bitterness of old age; in the midst of ease and delight, show compassion for the plight of those in trouble and adversity; and standing himself outside a matter, forgive the anxious heart of those caught within it.
Using crafty schemes to deceive the simple into a trap.

Whenever one uses crafty schemes and sets a snare so that a man falls into one’s trap, it is called deceit; and to work it upon the simple is pitiable beyond all else. For even though the simple fellow cannot take his revenge, in the secret darkness there will surely be those who take it for him! And so the simple man suffers no harm, while I have harmed myself first of all.

The Yuan Family Precepts say: “Wealth and poverty have no fixed estate, and lands and houses have no fixed owner: when a man has money he buys, and when he has none he sells; and the household that buys property ought to understand this principle. Besides, when a man sells his property, it may be for want of food, or because of debt, or because of sickness, death, marriage, or litigation; because he needs a large sum in cash he sells property worth exactly that sum. And the man who buys ought to deal generously and liberally, paying him the value of the property he sells; for although after the transaction the money will soon melt away, it is still enough to settle the one matter that drove him to sell. But the rich man without benevolence takes a special delight in using crafty schemes to deceive people: knowing perfectly well that the other is in urgent need, he outwardly affects the look of one who refuses to buy, while secretly he means to buy, and so beats the price down severely; and after the bargain is struck he dallies and stalls, unwilling to pay in full at once — or else he pays him off at a high valuation in grain and other goods, or fixes a term and pays him in dribbles. The man who sold the property forthwith consumes and scatters what he receives, and still cannot settle the one matter that drove him to sell; and the going back and forth to demand payment wastes the labor of his household, which has already swallowed up more than half of it. The rich buyer, meanwhile, is privately delighted with himself, thinking he has used a clever scheme; he does not know that the way of Heaven loves to return a thing upon its doer — sometimes the retribution falls upon the man himself, and sometimes the calamity reaches his sons and grandsons. Yet men for the most part remain deluded and do not awaken. And why should that be?”
Greed that can never be satisfied.

To take things in with the mouth is called greed; and the word describes a man’s covetous heart as being like the mouth at food, never sated, never reaching an end. Laozi said: “No sin is greater than excess of desire; no calamity is greater than not knowing when one has enough.” The man who knows enough is happy even in poverty and low estate; the man who does not know enough is sorrowful even in wealth and honor. The cravings of the men of the world, when their number is fulfilled, will in the end come to nothing and be scattered and gone. And that is a truth needing no further argument; yet a man will drag down upon himself a whole train of calamity and sin besides, which is harder still to be done with.

In the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Tang dynasty, the Vice Director of the Secretariat Yuan Zai — the chancellor of that day — indulged his several sons in interceding with officials for others and taking bribes; the capital and the provinces were alike affected by it, and men of loyalty and worth began to be pushed aside while corrupt and lawless men were advanced. And in Yuan Zai’s own house the luxury and extravagance of his pleasures were such that even the imperial palace could not match them. The emperor once warned him to restrain himself somewhat, but he did not change his ways; and afterward the emperor grew angry, and issued an edict placing Yuan Zai under arrest and granting him death; and Yuan Zai’s wife was granted death as well. His house was searched and his property confiscated; of the mineral stalactite seized there were as much as five hundred ounces, and the emperor issued an edict distributing it among the officials of the Secretariat, the Chancellery, and the Censorate; and of pepper there were as many as eight hundred bushels. Other goods besides were too many to be reckoned.
Zheng Xuan said: “Since ancient times, how many men who sat in the chancellor’s seat ever died of hunger and cold? Again and again they die of wealth and goods — and that is truly a laughable thing.”

In the Tianshun reign of the Ming dynasty, Li Ming of Jiaxing in Zhejiang came into possession of a precious hu vessel. The rich man Cao Yuan offered twenty bushels of rice for it, but Li Ming would not consent; he then showed it to Wu Ruhui, who offered a hundred bushels of rice, and only then did Li Ming agree and prepare to close the bargain. But Liu Zhu advised Li Ming, saying: “I have a plan that can bring you great profit. If you present the precious hu vessel as a gift to the eunuch Zhang, the garrison commander, and seek his consent to have the salt certificates of the whole Jiaxing prefecture entrusted to you to manage, then you may reap a hundredfold gain!” Li Ming agreed, and Liu Zhu went about making the connections and pulled the business off; when all was reckoned, they had gained more than three thousand ounces of silver, of which Liu Zhu gave Li Ming one third. Li Ming took the salt certificates and went home by boat; and as the boat crossed the river it capsized, and all the salt certificates were soaked and ruined. At that very time the prefect of Jiaxing, Yang Jizong, was pressing hard to recover the salt certificates; and so Li Ming was seized and thrown into prison, where he died; and Liu Zhu sold off all his property to make good the loss on the salt certificates.

An old saying goes: “No man lives a hundred years; in vain he plans for a thousand.” Why should a man harbor such greed that can never be satisfied? Is he scheming for his sons and grandsons? He does not know the proverb: “If my sons and grandsons are not my equals, what do they want with money? If my sons and grandsons are my betters, what do they want with money?”

Shu Guang of the Han dynasty once said: “Do you think I have grown so dotish that I will not plan for my sons and grandsons? I have old fields and an old cottage; if my sons and grandsons but till them diligently, these will be enough to furnish them food and clothing. To add surplus and abundance for them is to teach them idleness. If they are worthy and have much wealth, it injures their resolve; if they are foolish and have much wealth, it multiplies their faults. Moreover, the rich man is the target of the multitude’s resentment; and since I have no learning with which to teach my sons and grandsons, I do not wish to add to their faults and make them the mark of the multitude’s hatred.” From this we see it: the household precept of Sima Wengong — that to pile up gold is not so good as to pile up virtue — how can we fail to commit it to memory and put it into practice?
Laying a complaint before the spirits, or swearing an oath or a curse, calling on the gods to prove at once that one’s own case is right.

To curse and swear before the spirits need not be set down in writing or in a memorial; whenever a man in angry quarrel with another rashly calls upon and summons the gods, that too counts as a curse. As the Chapter on Curses and Oaths says: “Whenever a man utters a curse, those about him will for the most part curse him in return, and all the fierce and evil ghosts find their chance to slip in and work their mischief. Unless a man repents with a sincere heart and respectfully beseeches the gods of Heaven to descend and release him, it is no easy matter to cut off the harm of the curse.” How then can one curse?

In the early Wanli reign of the Ming dynasty, Wang Zhu, a village officer of Xihua, fell to quarreling with a taxpaying household over how much tax money was in arrears; and Wang Zhu swore an oath before the City God that he himself was in the right. That night he slept at the Yangshan Temple; at midnight he suddenly heard the cries of men clearing the way, and rising to look, he saw an official standing beneath a torch, wearing a headwrap and a red robe, with a great many guards about him. The official gave a loud command, and two strong men came toward Wang Zhu with knives in their hands. Wang Zhu at once snatched up the inkstone from the tea table and hurled it at the strong men; but he was pierced by the knife in their hands, and blood flowed from his mouth and cheeks. The monks of the temple, startled awake, rose and looked about, and saw not a single person; only then did they know that the official Wang Zhu had seen was the City God himself. The next morning Wang Zhu put on a prisoner’s garb and went to the City God’s temple to confess his fault and beg pardon; and the images in the temple were just as he had seen them the night before, and on the sword-bearing attendant at the City God’s right there was still a trace of ink! A month later the knife wound on Wang Zhu’s mouth and cheeks had healed, but the scar of the blade was plain to see.

You must know that in every matter there is a right and a wrong. If one’s cause is right, then the voice of the world’s opinion cannot be silenced; in time it will of itself become clear — why take the trouble to wrangle with another?
