If one’s cause is wrong, then on self-reflection one will feel that one is in the wrong — how would one dare to curse before the gods and lay the blame on another? Besides, in all things a man should act according to what is right, keeping to his own station and guarding himself. Once he curses before the gods, he will be loathed by the ghosts and spirits and will surely meet with Heaven’s condemnation. Can one then fail to be watchful and careful?
Given to drink and often drunk, defying reason and disordering the nature.

Wine can disorder a man’s nature, and if he is given to it by habit, the harm he suffers is very great. Reading the Admonition on Wine that the men of old wrote to restrain drinking, one sees how deep and far their forethought reached; reading the Ode to Wine, one sees how lofty the feeling was that they lodged in it. Thus the Book of Rites speaks of the offering of a single cup, host and guest bowing to each other in turn, and its very purpose is to keep men from losing propriety through drink. But the men of the world love wine and set no limit to it, and so their bodies and limbs are turned upside down, ritual and law fall into disorder, they shout and curse at the feast, they lie drunk in the streets, they break the law and offend their superiors; and in time their hearts are darkened and their virtue lost. Thus it is that scholars ruin their good name, officials lose their posts, farmers neglect their fields, merchants lose their goods, and in the gravest cases men lose their lives and destroy their families. Is this not a thing to make the heart ache? Fan Lugong of the Song dynasty admonished his sons, saying: “Beware, and love not deep drinking; / wine is a madman’s drug, no pleasant flavor; / it can turn a careful, generous nature / into the fierce and stubborn kind.” Cao Yuechuan said: “To nourish the nature, covet not the water that clouds it; to build a household, guard against the soup that wrecks a house.” Moreover, the source of every lewd and lawless act is mostly wine; and so among the four prohibitions, wine stands first. (The Abridged Pearl of the Lesser Learning, in its chapter on warnings, names wine, strong flavors, beautiful women, and high terraces and ponds as the four prohibitions.)

In a drunken man all good thoughts vanish, while evil thoughts blaze up fiercely; things he would never dare to do or say when sober, he dares both to do and to say when drunk. So the man who can keep his drinking in measure may call wine a brew of Great Harmony, or a friend who makes one forget one’s cares; but the man who cannot keep it in measure ought to look on wine as a soft demon, or as sweet poison.

Wine is the firewood of lust, and of those who give themselves to drink without giving themselves to lust there are exceedingly few. When the fire of the heart is at its height and desire is raging, it is hard enough to hold it in check; how much more so after wine, which only adds fuel to that fire! And to lie with a woman when drunk and full fed turns the five organs about within one, so that no small sickness comes of it. This above all should be sternly punished. And there are men who, drunk, babble of lewd and filthy things and so bring shame and death upon themselves; and then repentance comes too late.

The most laughable thing in the world is to contend for victory at a drinking feast. In our dealings with others we had best understand how to yield in every matter; and what is an occasional merry gathering of friends, with drinking games and guess-fingers, but a passing amusement? To win brings no glory, to lose brings no shame; the loser has lost nothing, the winner has gained nothing. It is just as the master of chess says: “To win is surely a matter for joy, and to lose is a matter for joy as well!” Some drinkers, not understanding this, muddle along and will not stop until they have won; and so they come to the point where they are not content until they are dead drunk — such men are fools past all reasoning. Others boast of their great capacity for wine, thinking that no one can match them, and count it a fine and gallant feat — never knowing that in moral character and learning, in degrees and official rank, they fall short of others in every single thing! Yet they must needs show off their capacity for wine before men — is that not a mistake far beyond all bounds? And there is yet another sort who boast that their drinking rules are strict and take a great pride in it, never reflecting that wine is meant to join hearts in joy and knit friendships together, and that each man should stop when his own measure is reached. Why must they force others to drink more, until it injures their health? The proverb says: “Tyranny is fiercer than a tiger.” I say: “A tyrant’s drinking rules are just as fierce as any tiger.” If such a man is at the feast, one should get away from him as fast as may be.

The Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom sets out thirty-five faults of drinking: First, in this present life one’s goods are emptied and exhausted — because, drunk, the mind knows no measure or restraint and spends without limit. Second, it is the root from which many diseases spring. Third, it is the root of blows and lawsuits. Fourth, one goes stark naked, shameless as cattle or horses. Fifth, drunk, one dances and curses at the feast, and an evil name goes abroad, so that men loathe and shun him and pay him no respect. Sixth, it clouds the wisdom. Seventh, what one ought to obtain one does not obtain; and what one has already obtained one loses. Eighth, one blurts out every hidden thing; and when sober again, one repents it. Ninth, one’s various undertakings fall into neglect and come to nothing. Tenth, drunkenness is the root of sorrow — for in drink one commits many faults, and when sober again one feels shame and grief. Eleventh, the body grows weak and strengthless. Twelfth, one’s health and the color of one’s face both grow poor. Thirteenth, one does not know to respect one’s father. Fourteenth, one does not know to respect one’s mother. Fifteenth, one does not know to respect the shramanas. Sixteenth, one does not know to respect the brahmins. Seventeenth, one does not know to respect one’s uncles and elders — all because, drunk, the spirit is bemused and cannot tell one thing from another. Eighteenth, one does not respect the Buddha. Nineteenth, one does not respect the Dharma. Twentieth, one does not respect the Sangha. Twenty-first, one joins with evil men in stirring up trouble. Twenty-second, one estranges the wise and the good. Twenty-third, one becomes a breaker of precepts. Twenty-fourth, one has no heart of shame. Twenty-fifth, one cannot master the six emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, delight, love, and hate. Twenty-sixth, one gives free rein to lust without restraint. Twenty-seventh, one is loathed by the many, and all dislike the sight of him. Twenty-eighth, one is cast off alike by the weighty kin of one’s family and by the good teachers of the world. Twenty-ninth, one does what is unwholesome. Thirtieth, one abandons the wholesome Dharma. Thirty-first, one is not trusted by the wise — and all because of the license that follows on drink. Thirty-second, one draws far away from nirvāṇa. Thirty-third, one plants the evil cause of delusion and madness. Thirty-fourth, when the body breaks up and life ends, one falls into the three evil paths, and even into hell. Thirty-fifth, if one is born a man again, the mind is often deranged. After drinking, such are the many faults that befall a man; therefore one must not drink.

There was a scholar named Liu in Fujian, a man who had always kept a strict rule over himself and who had many students. When he taught them, he would always tell them that they must abstain from lust. One day he got drunk and fell to fighting with a friend over a prostitute; when he sobered up he was overcome with regret, and ashamed to face his students again. So he shut his door and sat in quiet reflection for three days, gathering many instances old and new of the harm done by wine to serve as warnings to himself, and he gave the collection the name Classic of a Hundred Regrets. Again, there was a scholar named Ye of Zhejiang, a man most filial to his parents and affectionate to his brothers. One day, drunk, he quarreled with his younger brother, and the two cursed each other roundly; and when their father came out to mediate and persuade them, Ye spoke one or two disrespectful words to his father’s face. When he woke sober in the morning his wife told him how he had behaved in his cups; and when he heard it he was so torn with remorse that he hurried to his father’s door, knocked his head on the ground and wept, and knelt there waiting to beg his father’s pardon. Only then did his father’s anger subside.

Alas! The true nature of both these scholars was of the purest and most generous, and yet even they could not escape behaving without restraint when drunk. How much further, then, will men of loose and crooked habits go when wine has taken them — to what lengths of license and insolence, one cannot imagine! Wine has the name of the spring of calamity, and how truly it is called so!

Wu Yu of the Song dynasty held the post of Privy Counsellor. At that time Chen Zhizhong was relieved of the chancellorship and recommended Wu Yu to take his place as chancellor; but Wu Yu, who had been drinking with the emperor and had fallen asleep drunk, suddenly struck the couch and shouted loudly for his attendants. The emperor was angered by this and degraded him, sending him down to the Western Capital as a retired official of the Bureau of Receptions. Again, when Guo Zhi held the post of Vice Minister of Administration, the emperor once summoned him on business, but the reek of wine rose from him and offended the emperor’s nostrils; and for this he was degraded and transferred to Nanjing.

A slip of the tongue when drunk time and again brings great calamity. Formerly there was a famous scholar in Wuxi county, Jiangsu, a man still young and of high talent. One day, drunk, he exposed to his face another man’s shameful doings in his private chambers; and the man thus shamed before him laughed easily and said: “He is drunk, and what he says is the talk of a drunkard!” — putting on the look of one who bore no grudge at all. All who sat there greatly admired the breadth of the shamed man’s mind. But there was an old and seasoned man among them who, after the shamed man had gone, said to those who had been drinking with him: “To be shamed as he was just now and to be angry is the ordinary way of men; but to be shamed and not angry, and even to smile, is a thing no man can fathom!” Half a year after this, that young and gifted scholar was secretly done to death by someone; and so everyone suspected that the man who had held the knife was the very man he had once shamed to his face.

Alas! The calamity of wine can be as grave as this! If a man, drunk, falls into a river or tumbles into a pit, cuts his head and face, loses his goods, betrays a secret, or offends the ghosts and spirits — all such faults and disasters are the mischief that wine has wrought. Can a man then fail to abstain?
Story the Fourth:

Su Yijian, an Academician of the Song dynasty, once drank so heavily that blood came from his nose and mouth; sickness followed, and so he passed away. And Wang Quan, who held the post of Palace Secretary, likewise died when, after a great drunk, his navel split open.

You must know that wine is a madman’s drug, and that when it seeps into a man’s body in great quantity over long years, there are very few who escape sickness. If the poison of wine declares itself early, the sickness is comparatively light; if it declares itself late, the sickness is deep — and there is none whom it does not end by killing. So, looking through the long record of those ancient and modern who have enjoyed long life, they are all men who did not care for drink. Why, then, should any man take the useful body bequeathed him by his forebears and commit it to a life of drunken stupor and deathlike sleep in the company of wine?
Story the Fifth:

The household rules of the Zheng family of Pujiang say: “Sons and grandsons under thirty years of age shall not let wine touch their lips. Men in their prime may be permitted to drink a little wine; but those who give themselves up to drunkenness, or who make an uproar after drinking, must certainly be flogged as a punishment. In entertaining guests the chief thing is sincerity; guests must not be pressed to drink. The women of the house must not drink together with guests; but those who have passed the age of fifty may be left to do as they please.” These rules may serve a household for reference.

The ancients said: “Wine is a kind of go-between: if it meets with a good thing, it brings the good thing to pass; if it meets with a bad thing, it brings the bad thing to pass. Wine is also a condition that gives rise to good and evil: if it gives rise to a wholesome condition, wholesome deeds are accomplished; if it gives rise to an unwholesome condition, unwholesome deeds are accomplished. As for wine itself, it cannot decide a man’s right and wrong, good and evil — it is the man himself who decides what is right and wrong, good and evil.” So how can the two words “sparing” and “frugal” be left out of the account of wine?
Fathers and sons, elder and younger brothers — flesh and blood of the closest kin — quarreling in anger.

Zhang Gongyi of the Tang dynasty kept nine generations of his family beneath one roof, and all his household rested on a single word: forbearance. Anger and quarreling come of nothing but the inability to forbear. Among fathers and sons, brothers and kin of the same flesh, if one insists on being right, feeling will be wounded; and once feeling is wounded, one is no longer in the right at all. How then can kin of the same flesh quarrel in anger as they please? Yet the beginning of such quarrels most often lies in the mischief-making of women who come between. For a woman’s heart is not fair, and she is forever nursing jealousy; and the father- and mother-in-law, the uncles, and the sisters-in-law of her own generation whom she names as kin are, after all, only relations patched together by circumstance and addressed by courtesy against her will. They were never natural kin bound by Heaven’s own order; and so she will lightly cut off affection and lightly fall into angry quarrels; and let word be carried back and forth but twice, and the grudge hardens into hatred. Thus within the household trouble breeds upon trouble, and the disputes that spring up are too many to be counted. Only a man of deep and generous family feeling, of high understanding and far-seeing judgment, can discern the smallest thing and refuse to believe a woman’s slander; and then of itself the household will be harmonious and at peace together — and how could quarrels in anger ever arise among kin of the same flesh?

In the Ming dynasty, Zheng Lian of Pujiang had a household whose members, for two hundred years, never left their ancestral home to move elsewhere. Everyone called the village where he lived the “Righteous Gate.” The prefect of the time sent a plaque praising his family that read: “The First Story of All Under Heaven.” After the founding emperor Taizu of the Ming ascended the throne, he summoned Zheng Lian to the capital and asked him: “When your household begins to cook, how many people sit down to eat?” Zheng Lian replied: “A little over a thousand.” The emperor said: “Truly it is the first story under heaven!” At the time Empress Ma was listening behind a folding screen, and she said to the emperor: “Your Majesty obtained the realm by rising up as a single person; now Zheng Lian’s household actually numbers over a thousand. If they were to rise up, would it not be all the easier for them to take the realm?” Hearing these words, the emperor was genuinely startled, and asked Zheng Lian again: “What method do you use to keep your kinsmen dwelling together in harmony?” Zheng Lian answered with great cleverness: “I have no other method except that I simply do not listen to my wife’s words!” The emperor could not help laughing out loud. At the time Henan happened to present fragrant pears to the court, and the emperor therefore bestowed two pears upon Zheng Lian. Zheng Lian raised the pears above his head with both hands and walked out of the palace, whereupon the emperor had someone follow and watch him. After Zheng Lian returned home, he gathered his kinsmen, bowed his head to the ground toward the direction of the imperial palace to return thanks, and in two large vats of water crushed the pears and placed them in the vats, so that every person of the whole clan tasted the pears bestowed by the emperor. When the emperor heard of this, he was greatly pleased. Later, someone exposed the Zheng family, claiming they had colluded with a powerful minister to rebel. The emperor said: “There is no such person in the Zheng family; it is others who have falsely accused them!” Afterwards the emperor issued an edict ordering the Zheng family to select sons and younger brothers over thirty years of age to come to the capital, and the court conferred office upon them. The clan elder Zheng Ying came to the palace to return thanks, and the emperor himself came to the Fengtian gate, wrote the three characters “Filial and Righteous Family” with his own brush and bestowed them, and even affixed the imperial seal upon them!
A man who is not loyal, sincere, and good.

To exhaust oneself is called loyalty; to be upright and correct is called goodness. Man is the most intelligent of all beings, and among humans the man is honored. Since one has attained this body of a man, honored and intelligent, and yet is crafty and disloyal, unable to fulfill his own duty, and is wicked and unrighteous, unable to be an upright person — then he has not only betrayed his own intelligence, but has betrayed Heaven above as well!

The Song-dynasty Lord Wen Zheng Gong (Fan Zhongyan) lost his father at the age of two. When he grew older he stood on his own, and studied day and night, sitting in stillness and contemplating in silence. After six years of this he mastered the Six Classics. At the age of twenty he passed the imperial examination and served as the prefect of Hezhong. He was just and upright in office, governed his household with order, and knew well how to use both kindness and authority. In bestowing alms to relieve the poor and rescue the suffering, he spared no effort. For this reason Fan Zhongyan not only gained a great name for a time, but was also honored and revered by a hundred generations. So the word “man” may truly be said to be one that Mr. Fan was fully worthy of!
A woman who is not gentle and obedient.

The Record of Rites says: “The man leads, the woman follows.” It says again: “When a woman is young, she follows her father and elder brothers; after she is married, she follows her husband; after her husband dies, she follows her son.” The Family Instructions of Master Yan says: “The duty of a woman is only to preside over the proper usages of food, dress, and adornment in the household. If a woman possesses intelligence and talent, she should only assist her husband and make up for his shortcomings. If she places herself above her husband and meddles in outside affairs, she is like the hen that crows at dawn, or the long-tongued and garrulous owl. That the family fortune does not prosper has its beginning right here!”

The Lady Hou, wife of the Song-dynasty Cheng Xiang, was exceedingly humble and gentle. Even for the smallest matter she would report to her husband before acting. She governed her household well and never beat or scolded the servants. When her children reproved the servants, she would surely admonish them, saying: “Although people differ in high and low station, their personhood is equally honorable!” When her husband Cheng Xiang was angry, she would always gently advise him at his side, so that he could let go his wrath and his mood improve. Only when the children erred would she not cover for them. She often said: “The reason children turn out unworthy is that the mother protects and covers for them, so that the father never learns of the children’s faults!” Later her two sons, Cheng Yi and Cheng Hao, both became famous Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty, and their status was most exalted. Even after death they enjoyed the honor of having offerings placed for them in the Confucian temple.

The Zixia Formula for Building Fortune says: “For a woman who cultivates virtue, it is no different from a man. But a woman has no other business; if she can accomplish the three obediences and four virtues, only then is she a good woman. If there is a good deed, it is better to urge one’s parents and husband to do it. Therefore, if parents do three good deeds, the woman shares in one; if the husband does two, the wife shares in one. If it is brought about by the wife’s forethought and persuasion, then it is the same merit as the husband’s. If one can persuade a woman to do good, this merit is more precious than the woman doing good herself. Among sisters and sisters-in-law, if there is a good deed, they should praise one another; this merit is also equal. The most important thing is to rejoice in one’s heart and do good together, and not give rise to envy! If a woman can attain filialty and obedience, and assist her husband and teach her children, fulfilling her own duty, and moreover deeply believe in cause and effect, eat vegetarian food and recite the Buddha’s name, then in this present life she will naturally be at peace in body and mind, with flourishing descendants; and at death she will surely receive the compassionate guidance of the Buddha and be reborn in the Western Land. Therefore a woman should only cultivate quietly at home and should not rush about outside. In this way she will not waste her precious time, and may also avoid causing others to criticize her. Again, for example, if a child of the household is ill, and one prays to the spirits and performs offerings for protection, it easily costs a good deal of money. Why not instead, at ordinary times, do good deeds and release living creatures? Then one will naturally receive the protection of the spirits. Thus, within the inner quarters one can naturally cultivate virtue and build blessings. I hope that all women will encourage one another and strive to do this!”
Husband and wife who are not in harmony.

The common saying goes: “A harmonious household makes all things prosper.” The ancients said: “Only when husband and wife are in harmony is the family way prosperous.” If a woman has never studied and understood principle, and does something wrong, the husband should clearly explain and guide her. Certainly he should not indulge her, nor should he immediately become angry and resentful. But if a husband meets a fierce and shrewish wife, he will be subjected to her bullying; and if he meets a weak and simple wife, he instead humiliates and mistreats her. To bully the weak and fear the strong — is this what a husband should do? All the more there are foolish husbands who dote on a concubine and insult the primary wife, or who are infatuated with a courtesan and mistreat their wife, and even beat and rage at her. Such husbands especially do not come to a good end!

Gu Kai treated his wife with great propriety. He often went out early and returned late, so his wife seldom saw his face. Once, when Gu Kai was gravely ill and lying in bed, his wife came out to see him. Gu Kai ordered those at his side to help him up, and put on his cap and cloak, then exchanged greetings with his wife, and only after the ritual was completed did he tell his wife to return to her room.

From this we may see that between husband and wife, how can there be even a single moment without propriety? If husband and wife can treat each other with propriety, how could they ever fall out of harmony? Yet is it difficult to observe propriety? One only needs to be harmonious yet restrained, and loving yet respectful, and that is enough!

Wang Balang of Luoyang had a cruel temper and loved to beat his wife. He was infatuated with a courtesan and had nearly squandered his family fortune. His wife was already suffering hunger and cold, yet Wang Balang beat her all the more severely. His wife, having no recourse, could only entrust relatives and neighbors to help settle the matter. Wang Balang then ordered his wife to move elsewhere and lived with the courtesan in the same room. Not long after, Wang Balang fell gravely ill, and his property was already exhausted. At that point the courtesan drifted away on her own. Having no way out, Wang Balang then wished to take refuge with his wife again, but by then she avoided him. Suddenly Wang Balang died of an abrupt illness, and soon after his wife died too. The relatives and neighbors could only place the two corpses together. That night, they suddenly heard sounds of fighting and quarreling inside the house. When they opened the door and looked, the bodies of the couple Wang Balang were standing back to back.
A wife who does not respect her husband.

The ancients said: “The husband is the wife’s heaven.” The husband is the person a wife relies on for her whole life. So how could a wife fail to respect her husband? A wife who does not respect her husband is either a shrew or a wanton woman: either she contradicts her husband with harsh words, or she curses him. Yet she does not know that whoever is reborn as a woman, it is mostly because in past lives she created evil karma. If she again bullies her husband, in her next life she will fall into the three evil paths! As for a woman who, when her husband has just died and his bones are not yet cold, already wishes to remarry, who regards the children she bore her husband as strangers, and who does not even grieve at her husband’s death — when her husband was alive, how could she have respected him at all?

Du Qi was by nature extremely timid and weak. His wife, Lady Zhang, had always looked down on him. In his later years he was often ill, and his wife neither attended to him nor took care of him. Strangely enough, Lady Zhang died before Du Qi. After Lady Zhang was placed in her coffin, the coffin suddenly broke open, and Lady Zhang was transformed into a python that rushed straight into the forest.
Alas! The ancients said: “The husband is the wife’s heaven.” So to slight one’s husband is the same as slighting Heaven! Can Heaven be slighted? Let all who are wives think carefully on this!

In the Later Han dynasty, Liang Hong took the daughter of the Meng family as his wife. Meng Guang, when she married into the Liang household, was dressed in gold and silver and adorned most elegantly and luxuriously. After seven days had passed, Liang Hong would not speak a single word to her. So Meng Guang gathered up her hair, pinned it on top of her head, changed into plain clothing of coarse cloth, and set about the household chores. Only then did Liang Hong say with joy: “This is truly Liang Hong’s wife!” Thereupon he went with his wife into seclusion in the Baling mountains. Later, to avoid troubles, he went to the state of Wu and lodged in a small hut beside the residence of Gao Botong, where he was hired to husk rice. Every time Liang Hong returned home after work, his wife had already prepared his meal and set it before him, and she did not dare to lift her head to look up, her manner most respectful. Gao Botong, seeing how Liang Hong’s wife raised the tray (bowl) level with her eyebrows in serving her husband, said: “Liang Hong here is only a worker who husks rice, and yet he can make his wife serve him with such respect. He is surely no ordinary person!” So he invited the couple Liang Hong to move into his home.

There is no greater way for a wife to respect her husband than in these two matters: preserving her chastity for her husband, and being skilled at teaching her children. As the saying goes, “A virtuous woman does not serve two husbands.” When a widow preserves her chastity for her husband, even ghosts and spirits will respect her. For example, in the Ming dynasty the academician Huang Guan died for the state during the disaster of the Jingkang era. His wife, Lady Weng, and his two daughters were captured. To avoid the humiliation of herself and her daughters, Lady Weng seized the moment and took her daughters to drown themselves. Her act of preserving her chastity for her husband is revered by a thousand ages; and so to this day, in the temple by the Qinhuai River, Lady Weng’s memorial tablet is still enshrined. And in the Song dynasty, the father of Ouyang Xiu died when Ouyang Xiu was four. His mother, Lady Zheng, preserved her widowhood for her husband. Their life was very poor; besides working to earn money to support the family, she had personally to teach Ouyang Xiu to write and to read, enduring all hardship and bitterness. This so moved Ouyang Xiu to strive in his studies that he finally became a wise and worthy prime minister of the Song dynasty. Lady Zheng was also repeatedly granted by the court the titles of Grand Lady of Yue and Grand Lady of Wei. These two cases are models of respecting the husband, and all who are wives should take them as their own encouragement!
One who often delights in pride and self-conceit.

Laozi said: “He who does not think himself right makes his thought stand out; he who does not praise himself has his merit affirmed; he who is not proud is able to sustain the growth of his undertaking.” The Book of Changes says: “The way of Heaven, whatever it be: whoever is proud and self-satisfied it causes to lose, and the humble it lets gain benefit. The way of earth, whatever it be: whoever is proud and self-satisfied it causes to change, not letting him be forever satisfied, and the humble it lets be moistened and never dried, just as where a low place is, the flowing water passing by surely fills its defect. The way of ghosts and spirits: whoever is proud it causes to be harmed, and the humble it lets receive blessing. If one is high and noble yet humble, his virtue is all the more radiant; if one is low and humble yet humble, his virtue also cannot be surpassed. Therefore humility is a virtue the gentleman always preserves!” Great Yu was not proud and did not praise himself, and said: “Even the foolish man and woman have strengths in which they surpass me!” So Great Yu, not proud and not self-praising, was finally able to overcome a myriad difficulties, dredge the rivers, and tame the great flood, so that his merit extended to a myriad ages. And the Duke of Zhou, whose talent overshadowed the age, not only was not proud and not stingy, but was also exceedingly humble, respectful, diligent in government, and loving to the people, and finally completed the great enterprise of unifying the Eastern Expedition, laying for the Zhou dynasty a foundation of lasting peace. So it is said that the truly great sages and worthy men are all made bit by bit from a place of trembling caution, as if treading upon deep ice and facing a precipice! Great Yu and the Duke of Zhou were both sages; when did they ever parade their own virtue before others? Yet now people casually take pride and boast before others, not knowing what the point is. In fact, others merely see in them nothing more than the self-importance of the man of Yelang!

In the Han dynasty, Gu Yong had been enfeoffed as a marquis for three days, yet his family did not know of it. In the Jin dynasty, Xie An was playing chess with a guest, and the report of victory at the Battle of Fei River arrived, yet the guest did not notice. The Song-dynasty general Cao Bin, when he conquered Jiangnan and returned to the capital to be received by the emperor, in the memorial submitted at the gate just said: “Returning after handling official matters in Jiangnan by imperial command.” The Song-dynasty worthy minister Wen Yanbo, during the Zhihe era of Emperor Renzong of Song, was the first to propose establishing Yingzong as crown prince (Yingzong reigned four years). When Emperor Shenzong later ascended the throne, Wen Yanbo said it was entirely Han Qi’s merit. The emperor thereby knew that Wen Yanbo did not boast of his own merit. These worthies named above are all of first-rate character, and their contribution to the state was very great. They were still able to be so retiring and not proud. Why do people not realize they should emulate them?

A person of great capacity surely has thick fortune; a person of shallow capacity surely has thin fortune. And humility and pride are the very boundary between calamity and blessing, so how can one be careless? Moreover, what is there in wealth, nobility, and ability sufficient to be relied upon? If one uses them to be arrogant before others, let alone whether calamity will come on account of it — first of all one has already lost one’s own heart and knows no shame!

In the Jin dynasty, Shi Chong and Wang Kai vied in ostentatious display of wealth, seeing who was richer. Wang Kai made a purple-silk screen wall forty li long, and Shi Chong made a brocade screen wall fifty li long, precisely to outdo Wang Kai. Wang Kai once brought out a coral a foot long given to him by the emperor to flaunt before Shi Chong. Shi Chong picked up an iron ruyi and smashed the coral, whereupon Wang Kai flew into a great rage. Shi Chong then brought out corals treasured in his own home, all two or three feet tall, and offered one to Wang Kai in compensation. As for the other rare and precious objects, the two kept striving to see whose were better. Later, when Shi Chong, because of a crime, was about to be beheaded, he sighed and said: “Is not your purpose in killing me to get my family property!”

Alas! The words Shi Chong spoke just before he died were so wise! But if he had known earlier, surely he would not have boasted! And the calamity of pride and self-conceit is just this cruel. So in every word and act of ours, how can we fail to be careful and cautious?
One who often contends for favor and is envious.

Both men and women have hearts of envy. A man who sees another achieving fame is jealous; when he sees another wealthy and noble, he is jealous; when another’s position draws near to his own, he is jealous; when another’s ability surpasses his, he is jealous. All these come from the narrowness of his own mind! As for a woman who, to contend for favor, forms resentments, she often brings calamity upon the household, and may even cut off the line of descendants — this sin is all the more grave. To such a degree that while alive everyone gnashes their teeth at her in hatred, and after death she sinks forever into the three evil paths of hell, hungry ghosts, and beasts, to repay the wicked debts she has created. So to rectify the mind and cultivate the person, and to be a model for others — is that the responsibility of men alone?

In the Zhou dynasty, General Pang Juan of the state of Wei, out of envy of Sun Bin’s talent, had Sun Bin’s two feet cut off; later he was killed by Sun Bin. In the Tang dynasty, the eunuchs Yu Chaoen and Cheng Yuanzhen envied Guo Ziyi’s high merit and great office. Every time they wished to slander and harm Guo Ziyi, in the end they instead were both convicted; Yu Chaoen was executed, and Cheng Yuanzhen was demoted and banished to a distant place. The Song-dynasty treacherous minister Han Tuozhou envied Zhu Xi’s promotion to the post of acting grand secretary at the Huanzhang Pavilion, and therefore formed a faction to denounce Zhu Xi’s learning as false. For a time the gentlemanly men were all cast out and suppressed; later Han Tuozhou was killed by Shi Miyuan. In the Northern Qi dynasty, the monk Mingchen, whenever he saw anyone more accomplished than himself, would envy him greatly; later Mingchen in the forest was transformed into a python and crawled off into a mountain valley. And when Emperor Wu of Liang obtained a formula for stopping envy, one beside him said to Emperor Wu: “I wish Your Majesty would widely bestow this formula for stopping envy upon the assembled ministers, so that those without ability would not envy the able; those harboring selfishness would not envy the selfless; those not pure would not envy the pure; those covetous of wealth would not envy the incorruptible. This too is a means of reforming them.” Emperor Wu gladly agreed. From these historical cases, we see that the affliction of envy is not only among women; men too are subject to it!

In the Zhou dynasty, the wife of Su Bao of the state of Song was named Nüzong. She served her mother-in-law with great filialty, while Su Bao held office in the state of Wei, where he served for three years and there took another wife. Su Bao’s elder brother’s wife then told this news to Nüzong. Nüzong said: “For a wife to serve her husband, it is single-minded devotion that is chastity and good compliance that is obedience; it is not established as virtuous to monopolize the husband’s love! According to the rules of propriety, a senior minister may take three wives and a knight may take two wives. My husband is a knight, so is it not a good thing for him to have two wives? Moreover, a woman has the seven grounds of dismissal (the seven conditions by which a man in ancient times divorced his wife), and envy is the first condition for a wife to be dismissed by her husband! Instead of telling me the proper way of the inner chambers for a wife, you would make me envious and cause me to commit the act of being dismissed by my husband?” The ruler of Song heard of this and issued an order to honor her, calling her Nüzong, to serve as a model for women.

Lu Bian’s uncle served as the magistrate of Hucheng county, and Lu Bian went to Hucheng to visit him. When he slept at night he had a dream in which he came to a place where there were ten large millstones, and beside the millstones were countless women. The millstones kept turning without stopping, and ox-headed ghost soldiers scooped up the women with large dustpans and threw them into the holes of the millstones. The women’s bodies then turned and were ground with the millstones, their flesh and bones all crushed to powder, their cries of pain unbearable to hear. Lu Bian saw his aunt among them too; when the two met, they felt both grief and joy. Lu Bian asked his aunt the reason for her suffering here. His aunt said: “This is all because in my former life I was envious; after death I have come here to suffer!” Alas! The hellish retribution of envy is indeed this dreadful!

In the Jin dynasty, the wife of Jia Chong, Lady Guo, was naturally prone to envy. She once bore a son. One day, the wet nurse was just holding the son, and Jia Chong took the opportunity to make improper advances to the wet nurse. Just then his wife came upon them. Lady Guo beat the wet nurse to death with a whip. The son, missing the wet nurse, cried himself to death, and Jia Chong thereby lost all descendants.

Jia Chong was a great treacherous minister who misled the state, so Heaven caused him to marry an envious wife in order to cut off his posterity. Yet the number of people in the world who, because of envy, suffer the retribution of being cut off from descendants is by no means small! And these envious women, even if they do not know how grave their sin is and that after death they cannot escape the retribution of hell, should at least fear the retribution of losing children before their eyes, the pain of the separation of flesh and bone, and the desolation of having no one to make offerings to them afterwards. So all women should early consider how severe and dreadful the retribution of envy is, and naturally they will no longer dare to be envious. If we carefully examine the case of Jia Chong, the retribution of being cut off from descendants was originally ordained by Heaven; and that he should happen to marry the envious Lady Guo as his wife is itself an ingenious form of evil retribution. So how can men fail to think of accumulating virtue to turn back Heaven’s intent, and only blame the envy of women?

In the Later Wei dynasty, the wife of Du Chang, Lady Liu, was very envious. One time, after Du Chang had washed his hair, he called the maidservant Jin Jing to comb it. When Lady Liu saw this she flew into a rage and cut off Jin Jing’s fingers. Not long after, Lady Liu was bitten by a fox, and the fingers of both her hands thus dropped off. There was another maidservant named Yulian who sang very well, and Du Chang was very fond of her. Lady Liu cut out Yulian’s tongue, so that she could no longer sing. Later Lady Liu’s tongue grew sores and rotted, and her condition was most critical. She went to the Chan master Chou to confess. The master said: “My lady, you cut off the maidservant’s fingers, and your own fingers have accordingly dropped off; again you cut out the maidservant’s tongue, and now your tongue is about to be cut off as well. Therefore you must repent with utmost sincerity before this disaster can be removed!” Lady Liu bowed to the master and begged earnestly. After seven days, the master made Lady Liu open her mouth wide, and then recited a spell toward Lady Liu’s mouth. At this, two snakes slowly crawled out more than a foot from Lady Liu’s mouth. The master recited the spell all the more urgently, and then the snakes fell to the ground. Lady Liu’s tongue thereby recovered, and from then on she was never envious again.

Therefore, when one repents of one’s faults and mends one’s evil ways, both spirits and humans rejoice. Even if one has committed boundless evil karma, so long as from now on one repents and does not repeat it, the sins committed before can be immediately melted away.
[Conclusion]

The common saying goes: “A woman’s resentment is not easily ended; a woman’s temper also readily forms resentments with others.” So cruel, venomous, and treacherous things, a woman will do with her own hands and not feel a moment’s doubt! Only when a woman is not yet married should her parents and brothers instruct her in advance; and once she is married, one should tactfully restrain her, and not fan the flames of her temper. In this way her heart of envy may be somewhat diminished. And the duty of mediating and transforming her falls upon her husband. If the husband, greedy for female beauty and fond of licentiousness, causes his wife to roar like a lioness, then the gentleman lays the guilt of the debauched husband upon his head — and this is still to be counted especially light!
A husband who treats his wife unrighteously and unkindly.

In treating one’s wife, one should be gentle and respectful; in treating one’s children, one should be strict and upright. If one cannot treat one’s wife with propriety, one loses the righteousness of the husband leading and the wife following. If one cannot use principle to teach one’s children, one harms the kindness of a father in begetting and raising children. To be unrighteous and unkind is called being without proper conduct. Today many who are husbands, in treating their wives, are either harsh and ungrateful or irreverent and indecorous; in treating their children, they are either over-indulgent or over-severe. They themselves are already unrighteous and unkind — how then can they go and blame their wives?

In the Later Han dynasty, Zhang Zhan was by nature grave and dignified, and exceedingly fond of propriety. He often explained the principles of conducting oneself in the world to his wife and children, just as a ruler leads his ministers. So his wife too was able to encourage and urge herself and him, and they urged each other on mutually. Hence he had considerable reputation in his home district. Zhang Zhan’s example may serve as a model for teaching wife and children.

Shi Tang married his wife at a very young age. Later, when he passed the examination and attained rank, he often regretted that he had not been able to marry the daughter of a wealthy family, and so felt great remorse. He then stopped paying attention to his wife and no longer shared the room with her. Because of this his wife grew depressed and downcast; as time passed she fell ill, and the illness continued for several years. Shi Tang never once looked in on her. His wife thus felt great anguish. When she was about to die, she called out to Shi Tang from the next room: “I am about to die. Can you really bear not to see me one last time?” Shi Tang was hard-hearted enough not to see his wife even that last time. A year after his wife died, the underworld authorities, because Shi Tang had treated his wife harshly and ungratefully, without feeling or righteousness, stripped away his lifespan and fortune, and Shi Tang suddenly died of illness.

Wang Yao of Zhuozhou doted excessively on his two sons, and so fostered evil dispositions in them. He himself could not control his sons and had to take them to the authorities. Later both sons died, and Wang Yao was thus left without posterity. After Wang Yao died, on the night of the fifteenth day of the second month of the following year, Liu Jin, the shrine keeper of the City God temple of Zhuozhou, saw a man holding a petition requesting from the City God an offering at the Qingming festival. The City God angrily said: “Wang Yao, you had sons and yet could not discipline them properly, bringing it about that your posterity was cut off. Who will come to make offerings to you?” After saying this, the City God ordered the ghost soldiers to drive Wang Yao off. Wang Yao could only wail and go away. The next day the temple master went to visit Wang Yao’s home, and only then learned that Wang Yao had been dead for more than a year.

A saying of old goes: “Confucius’s sons did not know cursing; Zengzi’s sons did not know quarreling.” These are all the result of habit becoming nature! It says again: “Raising sons and younger brothers is like raising orchid and fragrant grass: one must both accumulate learning to cultivate them, and accumulate good to nourish them.” A father must not dote excessively on his sons. Sons and younger brothers should be strictly disciplined from early youth; once grown, they will not have the regret of unworthy offspring. It says again: “If the household has several children, food and clothing should be distributed fairly; the precedence of elder and younger, high and low, must be strictly carried out; right and wrong, good and evil, good and bad, must be clearly distinguished. When sons and younger brothers are small, teach them fairness, and when grown there will be no disaster of contending over property; discipline them strictly from early youth, and when grown there will be no disaster of insubordination and arrogance; from childhood teach them to distinguish good from evil and right from wrong, and when grown there will be no disaster of becoming ruffians and bandits. Taken together with what has been said before, one will then know how to act.”
A daughter-in-law who is not filial and not respectful toward her parents-in-law.

A daughter-in-law serving her parents-in-law is like a son serving his parents: her attitude should be gentle and pleasant-spoken, with a soft voice and lowered tone; she should be concerned for her parents-in-law’s cold and warmth, illness and itch, and support them when they come and go. If she is in the least lacking in propriety toward her parents-in-law, it is unfilial; and this sin of unfiliality reaches the heavens and may even bring upon her the retribution of being struck dead by thunder and fire. Alas! The relation of daughter-in-law to parents-in-law is formed by her marriage to the son; while the relation of son to parents is the innate kinship of blood! From ancient times, is there such a principle that a son is unfilial to his parents, yet a daughter-in-law is filial to her parents-in-law? So whenever a daughter-in-law fails in propriety toward her parents-in-law, it is all caused by the son. So how could ghosts and spirits single out the daughter-in-law’s unfiliality to punish? I hope that all who are sons will ponder this deeply!

On the twenty-second day of the third month of the fifth year of the Chongzhen era of the Ming dynasty, the wife of Mao Jizong of Shanyang county in Huai’an, Lady Feng, was by nature utterly filial. Her mother-in-law was advanced in age and gravely ill, and Mao Jizong just happened to be transporting grain to the capital. Lady Feng, having no recourse, that night bathed and changed her clothes, prayed to Heaven to die in her mother-in-law’s place, and then took a knife and stabbed herself in the side, so that the tip of her liver protruded. At that moment she suddenly heard her son cry out; fearing it would wake her mother-in-law, she used a handkerchief to temporarily cover the wound, went into the room to soothe the child. Afterwards, she worried that a little liver might not suffice to cure her mother-in-law’s illness, so she prayed devoutly and then cut again. At that time the moon had not yet come out, but the sky suddenly became bright and clear, and the stars shone forth brilliantly, shining upon Lady Feng as brightly as broad daylight. She cut another piece of her liver, immediately cooked it into a soup, and gave it to her mother-in-law to eat. As soon as her mother-in-law put it in her mouth, she found it exceptionally sweet and asked her: “What is this? How is it so delicious?” Lady Feng pretended and said: “A neighbor caught a deer; this is deer liver.” Her mother-in-law then drank up all the soup. Strangely enough, her illness was cured. Because Lady Feng at the time was moved by utmost sincerity, her wound did not feel painful. But the bloodstains were hard to conceal, and were detected by her young sister-in-law. The whole family spread the news in astonishment, and only then did the mother-in-law learn that it was her daughter-in-law who had saved her. Moved to sobs and tears, she cherished her daughter-in-law all the more. At the time the scholars of the village decided to write up this deed and present it to the emperor, but they were troubled by the boundless extortion of the officials and could not get the matter up to the emperor’s knowledge. Fortunately there was a scholar of Huizhou, Jiang Tianyi, who wrote a book, The Collection of Startling Filialty That Moved Heaven, and so this deed was passed down.

In the Song dynasty, Jia Dan served as the military governor of Huazhou. At the time there was a common woman who served her mother-in-law unfilially. Because the mother-in-law was old and blind, the woman gave her filthy food to eat; the mother-in-law found the taste strange. When the son returned from outside, she pulled at the son and asked. The son, seeing that his wife had actually given filth to his mother to eat, raised his face to heaven and wept bitterly. Suddenly, a peal of thunder flashed, cut off the woman’s head, and joined a dog’s head onto her neck. When Jia Dan learned of this, he ordered the woman to be led out and paraded through the streets within his jurisdiction, to warn the unfilial.

Alas! People today are forever saying that a woman’s disposition is as changeable as water, and so it is hard to achieve an immediate and perfect effect in instructing her; a claim like this is truly without reason! Now that a woman is born, if her parents have already failed in the way they nurture and teach her, and when she is married into another’s household as a daughter-in-law her dull-witted husband is unable to serve as a model she can learn from, then she comes to feel that the evil habits of perversity, lewdness, and jealousy cannot be suppressed. But if a girl’s parents, from her childhood until she is given in marriage, instruct her and educate her in the principles of filial obedience to her parents-in-law, respect for her husband, and the need to be gentle and compliant, then even if she marries a husband without ability, she will still know how to stand on her own feet and help her husband establish the family estate; and if the husband she marries is a good man worthy of learning from, then all the more can she give full play to the virtue and capability of a worthy wife and good mother. Therefore to educate a daughter is exactly as important as to educate a son. This truth should be made clear to all the world!
Despising and slighting the spirits of one’s ancestors.

After one’s ancestors and parents have died, their yin spirits remain, and these are called the former spirits (xianling). Whenever the funeral rites lack propriety, the mourning period violates the norms, the burial is not carried out promptly, the sacrifices and prayers are not sincere, the grave-sweeping is not diligent, the ancestral hall is not kept clean, or the incense is lit intermittently—these are all ways of slighting the former spirits. Water has its source and a tree has its root; how can a person forget the spirits of those who came before him? If one is remiss in this, then one does not deserve to be called a human being!
Violating the command of those above.

All persons in a lower position who receive commands from those above are under an ‘upper command’: for example, a minister receiving a command from the ruler, a child receiving a command from a parent, or a disciple receiving a command from his teacher. As for these commands from above—the orders, directives, commissions, and summons—if they are contrary to reason and cannot be carried out, one should explain gently and offer remonstrance beforehand, making clear the reason one dares not accept the command. If, on the other hand, they accord with reason and ought to be done, and one still fails to carry them out diligently, there is already fault in that—how much more so in rebelling against them! And the one who rebels against the command of those above is precisely he who will in time become a rebellious minister or a treacherous son.
Doing things that bring no benefit to oneself.

All the affairs of the world turn empty in the blink of an eye. Only the merit and virtue one cultivates oneself, and the good one does to benefit society by promoting what is beneficial and removing what is harmful—these alone can one carry with oneself, life after life and world after world, in boundless enjoyment. These are the things that are truly beneficial. But building great houses, buying good fields, clothing, and carriages, and collecting every kind of poem, painting, and antique—these are all profitless undertakings, and moreover they can ruin one’s resolve and burden one’s body, with not the slightest benefit. As for hanging lanterns and draping festoons, singing and dancing and performing plays, drinking wine and smoking, gambling and visiting prostitutes—these not only bring no benefit but also do great harm!
Harboring false intentions in secret.

A minister deceiving his ruler, a child rebelling against his parents, a wife betraying her husband, brothers harming one another, and friends overthrowing one another—all these conduct arise from harboring false intentions in secret. Yet harboring false intentions does not need to wait until it is manifested in deed; the moment such a thought stirs, though others may not know it, the ghosts and spirits have already condemned his heart.
Cursing oneself, and also cursing others.

This sentence refers to one who curses without any just cause to plead. Whenever one is angry and resentful beyond bearing, curses oneself to die, and curses others to die too—this is the first sign of disaster befalling the petty man or the woman. It often happens that before one’s time to die has come, one dies at once just as one had cursed, and so how can one be anything but cautious?
Having one’s likes and dislikes perverted by partiality.

The scope of partial dislike or partial affection is wide. Whenever it is a ruler toward his minister, a father toward his son, a husband toward his wife and concubines, or a master toward his servants, this is often present. But for a woman toward the children born of the former wife and the children she herself bore, the case of partial dislike and partial affection is especially severe. Therefore, in ancient times, Master Zeng, after his wife died, never remarried for the rest of his life. Zengzi said: “Yin Gaozong, because of his later wife, killed his own son Xiaoji; the Zhou minister Yin Jifu, also because of a later wife, killed his own son Boqi. I am not the equal of Gaozong, nor of Jifu—how could I be sure not to commit the same error as they?” Excellent! Excellent! Zengzi spoke most truly. Zengzi, fearing that he himself might fall into the fault of partial dislike and partial affection, was the best model of one who could preserve the grace of a father. Yet after his wife had passed away never to remarry—this too is a thing hard for human feeling to achieve. We can only ask that one who remarries constantly bear in mind Zengzi’s words, and perhaps he may not, through partial dislike and affection, commit a great error.
Stepping over wells and stoves.

The benefit of a well to mankind is very great, and there is a spirit of the spring that presides over it, called Guan, whose form is like that of a beautiful woman; moreover the water of the well can supply men and animals, birds and beasts, and can too be used to sacrifice to the gods and make offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—how can one profane and slight it? And among the spirits of the five kinds of sacrifice, the hearth god is one of them; he is the Fire Spirit of Great Unity, surnamed Zhang, named Zhuo, styled Ziguo. He is in charge of the fortune and misfortune of a whole household, and exclusively examines good and evil, knows beforehand auspiciousness and calamity. If one steps over the well or the stove, one slights and insults the spirits, and the offense is very great. And it is not only stepping over them: for example, sitting on the well’s rim, trampling the stove door with one’s foot, or baking filthy things upon the stove—all these are acts that offend and defile the spirits!
Leaping over food and over people’s bodies.

Food is the provision that sustains life, and man is one of the Three Powers, standing alongside Heaven and Earth as the Three Powers (for it is because man can aid Heaven and Earth in transforming and nourishing all things that he stands with them as one of the Three Powers). Therefore to leap over food and to leap over a person’s body are both offenses.
Harming an already-born child and aborting a child still in the womb.

The human body is supremely precious; to obtain a human body is exceedingly difficult. Moreover, at the time a person is born, the heavenly spirits rejoice and the god in charge of destiny settles his reckoning; it can be said to startle heaven and move earth, and its preciousness is beyond description! And when a child is just born, what has it done to owe anything to its parents? Yet some hard-hearted parents dare to kill the infant. Then there is the woman who elopes in lewdness, and after conceiving aborts the child; such conduct is worse than that of birds and beasts, and cannot be guided or made to understand. As for those who, because the family is poor and dislike having too many children, drown the child at birth or abort it before it is born—know that the offense of killing a person is beyond expiation. Even the smallest creature’s life is so precious that one should wish to spare it and avoid killing it—how much more one’s own child! Whenever in this life a person has no child, or raises a child only to have it die, or in old age has the child die before him—these are all fruits born of such evil karma committed in past lives.

When Qian Bangwei served as magistrate of Guixi county, because the local custom was that when a daughter was born many were unwilling to raise her and drowned the infant girls, Qian Bangwei employed both kindness and severity—heavy rewards and heavy punishments—to strictly forbid the drowning of infant girls. If one killed an infant girl, five households were held jointly guilty and punished, and in this way he saved the lives of many baby girls. Qian Bangwei was later promoted to be prefect of Tingzhou, enjoyed a long life, and his descendants all prospered.

Just because he prohibited the people from harming children and aborting the unborn, he was able to obtain such blessings. Today people should at all times counsel others not to commit this evil deed, and the merit too is not small!

Once there was Guo Yin’s daughter, Guo Yinfeng, whose soul was seized by two ghosts and taken through all eighteen hells. She saw that in the last hell there was a King of the Underworld seated in the hall, and beneath the hall several hundred women stood drawn up in order; and each of them had children embracing their feet, weeping and crying: “Give me back my life! Give me back my life!” Some of these women, because they had borne too many daughters, had drowned the infant girls; some were so poor they had raised children and then killed them; some were wives who, jealous of a concubine’s pregnancy, beat the child from her womb; some had conceived an illicit child and then poisoned it; some, through quarrels and fighting, had disturbed the fetal energy and caused a miscarriage; some, disliking the child’s crying, beat or threw the child until it died; and some, being careless and unguarded in caring for the child, brought it to an untimely death. The King of the Underworld questioned each of them one by one. Every woman’s body was bound with chains, her face gaunt and her body thin, looking utterly pitiable. After Guo Yinfeng returned to the living world, she told her father all she had seen. Guo Yin wrote this matter upon the wall of Tianning Temple to warn the world.

The woman Yang Asheng had been poor and sickly from childhood, and in her later years was even more destitute. At the moment of her death she said to herself: “In a former life I was a physician. When I attended the sick I did not examine the illness carefully. On one occasion a woman said there was a poisonous worm in her belly; I could not tell that she was already with child, and at once gave her wine infused with Daphne genkwa, to drive out the worm. As a result the woman died together with the twins in her belly. Because I misdiagnosed the illness and gave the wrong medicine, I killed three lives. The underworld officials punished me for this crime of killing; when I had endured my suffering in the underworld, I was condemned to be reborn as a woman, and this is already the third time in this life; and in life after life I must be a lowly slave, forever enduring the torment of poverty and hunger and thirst, with scarcely a single day of peace. My plight may be told to the physicians of the world, that they take me as a warning!” When she had spoken, Yang Asheng died.

The Emperor Lord Wenchang said: “Children who are not filial to their parents will naturally be punished and executed by the laws of Heaven. But children who are without fault, and are yet killed by their parents—this is the same as killing the people of the world! And when parents wish to kill their children, why do they not restrain their desires? How can they dare to kill people without regard for the principles of Heaven? In this present age, how can one guarantee there are no such persons? I look upon those suffering punishment in the ghost city of Fengdu, and many of them have committed this very offense! Therefore I hope the people of the world will reflect and awaken quickly, and not bring Heaven’s chastisement upon themselves all the sooner!”
Conduct that is largely dark and unrighteous.

Conduct that is hidden and perverse—such things as adultery, robbery, and lewdness—whatever cannot be told to Heaven or spoken before another, all of it is included. Yet among these, the greater ones must surely be the matter of lewdness. Therefore the Most High writes ‘conduct that is largely hidden and perverse’ immediately after ‘harming children and aborting the unborn’—and there is reason for it.

Master Mao Qizong of the Ming said: “North of Fuliang there was a man named Zhang Mingsan, who accompanied his father, who had been transferred to an office, to Qiongya in exile. The official residence they occupied was next door to that of Commander Li. Commander Li’s two daughters were very beautiful, and Zhang Mingsan secretly carried on an affair with them. Later, when Mingsan wanted to return to his old home in Fuliang, he secretly eloped with Commander Li’s two daughters, hiding them first in a boat. Just as they were about to cross the sea, Commander Li rode up in hot pursuit. Mingsan, at his wit’s end, quickly pushed the two sisters into the water and drowned them. Ten years later Mingsan fell ill with a pain in his waist and hired the physician Sun to treat him. After taking the medicine Sun prescribed, the pain in his waist somewhat eased. That night Sun dreamed that he was catching fish on the beach near Limei when suddenly two women, naked, came out of the water toward him and seized his clothing, saying: ‘We two sisters are from Hainan, and have come here especially to treat Zhang Mingsan’s illness. Are you trying to seize our merit?’ And with that they pulled Sun the physician into the water. Sun woke with a start, drenched in a cold sweat. The next morning Sun told Mingsan of his dream, and Mingsan beat his breast and sighed: ‘Alas! My offense has already come before me—is my death near?’ And indeed, after a month or so, Zhang Mingsan died.”

This is a case of conduct darkly hidden between a man and a woman, and of each receiving retribution! Zhang Mingsan and the two sisters first met in secret, and then fled together in secret; yet the two sisters came to die at Zhang Mingsan’s hand, and ten years later Mingsan died at the hands of the two sisters’ vengeful ghosts. One could say the retribution was wonderfully exact and never the slightest bit off. In general, to commit adultery with another’s wife or daughter, and to harm another’s career and reputation—these two matters are the most hidden and perverse of all, and the most wounding to the heart and to the principles of Heaven. Therefore, he who commits adultery with another’s wife or daughter will surely have his own wife or daughter commit adultery with another; and he who harms the career of another will surely have his own career harmed by another. As the saying goes: “In a dark room, if one does something to wrong one’s conscience, the eyes of the spirits see as clearly as lightning!” And so how can one do evil?
Singing, dancing, and performing plays on the days of obscuration (hui) and the winter sacrifices (la).

Hui is the last day of each lunar month, the day on which the hearth god in charge of destiny makes his report of the world’s merit and faults to Heaven. La has five observances, the days on which the heavenly spirits assess the good and evil, offense and blessing, honors and rank, allotted years, and the auspicious and inauspicious, the life and death of people. The first day of the first month is Heaven’s La; the fifth day of the fifth month is Earth’s La; the seventh day of the seventh month is called the La of Virtue; the first day of the tenth month is the Year’s La; and the eighth day of the twelfth month is the La of Princes and Kings. Whenever these days come, if one should have a fault and it be recorded in the black register of the heavenly spirits, it is very hard to redeem it! Moreover, the Northern Emperor of Fengdu and the Great Lord of the Moon bring out, on these very days, the distant ancestors, parents, and kindred of the living, together with the ghosts of the prison-realms, and question them about the length of their time in the underworld, what offense brought them there to suffer, and in what place their graves now lie; and what are the names of their descendants. Having obtained the names and surnames of the descendants, brothers, kindred, and nine generations, they then begin to assemble and verify, to make up the record of offenses of the living descendants. If, from the distant ages, the living descendants have not yet offered rites of release, then the living descendants are sure to be implicated. Moreover, on these days the yin spirits of the ancestors and kindred are all released, each returning to his own home to receive the sacrifices of his descendants. And as descendants, one ought of course to rely upon the power of the Dharma to sacrifice to the former spirits, to redeem the offenses the forebears committed in the past. If instead one carelessly sings and dances, one offends Heaven and Earth, the ancestors, and one’s kindred! Therefore, on the days of hui and la, should one be making offerings for the ancestors, or should one be singing and dancing?

Master Yu Yubi said: “People should on the days of hui and la weigh the merit they have accumulated in daily life, examine and reflect upon themselves, and rouse themselves to reform and advance.” Therefore the Patriarch often urged people, saying: “If one does not first make a round of preparation, when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, you may be sure you will meet with a fine commotion” (that is, at the moment of death one will be all in a flurry). And again he said: “Each of you, try examining yourselves: from childhood to old age, from birth to death, your mind has been fused into one mass with the five desires, the six dusts, afflictions, and karmic consciousness—what, in the end, will be the result? And what is that one turn that is true turning back?” (that is, have you ever reflected and examined yourselves?) “In a sudden instant, breathing stops, the eyes are shut, and this wandering soul after death must follow the good and evil karma made in a lifetime to receive its retribution! Playing such a part, one has gone for nothing through the world of men—this is what is called living in vain and dying in turbulence!” In the ritual of Master Yunqi Lianchi warning the aged, on the last day of each lunar month people are reminded: “Human life is impermanent, swifter even than the breath! Like a fish in a boiling pot, soon to be cooked until it is burnt and rotten; like a lamp before the wind, to be blown out in an instant. Moreover this body must not long from now pass to death, and the road ahead is a blank mist—who knows where one goes? How can one not suddenly reflect and awaken to the impermanence of life? Therefore one must be watchful and cautious, alert and striving, casting down all conditions and fixing the mind on Buddha-recitation!” The Patriarch exhorted and warned everyone with such bitter words and such a compassionate heart—how can we still go singing and dancing on the days of hui and la?

Qiang Fu of Huaiyin was always most careful in guarding his conduct throughout his life, and in dealing with people he was very humble and gentle. Every morning of the first, fifteenth, and la days he recited Buddhist scriptures, bowed to Heaven and Earth and the spirits, never once skipping it. One time, on the dawn of the New Year’s Day, the Heaven’s La, a petty man came drunk and cursed Qiang Fu. Qiang Fu simply shut his door and paid him no heed. His family and neighbors could hardly contain themselves, but Qiang Fu said: “On a fine festival such as this, who is it that does not drink? And when a man is drunk and raves, it is only human nature. If I contended with him, would it not only show how narrow my own heart is?” These words of Qiang Fu touched the heavenly spirits. That evening, as he was dozing, he dreamed he had come to a place where he saw a man wearing a golden crown and a purple robe, who said to him: “Though you endured, on the dawn of the Heaven’s La of the first day, an insult that others could not bear; God has therefore commended you and gives you blessings and long life, and your descendants shall enjoy rank for generation after generation.” Just then Qiang Fu was awakened by his family. Later Qiang Fu indeed lived to be over eighty, and his two sons and one grandson were all recommended to office as tribute students; and his great-grandsons and great-great-grandsons were all scholars of fine repute in the world of education.
The case of Qiang Fu is an example of the retribution of reflecting on oneself on the days of hui and la. If one instead, on these days, wildly shouts and sings,

dances, indulges in wine, and is given over to wanton conduct—since one has already violated the precepts of Heaven, the mind of self-examination is surely lost as well. Such evil karma is indeed enough to consume one’s blessings and emolument and to cut off one’s allotted years!
On the first day of each month and at the dawn of every day, crying out loudly and cursing angrily.

The deeds of a single month take the first day as their foundation, and the deeds of a single day take the morning as their foundation. At such a time one ought to purify the mind, so as to accord with the Way. If one roars and shouts in anger, then the muddy vapor rises with the liver-fire, and the true energy is scattered with the voice; whereupon a person becomes dim of spirit and muddy of breath, and the thoughts of good all vanish! An old poem says: “All the many afflictions arise from not forbearing; at the moment of encounter, as before a mirror, the wonder lies in brightness. The Buddha’s words seek non-contention, and the Confucian books value non-striving. Here is a fine, happy road—yet few in the world walk it.” The Buddhist scriptures say: “Anger is the root of losing all good dharmas and the cause of falling into the evil paths; one should cast it off quickly and not let it grow!” Therefore crying out and raging gravely afflicts and burdens people. Even in ordinary times one should be careful and cautious—how much more on the first day and in the early morning?

Chen Ying’s wife, nee Zhao, was of a strong and quarrelsome nature. Every time the first day of the month came round her condition grew worse, and those going in and out of her house heard only her voice shouting and cursing without end. Then one day a Daoist came to her home. Zhao said to him: “Why have you come to my house?” The Daoist said: “I have come to sell a miracle pill; once you take my pill you can live to be a hundred.” Zhao was delighted at this, bought the pill, and swallowed it, and at once turned dumb.

In the Han, the Minister of Works Diwu Lun, because his mother was old and could not come to live with him in his official residence, every time the days of hui, la, the new moon, and the full moon came round would think of his mother and often weep in grief; he bowed to Heaven and prayed for his mother’s longevity.

Alas! The gentlemen of old thus grieved for their kin in sympathy with the seasons. Then those who on the days of hui and la sing, dance, shout, and rage—for what reason do they do so? Moreover, what has already been said about making offerings and delivering the ancestors in their distant ages is very detailed—why not make a little reflection upon oneself?
Blowing the nose, spitting phlegm, spitting saliva, and urinating while facing north.

The north is where the Lord of the Big Dipper dwells, and the North Pole is the pivot of Heaven; the three realms, the ten directions, and the ten thousand spirits all belong to the North Pole, and so the Dipper of the Midmost Heaven is called Supreme. How then can one defile the place where this honored one resides? According to the rules of propriety, a son or daughter-in-law may not, beside father and mother or parents-in-law, vomit, sneeze, spit, or blow the nose, for to do so is disrespect! Since this is so, to blow the nose or spit against the north, the direction of the spirits, is not permitted—how much more to urinate?

In the state of Wu of old, there was a man who, waking in the night pressed by thirst, rose and went outside the door, and naked, urinated toward the north. He suddenly saw the whole sky filled with black banners and beheld the True Warrior appearing in his form. Startled, he crawled from outside back into his room, lay down on his bed, and was ill for several months; only after repenting did the illness mend.

The ‘Scripture of Long Life’ says: “Spring is the east, summer the south, autumn the west, and winter the north; these are the directions pointed to by the monthly orders, the directions in which the handle of the Big Dipper turns, and they are all offenses against the handle of the Dipper; and by them the shortening of life is most swift.” Looking again at the case above, one comes to know that there are precepts for every direction, and not only for the exact north.

The Qian family of Changshu county in Jiangsu was a great clan of the region. In the Zhengde era of the Ming, the family’s houses caught fire and burned for three days and three nights before going out. Yet in the midst of the ashes of the row upon row of burned buildings, only a small three-story tower was not burned. It was the tower where the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law of the fourth branch of the Qians, both widows, lived. When the flames came pressing in on all four sides, the two, having nowhere to flee, and since they had always reverently worshipped the Dipper Spirit, could only kneel and knock their heads and pray to the Dipper with all their might. Suddenly they saw seven persons in red standing beneath the eaves, who raised their sleeves and waved the fire away, and the fire at once scattered. Thereupon the mother-in-law and daughter-in-law were safe and unharmed. The houses all around were burned to the last stick of timber. The miracle of the two women’s prayer to the Big Dipper affecting their safety moved the people of the region, who all devoutly served the Big Dipper.

All who revere the Big Dipper obtain blessings of lengthened life, removal of illness, preservation of life, escape from disaster, bestowal of happiness, and continuation of descendants; and the examples of the floods, fires, robbers, demons, ghosts, and pestilences that do not harm them are beyond counting. Since one understands this much, how could one blow the nose, spit, or urinate facing north?
Singing and weeping before the stove.

The Yellow Emperor’s ‘Scripture of the Stove’ says: “At the place of the stove one may not sing, intone poems, weep, curse, rage, or shout.” And intoning and weeping, though grief and joy differ, are both acts that slight the spirits, and surely will cut off one’s emoluments and longevity. Now people today, before the authorities, do not dare to speak loudly or tell lies—why then do they dare behave recklessly before the spirits? These are things that every person ought earnestly to refrain from! As for the blessings and calamities of reverence and profanity, these have already been explained in detail earlier.
Again, lighting incense with the fire of the stove.

According to the ordinances of the school of the Heavenly Master: “The gray fire beneath the stove is called the secret dung of the crouching dragon.” Therefore one may not use the fire of the stove to light incense. And the taboos of incense and fire spoken of in the religious canons are not confined to this one matter alone. For example, using a paper spill soiled and stained by grease as tinder to burn paper money—this is called vainly piling up wax money; such vainly burned wax money piles up at Mount Tai as high as a mountain, and the assemblies of Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, are all unwilling to accept it.
