Again, in offering to the True Warrior: in summer one may not offer plums, and in winter one may not offer pomegranates; and in inviting the supreme truths to descend, one may not burn nipple-wood incense. Moreover sandalwood is called bath incense, the rose is called the out-of-season flower, and the tung-flower is called the ghost flower—all of these should be avoided. Rather than offend by not avoiding them and bring guilt upon oneself, why not reverently observe the rules of the teaching?

The ‘Collection of the Essentials of the Sutras’ says: “Because there are forms, one may awaken to principle; therefore one must rely upon forms to draw one into the true meaning. So one gazes upon the holy countenance, and relies upon flowers and incense in making offerings.” The Buddha said: “After the Thus-Come-One is extinguished, if a man can use a single flower or a single incense to make offering to the Three Jewels, use one handful of pure water to cleanse the offerings, and with a reverent heart come before the Buddha and call the name of Namo Buddha once—that man falling into the three evil paths is an impossibility.” The ‘Commentary on the Vimalakīrti Sutra’ says: “Incense is the name for turning away from filth, and it has the function of spreading fragrance, scattering its perfume, and lifting its fragrance aloft.” The ‘Record of Mystery-Responses’ says: “The foul breath of the human world rises up to Heaven for four hundred thousand li; and the heavens being pure, none of them but loathes the foul breath of the human world. Yet because they have received the Buddha’s entrustment, and the Buddha commanded the heavenly spirits to protect the Dharma, and the Buddha himself still lived among men, therefore the heavenly spirits dare not but come to the human world. Thus in the Dharma of the Buddha, incense may well be called the foremost in Buddhist worship.” The ‘Avataṃsaka Sutra’ says: “In the Good-Dharma Hall of the Heaven of the Thirty-Three there is an incense called pure and majestic; if one burns a single ball of the pure and majestic incense, its fragrance pervades all the heavens, causing the heavenly spirits to think of the Buddha and to attain the Buddha-recitation samadhi.” This being so—can lighting incense with the fire of the stove really go unadmonished?

In the Song, Zhou Kaishan could recite the ‘Avataṃsaka Sutra,’ and there was another monk who could recite the ‘Diamond Sutra.’ The two suddenly died at the same time. The King of the Underworld asked Kaishan to recite the ‘Avataṃsaka Sutra’ and treated him with great reverence; and asked the other monk to recite the ‘Diamond Sutra,’ and his heart was not so reverent. After they had finished, the King said: “You two, because of the merit of reciting the sutras, have both had your lives extended by twenty-four years; but Kaishan, who holds the ‘Avataṃsaka,’ is to be the more highly regarded; and he will not be coming to the underworld again.” At this, the monk who recited the ‘Diamond Sutra’ was deeply ashamed, and asked where Kaishan dwelt, desiring to go visit him. When he awoke, the monk went directly to Luzhou to visit Kaishan and ask him the reason. Kaishan said: “Whenever I recite the sutra, I first put on clean clothes, sprinkle and sweep the room with perfumed water, and then use stones to strike fire or drill wood to draw fire to light the incense. When making the offering, I first revere my own mind, and when I open my mouth to recite, I am as reverent as if I stood before the true Buddha, never daring to be careless or slight. If there be no purification of fire, I absolutely dare not use any other fire to light the incense.” The monk who recited the ‘Diamond Sutra’ thanked him, saying: “I have sinned! Whenever I recited, I often used the fire of the stove to light the incense. For this alone my disrespect is far too great!”

Master Yu Bi said: ‘On the days of hui and la — the last day of the lunar month and the la month of year’s end — a man should weigh the merit he has gathered in ordinary times, examine and reprove himself, and rouse his will to press on in the practice.’ Therefore the patriarchs often exhorted people, saying: ‘If you have not done the work of preparation beforehand, then when the thirtieth of the twelfth month arrives, you may be sure you will get a lively scene — that is, at the moment of death you will be thrown into confusion.’ They also said: ‘Each of you would do well to examine himself a little: from youth to age, from birth to death, your mind has mingled into one mass with the five desires and the six dusts, with afflictions and karmic consciousness — what result will it all come to in the end? And which is the one move that turns you back? (That is, have you ever examined and reproved yourselves?) All at once the breath stops, the eyes close tight, and the wandering soul after death must follow the good and evil karma of a lifetime and go to receive its reward. In such a case, has your life in this world not been a journey taken in vain? This is what is meant by living and dying to no purpose.’ In Master Lianchi of Yunqi’s exhortation for the aged, on the last day of every lunar month he would remind the assembly, saying: ‘Human life is impermanent — more fleeting even than a breath. It is like a fish in a pot already coming to the boil, which in a moment will be scalded and cooked to shreds. It is like a lamp before the wind, which in an instant is blown out. Moreover this body must before long go down to death, and the road ahead is a vast blur — who knows where it leads? How then can one fail to turn back with a start and awaken to the truth of life’s impermanence? Therefore you must be anxiously on your guard, spurring yourselves on, setting down all ten thousand conditions and single-mindedly reciting the Buddha’s name.’ Thus the patriarchs, with tireless and earnest words, exhorted and warned everyone — how then can we still sing and dance on the days of hui and la?

Qiang Fu of Huaiyin was exceedingly careful in his personal conduct and most courteous in his dealings with others. On the mornings of the first and the fifteenth of each month and of the la days, he would recite the sutras and bow in worship to the gods of heaven and earth, never once failing to keep this up. One year, on the morning of the Heaven-la — the first day of the first lunar month — a petty fellow, drunk with wine, reviled and cursed Qiang Fu. Qiang Fu closed his door and paid him no heed. His family and the neighbors on either side could scarcely restrain their anger, but Qiang Fu said: ‘On a festival day like this, who does not drink? And for a man to run wild when drunk is but human nature. If I were to take him to task, would that not only show how small my own heart is?’
This case of Qiang Fu is exactly the retribution that comes of examining oneself on the days of hui and la. But those who on such days shout wildly and sing,

and dance, giving themselves up to drink and loose behavior — since they have already offended against the statutes of Heaven, the very mind of self-cultivation must be lost to them; and such evil karma is truly enough to wear away a man’s blessings and emoluments and to cut short his allotted years.
To shout aloud and cry out, or to bellow in fury and rage, on the first of the month and at the break of every day:

What a man does within a month has the first of the month as its foundation; what a man does within a day has the early morning as its foundation. At such times one should rather clarify and still the mind, for only so can one accord with the Way. But if one roars and bellows and gives way to anger, then turbid qi rises along with the fire of the liver, and true qi scatters along with the sound of the voice; and so a man grows muddled in spirit and foul in breath, and every good thought is lost. An old poem says: ‘All the afflictions of the mind / spring from a heart that cannot bear; / facing the moment as before a mirror, / the wonder lies in clarity. / The Buddha’s word seeks non-contention; / the Confucian books prize not striving. / A fine and joyous road this is — / yet few in the world will walk it.’ The sutras say: ‘Anger is the root of losing all good dharmas and the cause of falling into the evil paths; it must be cast off with all speed, and must not be allowed to grow.’ Thus shouting and rage weigh heavily upon men and drag them down; and so in ordinary times one should be careful and circumspect — how much more on the first of the month and at daybreak?

The wife of Chen Ying was a woman of the Zhao family, fierce by nature and fond of quarrelling; and whenever the first of the month came round she grew worse still. Those who came and went from her house for the most part heard nothing but the unbroken sound of her shouting and reviling. Suddenly a Daoist priest came to her house, and Dame Zhao said to him: ‘What have you come to my house for?’ The priest said: ‘I have come to sell a miraculous elixir; once a man has swallowed it, he will live a hundred years.’ Dame Zhao was greatly delighted, and bought the elixir and swallowed it; whereupon she at once became mute.

The Han-dynasty Minister of Works Diwu Lun, because his mother was advanced in years and could not come to live with him at his official residence, would think of her on the days of hui, la, and the new and full moons, and often weep in his sorrow; he would bow in worship to Heaven and pray that his mother might be granted long life.

Alas! Thus did the noble men of old feel the season and cherish their kin. And those who sing and dance, or shout and rage, on the days of hui and la — for what reason do they do it? Moreover, what was said above concerning the rites for seeking out the distant dead and delivering one’s forebears was set forth in the greatest detail; why will people not examine themselves a little?
To blow the nose, spit, expectorate, or urinate toward the north:

The north is where the Lord of the Northern Dipper resides, and the North Pole is the pivot of Heaven. The three realms and the ten directions, the ten thousand spirits and all the perfected, are all subordinate to the North Pole; hence the celestial pivot of the Dipper is called the Most Honored. How then can the place where the Honored One dwells be defiled by transgression? According to the rules of ritual, a son or daughter-in-law may not retch, sneeze, spit, or blow the nose beside father and mother or father- and mother-in-law, for to do so is disrespectful. How much less may one urinate toward the north, the quarter in which the gods abide — when blowing the nose and spitting there is already impermissible?

Formerly in the region of Wu there was a man who woke at night with a full bladder, rose and went out beyond the door, and, naked, made water toward the north. Suddenly he saw the whole sky filled with black banners and beheld the Dark Warrior Zhenwu manifesting his form. He was so frightened that he crawled back from the doorway into the house; and thereupon he took to his bed and was ill for several months; only after he had repented was he healed.

The Scripture of Long Life says: ‘The east in spring, the south in summer, the west in autumn, the north in winter — these are the directions indicated by the monthly ordinances, that is, the directions in which the handle of the Northern Dipper turns; to offend against the Dipper’s handle in this way cuts short a man’s allotted years more swiftly than anything else.’ And when we look at the case just told, we understand that each direction has its own prohibition — it is not the due north alone.

The Qian family of Changshu county in Jiangsu was one of the great clans of that place. In the Zhengde reign of the Ming dynasty, the houses of the Qian clan were set ablaze and burned for three days and three nights before the fire went out. Yet amid the ashes of those whole rows of dwellings, three small upper chambers alone were untouched; these were the chambers in which the youngest branch of the Qian family, a mother-in-law and her daughter-in-law, lived together in widowhood. When the great fire closed in from all four sides, the two women were driven by the flames until there was nowhere to flee. Because they had always reverently served the Dipper gods and knew only to knock their heads to the ground and cry out desperately for rescue, they suddenly saw seven men dressed in vermilion standing beneath the eaves, who lifted their sleeves and waved them at the fire, whereupon the fire at once dispersed; and so the two women, mother-in-law and daughter-in-law, came through unharmed, while the houses on every side were burned until not a single beam remained. This miracle — that the two women, by praying to the Northern Dipper, came through unscathed — moved the people of that place, and all of them devoutly served the Northern Dipper.

All the blessings that come of revering the Northern Dipper — lengthened years, freedom from illness, preservation of life, escape from calamity, the granting of happiness, the continuation of one’s line — and all the instances in which flood, fire, robbers, demon-spirits, ghosts, and pestilence were kept from doing harm, are too many to be numbered. One who understands these principles — how could he ever blow his nose, spit, or make water toward the north?
To sing or to weep before the stove:

The Yellow Emperor’s Scripture of the Stove says: ‘At the stove one may not sing, chant poetry, weep, curse, revile in anger, or shout.’ Moreover, chanting and weeping, though grief and joy are not the same, are alike acts of disrespect toward the gods, and a man’s wealth and years will surely be cut short for them. Yet people of today, standing before a magistrate, dare not even speak aloud or tell a lie — why then, before the gods, do they dare to be so utterly unbridled? These are things every man should strictly guard against. As for the blessings and calamities that follow reverence and profanation, these have already been set out in detail above.
To light incense from the stove fire:

According to the regulations of the Celestial Master’s school: ‘The ash and fire beneath the stove are called the dung of the hidden dragon.’ Therefore one may not light incense from the stove fire. And the taboos concerning incense and fire set out in the scriptures are not limited to this one matter. For example, to use a wick of paper soiled and stained with grease as kindling to burn gold paper — this is called ‘accumulating wax-money in vain,’ and such vainly burned wax-money piles up in the Eastern Peak as high as a mountain, while the bureaus of heaven and earth, of yin and yang, will not receive it. Again, when making offerings to Zhenwu, in summer one may not use plums, and in winter one may not use pomegranates; and in inviting the High Perfected to descend, one may not burn nipple incense. Further, sandalwood is called bathing incense, the monthly rose is called untimely flower, and the golden tung is called ghost flower — all of these should be avoided. Rather than failing to avoid them and bringing the guilt of offense upon oneself, would it not be better to reverently observe the ordinances of the teachings?

The Compendium of the Sutras says: ‘It is by means of the phenomenal that one may awaken to principle; therefore one must rely upon the phenomenal in order to be led into the truth, beholding the sacred countenance and making offerings with the support of flowers and incense.’ The Buddha said: ‘After the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, if a man can make offering to the Three Jewels with a single flower and a single stick of incense, or wash and cleanse the offerings with a handful of pure water, and with a reverent heart come before the Buddha and recite once the name of Namo Buddha, then for such a man to fall into the three evil paths is an impossibility.’ The Jingming Commentary says: ‘Incense is the name for that which departs from defilement, and it has the power to diffuse fragrance and scatter sweetness, to lift up its perfume.’ The Records of Spiritual Response say: ‘The stench of the human world rises and fumes upward to the sky for four hundred thousand li, and the heavens in their purity find nothing so hateful as the stench of the human world. Yet because they have received the Buddha’s charge, and the Buddha commanded the heavens to protect the Dharma, and the Buddha himself still dwells among men, the heavens dare not but come among men. Therefore in the Dharma, incense ranks first among Buddhist observances.’ The Avataṃsaka Sutra says: ‘In the Hall of Good Dharma in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven there is an incense called Pure and Adorned; if one burns a single pellet of this Pure and Adorned incense, it will perfume all the heavens, causing the gods to fix their minds upon the Buddha and attain the samādhi of Buddha-recitation.’ This being so, can lighting incense from the stove fire go unprohibited?

Zhou Kaishan of the Song dynasty could recite the Avataṃsaka Sutra, and there was also a monk who could recite the Diamond Sutra; the two died suddenly at one and the same time. King Yama asked Kaishan to recite the Avataṃsaka Sutra, and treated him with the greatest reverence; then he asked the monk to recite the Diamond Sutra, and in his heart was somewhat less respectful. When the recitation was done, King Yama said: ‘You two, by the merit of your recitation, are both granted an extension of twenty-four years of life; and Kaishan, who upholds the Avataṃsaka Sutra, is all the more to be held in esteem — moreover, he will never come again to the underworld.’ At this the monk who recited the Diamond Sutra felt great shame in his heart; and so he asked where Kaishan lived, wishing to go and visit him. After he revived, the monk went straight to Luzhou and called upon Kaishan, asking him the reason for it all. Kaishan said: ‘Whenever I recite the sutra, I must first put on clean garments and sprinkle and sweep a pure room with scented water; then I strike fire from stone, or drill wood to make fire, to burn incense. When I make my vows I first make my own mind reverent, and when I open my mouth to recite, I am as reverent as if I stood before the true Buddha — never once have I dared to be careless or slighting. And if I have no pure fire, I would never dare to make so bold as to use any other fire for burning incense.’ The monk who recited the Diamond Sutra thanked him, saying: ‘I have done wrong. Whenever I recite the sutra I have constantly used stove fire to burn incense; in this one matter alone my disrespect has been very great indeed.’

You must understand that the purpose of burning incense is to express one’s own reverence. Therefore it must be clean and pure before it may be burned. If perchance there is filthy firewood in the stove, and one burns incense with the stove fire kindled from that filthy wood, then reverence turns instead into profanation. This is why Taishang forbade lighting incense from the stove fire.
To cook rice and prepare dishes with filthy firewood:

Though firewood burns beneath the stove, its qi rises upward. Because filthy firewood is unclean, the foul and turbid qi it gives off offends the Stove God — this is the first reason it may not be done. Since one uses filthy firewood to cook food, one will inevitably use it as well to make offerings to the Buddhas and the gods and to sacrifice to the ancestors, and in every case one offends — this is the second reason. The smoke from filthy firewood rises straight up through the void, and the gods, seeing it, are easily angered — this is the third reason. Therefore those who cook food must never use filthy firewood.

In the seventh year of the Zhenghe reign of the Song dynasty, Li Ba contracted leprosy and was ill for three years; every kind of medicine he took was of no avail. Yet before he fell ill, Li Ba had constantly read and recited the Great Compassionate Avalokiteśvara Sutra until he had completed three thousand recitations. One day a monk suddenly appeared and gave Li Ba a pill, telling him to swallow it, for it would cure his illness; but Li Ba kept the pill and would not swallow it at once. That night Li Ba dreamed that the monk who had brought the medicine by day said to him: ‘I am Avalokiteśvara. Because you were wont to cook rice and prepare dishes with filthy firewood, you offended the ghosts and spirits, and so you contracted this leprosy; and because you had once recited the sutra three thousand times, I have today granted you this one pill of the Elixir of Deliverance from Suffering — why will you not take it?’ When Li Ba woke, he swallowed the Elixir of Deliverance at once; and after seven days all the rotten skin over Li Ba’s whole body peeled away, and his beard and eyebrows grew out anew.

That using filthy firewood to cook food offends the gods is a thing that should certainly be prohibited. As for using the branches and trunks of peach and willow trees as fuel for cooking — this too offends the Stove God. It is a taboo handed down in the scriptures of Daoism, and it should likewise be known.
To rise at night with the body unclothed:

A gentleman is watchful of himself before others in open and visible places, and stands in awe of the ghosts and spirits in dark and unpeopled places. Therefore, though he be in a dark room or a hidden corner where no one can see him, he still keeps up a reverent demeanor, as though he stood before the gods. Moreover the ghosts and spirits dwell by nature in dark places, and so are everywhere present; and night belongs to yin, and is all the more the time when the hundred gods meet and peer down. How then can one fail to be careful and circumspect, and so bring down calamity and guilt upon oneself?

Formerly in Pengcheng there was the daughter of an official’s household. Less than a month after she was married, she took for no reason to babbling and talking wildly, and to running about stripped naked, having lost all sense of shame. Many physicians were consulted and prayers were offered to the gods everywhere, but none could cure her illness. Just then it happened that Master Zhang the Perfected was returning to the capital, and the master of the official household sent him a letter asking for his help. Master Zhang at once sent a disciple to counter the affliction with talismans and incantations, but the disciple came staggering back in defeat, and the official’s daughter went on raving and running naked as before. So Master Zhang went himself to perform the rite, and summoned the spirit generals to manifest beneath the altar. The Dark Emperor Xuan had only just arrived when the young woman changed her manner and said: ‘You common woman — to dare to go naked in the night and offend the gods of Heaven is a crime deserving of beheading. Yet you have troubled the High Perfected to come in person, and now your guilt is pardoned.’ When the woman had finished speaking, she fell to the ground in terror; and thereupon her illness was cured.
To carry out death sentences or terms of penal servitude, or to put prisoners to torture, on the days of the eight seasonal nodes:

The eight nodes are the eight festivals of the Beginning of Spring and the Spring Equinox, the Beginning of Summer and the Summer Solstice, the Beginning of Autumn and the Autumn Equinox, the Beginning of Winter and the Winter Solstice. These days are the days on which the gods record the offenses and blessings of the people of the world; and so on such days the people of the world should strive to examine themselves, to cut off evil and cultivate good. Then, on the one hand, they may accord with the mind of Taishang and the assembled gods, who seek to transform and deliver living beings; but if they are utterly without restraint and carry out punishments on the eight nodes, they will wound the harmonious qi between heaven and earth and gravely harm the blessings of their own persons and households.

In the third year of the Wude reign of Emperor Gaozu of the Tang dynasty, an edict was issued providing that in the three months of the first, fifth, and ninth lunar months, and on the ten fasting days of each month, the officials of every level of government might not carry out punishments. And in earlier dynasties it was likewise provided that on the first day of each month punishments were forbidden, as was the slaughter of domestic animals. These were among the measures by which the rulers showed their compassion for the people and their love for all creatures. Those who nowadays serve as the father-and-mother officials of the local people — have they ever understood the deep meaning contained in such measures?

In the Tang dynasty, Dou Gui, a cousin of Emperor Gaozu’s Empress Tai Mu, served as commander of Luozhou. He was by nature harsh and severe and delighted in killing, and for this reason he punished many of the common people and men of letters. When a verdict was to be pronounced, he would not consent to the slightest delay even during the periods when the imperial court expressly forbade punishment and slaughter. Dou Gui also once brought about the death of the Minister Wei Yunqi. In the second year of the Zhenguan reign Dou Gui fell ill, and his illness was grave. Suddenly he said: ‘Someone has brought melons!’ Those about him all answered: ‘No one has.’ Dou Gui said: ‘It is plainly a platter of fine melons — how can you say there are none?’ After a while Dou Gui stared in terror and said: ‘It is not a melon! It is a human head, come to demand my life!’ Then he said: ‘Quickly, help me up; I must meet with Minister Wei.’ Having spoken, Dou Gui died.

To carry out punishments on the eight nodes does not refer to killing alone; even the flogging of prisoners is impermissible. You must understand that generosity and compassion, cruelty and inhumanity, turn upon a single thought of the mind alone; yet the calamity or the good fortune each brings is as far apart as heaven is from earth. Therefore whether one holds office or governs a household, one should be careful and keep the prohibition.
To spit at shooting stars, to point at the rainbow, and often to point at the sun, the moon, and the stars, or to gaze long at the sun and the moon:

The stars and constellations are in heaven, passing through their palaces and coursing through their degrees, drifting and shifting from time to time, and they do not meddle with the people of the world at all — why then should men spit at shooting stars? Foolish men without wisdom recklessly point at shooting stars and take them for monsters, believing that by spitting at a shooting star they can get the better of it — such absurd talk in fact comes from rustic legend. In truth, it is because the words and deeds of the common people have failed in virtue that the celestial signs show forth changes in order to warn the people of the world. So the flight of a comet is in fact drawn forth by the people’s failure in virtue. At such a time one should rather be on guard with fear and dread and redouble one’s self-examination, piling up virtue and doing good in order to dispel the calamity — how then can one spit at a comet? Duke Jing of Qi spoke three words of good sense, and the planet Mars withdrew from its station — this is the response that comes of cultivating virtue.

The red-and-white is called hong, the blue-and-white is called ni; these are the qi produced when heaven and earth, yin and yang, join and meet. The Book of Songs says: ‘The rainbow appearing in the east — no one dares to point at it with the hand.’ The Chunqiu Yundou Shu says: ‘When stars disperse, they become a rainbow.’ Therefore the rainbow is the residual qi of the Dipper stars, displaying its shapes and colors. Thus when Confucius of old composed the Spring and Autumn Annals and the Classic of Filial Piety, and had finished them, he prayed to the Northern Dipper, and a red rainbow descended and became writing cut in yellow jade. Who then can say that the rainbow is not the residual qi of the Dipper stars? And so, to point at the rainbow with the hand — how could there be no guilt in it?

The sun, the moon, and the stars are called the three luminaries, and are also called the three chronograms; they are what Heaven has spread out to illumine and observe the world below and to hand down its laws. Taishang said: ‘When you see the sun, the moon, the Northern Dipper, or the Southern Dipper, you should solemnly bow your head and beg for protection, asking that your faults be pardoned and forgiven; you must not be careless or disrespectful, lest you bring calamity upon yourself.’ In the scriptures of Daoism, men are taught to sacrifice to the sun and the moon, thus: ‘On the first day of the second lunar month each year, sacrifice to the sun; on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month, sacrifice to the moon. You should prepare offerings of incense, flowers, and vegetarian food, and bow in worship and pray to the sun and the moon, in order to repay the sun and the moon for their kindness to us; this can increase a man’s blessings and lengthen his years.’ This being so, can the sun, the moon, and the stars be pointed at with the hand as one pleases, or gazed at long with the eyes?

Zhou Hong says: In my native place, there was once a time when many of the villagers had gathered to drink together, and they saw an unusual light appear on the face of the sun in the sky, and all of them pointed at it with their hands. Suddenly wind and rain came upon them out of nowhere, and down from the sky dropped a monster that looked very much like an ape, with two eyes shining brightly; the people were so frightened that every one of them fell flat on the ground. After a while the monster went away. By then the ears of everyone present were filled with mud, and every person there, from sheer terror, contracted a malady of the heart.

Cai Jing, a chancellor of the Song dynasty, could gaze at the sun for a long time without his eyes blurring, and some said: ‘This is the sign of a man destined for high honor.’ Yet Cai Jing relied on his own eyesight and dared to pit himself against the sun; and one who understands principle knows that in his heart there was no longer any emperor. In the end Cai Jing was indeed degraded and died for having usurped authority and ruined the state.

Sun Jin of the Yuan dynasty grieved exceedingly over his father’s death and walked barefoot in the bitter cold of winter. His father’s coffin had not yet been buried, and Sun Jin was so busy that he never loosened his belt. When he carried his father’s coffin by boat across the river, the wind and waves on the river were so fierce that the sky turned dark and the earth dim; and Sun Jin prayed devoutly to the sun, the moon, and the stars. Before long the wind actually stopped and the waves subsided, and even the sun came out. Sun Jin was especially filial in serving his stepmother, Dame Tang. When his stepmother developed sores, Sun Jin sucked the poison from the sores with his own mouth; and when his stepmother’s eyes went blind, Sun Jin prayed to the sun, the moon, and the stars, and then licked his stepmother’s eyes with his tongue, and his stepmother’s eyes were able to see the light again. Ten days after his stepmother died, when she was about to be buried, the spring rain was falling without cease, and Sun Jin in his distress wept aloud at night, and the rain stopped on that account, and the clouds in the sky parted and the sun came out. When they reached the burial ground and were ready to lay her to rest, it was already night and there was no light, so Sun Jin again wailed and wept aloud; and then the starlight in the sky shone out brilliantly. It had been a night without a moon, yet suddenly it grew bright and gave forth great light, as though it were day.

Judging from this case, the sun, the moon, and the stars not only have the kindness of shining down upon the world, but can also be prayed to at any time and will respond at any time. How then can people point at the three luminaries of sun, moon, and stars as they please, or gaze at them long, and so bring grave fault upon themselves?
In spring, to burn the mountains and hunt:

Even for ‘shooting birds to kill them and chasing beasts to catch them’ Taishang has an explicit prohibition; how much more for burning the mountains to hunt, when the lives slain are beyond counting. Yet Taishang speaks here of spring because spring is the season in which the ten thousand things grow and flourish; and to burn the mountains and hunt in spring is nothing less than to defy the course of Heaven above and to kill living creatures below — cruelty at its utmost extreme. It does not mean that in the other seasons there is no need for the prohibition.

In the Tang dynasty, Liu Mo’er and his son died on the same day. A neighbor named Qi fell ill and died, then came back to life; and so he told others how he had gone to the world below and had seen Liu Mo’er and his son in a boiling cauldron, their skin and flesh entirely gone so that only white bones remained; after a long while they returned to their former shape, and then the skin and flesh vanished again; and after another long while they returned once more to their former shape — thus again and again they suffered the punishment of the cauldron without any respite. King Yama said: ‘This is because Liu Mo’er and his son were devoted to hunting with fire; hence they receive this retribution.’

You must understand that all living beings possess the Buddha-nature — how then can they be killed as one pleases? Hunting is already impermissible; how much more is hunting with fire. For then all things are scorched and burned to ashes by the flames, and even the various insects that lie hidden beneath the ground are burned to death. Thus the harm of hunting with fire is so great that one cannot bear to speak of it. The Book of Rites, in its Monthly Ordinances, contains very detailed provisions forbidding hunting with fire; and Taishang here again lays down the prohibition because hunting with fire is bound up with so many lives — and this is why he warned of it again and again.
To curse malevolently toward the north:

To spit and to blow the nose are small matters indeed; yet even for spitting and blowing the nose toward the north there is still guilt — how much more for cursing malevolently toward the north. Foolish men without wisdom, driven on by their own angry hearts, have no leisure to consider what they ought to scruple at; but they never reflect: if I would give vent to my anger, then how is the anger of the gods to be given vent?

The speech-karma of the people of the world falls into four kinds, and among them malevolent cursing is the most serious. The sutras say: ‘The three poisons of greed, hatred, and delusion in ordinary men are exceedingly fierce, and the fire of anger is constantly being set alight. As soon as they meet with an object, hatred arises; as soon as they encounter an evil condition, obstruction arises. And so when they speak, once anger rises it comes rushing from the mouth and sears another man’s heart, making him feel pain as though cut by a knife, and bringing him immeasurable affliction. Though the body commits no fault, if a man does not guard his speech-karma, he too will fall into the evil paths.’

There was a woman of Xin’an, fierce by nature and childless, who was jealous of the child borne by her husband’s concubine. Every time dusk fell she would curse and revile malevolently toward the north. One evening at dusk, as she again cursed and reviled toward the north, she suddenly saw a star fall to the earth, as large in shape as a bushel, and the sound it gave forth was like thunder; the woman was so frightened that she fell ill, and her belly gradually swelled until she looked as though she were with child. When the time came for her to give birth, she labored for seven days and could not deliver — and in truth there was no child within her belly at all. Only after she had repented with a sincere heart was she healed.

You must understand that the awe-inspiring virtue of the gods is in truth everywhere present. Why then does the text single out the north in particular? It is to stress where their importance lies. How then can men fail to keep ever in mind the fact and the principle that ghosts and spirits are present everywhere, and so hold fear in their hearts and redouble the work of their own cultivation and self-examination?
To kill turtles and beat snakes without cause:

The Perfected One Yingshi said: ‘No living creature may be killed; and the turtle and the snake are the yin essence, corresponding to the constellation of Zhenwu in the north, and so above all may they not be killed. If a man kills them without cause, he will surely meet with cruel retribution.’ Therefore men of compassionate heart are always earnest in rescuing and protecting them.

In Yuezhou there was a villager who drained the water from a pond to catch fish, and so took a great many turtles. He stripped the flesh from the turtles entirely, and carried their shells to Jiangling to sell, and by this made a very great profit. When he returned home, his whole body broke out in sores, and the pain made him bellow aloud in a way that was dreadful to hear; a great basin had to be filled with water, and others had to rub him with their hands before his suffering could be somewhat eased. In the end his skin and flesh sloughed away and his bones lay bare, so that he came to resemble a turtle; and he died with his skin and flesh split open and festering.

There was a rich man who had beside the house he lived in a great withered tree, and the rich man made ready to cut the dead tree down. As he slept at night he dreamed that a man came leading a great many people to beg a favor of him, asking the rich man to grant them a little more time, until they had finished moving away, before he cut the dead tree down. When the rich man woke he sent men to climb up and look into the withered tree, and saw that within it a great many snakes lay coiled and knotted together. So the rich man ordered his men to set fire to it and burn the snakes to death. Before long, in the rich man’s household, in the dead of night, flying flames were constantly seen to fly into the rooms; yet when they rose to put out the fire, there was nothing at all, and this happened so many times in succession that at last no one thought it strange. Then one night a maidservant in the rich man’s household was careless, and set fire to the firewood with a flame, and so the fire blazed up; the rich man’s family took it for the same thing as before, and went on sleeping soundly. By the time they realized that something was wrong, it was too late to escape, and the whole family was burned to death.

When Liu Yanhui’s father was serving as prefect of Huzhou, a man came from the Silver Pit and presented his father with a great turtle, saying: ‘If a man eats the flesh of this turtle, he may live to be a thousand years old.’ His father took the turtle and secretly sent it back again to the place where it had lived. After Yanhui’s father had passed away, Yanhui served as Commandant of Knights in Fangzhou. Suddenly a mountain flood burst forth, and the level ground was submerged to a depth of several feet, and Yanhui’s whole household had no road by which to escape. Yet they saw a great turtle leading the way before them, always by the shallow places; and so the whole family came through that calamity. That night he dreamed that a man in white told him: ‘I am the turtle that your father released into the Silver Pit. I have come here to repay the kindness of your father in saving my life long ago.’

In the Tang dynasty the Perfected One Sun (Sun Zhenren) was once walking in the mountains when he saw the villagers beating a green snake. He bought the snake from the villagers and set it free. Before long a young man came to welcome the Perfected One Sun to a kingly palace, where a man in crimson robes came out to greet him and said: “Yesterday my little son met with calamity; fortunately, sir, in your compassion you came to his rescue. Therefore I have sent my eldest son to welcome you to the palace, to express a little of my gratitude.” He then led the Perfected One Sun deep into the palace. At that point a consort brought out a child dressed in green, who bowed and thanked the Perfected One Sun, over and over expressing gratitude for the life he had saved. The Dragon King kept the Perfected One Sun in the dragon palace for three days, setting before him every delicious delicacy the palace held, its fine silks and its precious jewels, for him to choose as he pleased. The Perfected One Sun accepted none of them, taking only the thirty divine prescriptions that the Lord on High had bestowed upon the dragon palace, and carried them back into the world. By these he saved countless sick people. The Qianjin Fang (Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold) handed down to the present day is precisely what the Perfected One Sun drew from those thirty prescriptions.

As for the various offenses set forth in the preceding passages, the god who presides over destiny (the Director of Destinies) will, according to the weight of the offenses this person has committed, take away his allotted years. For grave offenses he takes away twelve years of life; for lighter offenses, a hundred days. When a person’s allotted span of years has been entirely taken away, then his day of death arrives. And if his crimes deserve more than death, the calamity extends to his descendants.

“Offenses such as these” is the phrase that sums up the preceding passage; it refers to the offenses from “acting contrary to righteousness” all the way to “killing turtles and striking snakes.” The text that follows, beginning with “the god who presides over destiny,” explains the fact that one receives retribution in accordance with the karmic offenses one has committed. The sutras say: “Karma arises from the mind, and the mind is the functioning produced by karmic power. Karma takes shape depending on the mind’s activity, and the mind, following karma, manifests the various states, just as a shadow follows the body!” And the distinction in the mind between right and wrong, good and evil, is like an echo answering a sound; the rewards and retributions that arise from them differ in magnitude and are never in the least off. As for the statement that calamity extends to descendants, this too speaks of retribution across the three periods of time. In short, whether it be distant in our descendants or near in ourselves, the fact of retribution is clear and unfailing; for ever since the minds and conduct of the world turned deceitful, they have amassed too much evil karma, and have wounded the Lord on High’s love of life and violated the protection of the ancestors, and so have brought about the results of descendants in hardship and the ancestral line cut off. Some blame it on fate, others attribute it to their natural constitution. Alas! The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life; even plants, trees, birds, and fish Heaven and Earth cannot bear to see destroyed. Moreover, since humans are the most intelligent of all creatures, how could Heaven and Earth bear to harm people’s descendants? Thus, unless a person has committed extremely grave offenses, his descendants will not be cut off. Yet again that evil retribution, not being exhausted, reaches to the descendants — this too is an eternal and unchanging fact and principle!

In the Sui dynasty the minister Yang Su strongly urged Emperor Wen of Sui to depose the heir apparent Yang Yong and establish Yang Guang in his place — the future Emperor Yang of Sui — which endangered the dynastic line of the Sui. And Yang Su’s son Yang Yuangan had his entire family slaughtered by Emperor Yang. In the Tang dynasty, the founding minister Xu Shiji (granted the imperial surname Li) was consulted when Emperor Gaozong wished to depose Empress Wang and establish Consort Wu (the future Empress Wu Zetian) as empress. Facing opposition from his ministers, Gaozong asked Xu Shiji’s opinion. Xu Shiji, who bore a grudge from having once been exiled by Emperor Taizong, replied: “This is a family matter of Your Majesty; let Your Majesty decide for yourself.” This led to Gaozong’s establishing Empress Wu, thereby sapping the very lifeline of the Tang imperial house. And his grandson Xu Jingye was put to death by Wu Zetian.

The two precedents mentioned above are precisely facts of the calamity extending to descendants. As the saying goes, “he who began it in this way shall end it in this way.” Retribution that comes back in reversal upon oneself surely cannot be denied. Yet people today mostly look only at what is before their eyes. When they see someone who has done much evil and yet seems to come to no harm, they say: “Heaven has no eyes!” When they see someone do evil and yet his family prospers, they say: “One can do evil and still gain fortune!” Let them know that the Book of Changes’ principle — “a family that accumulates good deeds will have surplus felicity; a family that accumulates evil deeds will have surplus calamity” — is the truth; and the word “surplus” in it covers a very wide range! Reckoning from after our own death, it refers to our descendants; how could it refer only to retribution in this present life! Nevertheless, the Lord on High loves life; what is called surplus calamity reaching one’s descendants is likewise a means of punishing evil and encouraging good. If filial sons and compassionate grandchildren cultivate their minds and establish themselves, accumulate goodness and pile up merit, in order to atone for the offenses committed by their forebears and to lighten their own punishment, they can still turn calamity into fortune! This too is what Taishang and the Lord on High earnestly desire.

“Again, as for all who take others’ wealth by force, Heaven reckons it against their wives, children, and household, until death and bereavement gradually come upon them. If they die not, then there shall be flood and fire, thieves and robbers, lost possessions, sickness, and quarrels, to balance the value of what they wrongfully seized.”

There are also many who use their power and influence to seize others’ wealth by force, mostly calculating for the sake of their own wives and families; yet the god who presides over destiny is likewise reckoning against his wife and family in requital for his greed and wickedness, so that the retribution may be proportionate. If by degrees he reaches the point where his evil is full and his years are exhausted, he himself cannot escape death and bereavement. If, fortunately, his offenses are somewhat lighter and he does not yet die, then there will come floods and fires, thieves and robbers, lost possessions, sickness and medicine, quarrels and lawsuits, and many other misfortunes, to repay the total of what he originally wrongfully seized from others.

The preceding passage has already explained that one receives retribution for one’s deeds, and this section again sets forth the calamity of seizing by force. It is spoken chiefly for those who have power and influence! Because this offense is the most unkind and unrighteous, and moreover is the one people find most difficult to avoid, it is specially brought up again in order to warn the world.

You should know that those who seize others’ wealth by force do so mostly for the purpose of enabling their own wives and families to live a good life; yet they do not know that the god who presides over destiny is also reckoning against his wife and family in requital for his greed and wickedness — is this not a case of benefiting where one only harms? Trading the flesh and blood of one’s beloved for heartless money — is this not a great pity? Moreover, when one’s evil is full and one’s years are taken away and the day of death arrives, of what use is all that money? If one wishes to use money to bribe one’s way through the underworld, I fear the underworld will not allow it! When it comes to this point, who would not be willing to see through it all? But it is always too late; why not, before this moment arrives, put oneself in one’s own place and think it over. If one’s offenses are somewhat lighter and one does not die, then one will meet with many calamities, or else unfilial descendants, to scatter the wealth one forcibly seized from others. Know that for those who seize others’ wealth by force, in the unseen world there will surely be a power that takes away the fortune they extorted; so in the end the money comes to nothing at all! And then there are the terrors of flood and fire and thieves, the vexation and regret of lost belongings, the pain and sorrow of sickness, the anger and shame of quarrels and lawsuits, the disgrace of unfilial descendants — one suffers loss for nothing and has no way to recover; and moreover one still bears countless karmic sins, unable to attain ease and never able to make them good, until one is utterly at a loss. Therefore those who seize others’ wealth by force, when they think of this, are not only chilled to the heart, but utterly disheartened.

In the reign of Emperor Xuanzong of Tang, Xing Shou was sent on a mission to Silla. After completing his mission, on the way back he stopped temporarily at Tanshan. Seeing more than a hundred merchants whose several boats were laden with goods worth several hundred thousand strings of coins, Xing Shou sent men to raid them, killing all the merchants and seizing their cargo. Later, when his son plotted rebellion together with Wang Hong, the court sentenced the entire family to execution, and not a single descendant was left! And Wei Gonggan served as governor of Qiongzhou; relying on the power of the government he forcibly extorted a great deal of wealth. When his term of office ended and he returned home, the boat he rode capsized, and all his wealth and goods sank beneath the water, so that he barely kept his old life! Lü Shizao, prefect of Chizhou, plundered the people’s wealth, and while sailing home fully laden his goods were all of a sudden burned up by fire; only the boat and his person escaped harm.

In the Song dynasty the treacherous minister Ding Wei was demoted and exiled to Zhuya by the court. He met with robbers and lost all his property; not long afterward Ding Wei died. Ma Xiang was extremely covetous. Serving as transport official in Xichuan, he happened upon the rebellion of Liu Xu. Ma Xiang hid his gold in a well. After Liu Xu’s rebellion was put down, Ma Xiang went to the well to retrieve the gold he had stored, but search as he might he could not find it! And all of his wealth was likewise gone. The two men Hu Yinggui and Lu Yiqi conspired together to lure the son of an official family into gambling, in order to seize the family’s property. Suddenly Hu Yinggui went blind in one eye and Lu Yiqi became lame in one foot; both were crippled and lived out their lives in poverty and destitution! Qiang Huairen grew rich by means of greedy extortion, yet his son was a reprobate who loved gambling, debauchery, and every kind of lawless deed. Every day there were quarrels and lawsuits, disputes and litigation; in less than ten years the family’s property was all spent. From then on he lived in poverty and hardship, and his descendants never recovered.

The precedents cited above are all instances of people who forcibly seized others’ wealth and then, as calamities came upon them, made good the total of what they originally wrongfully took from others. And the gravest of them was the execution of the entire family of Xing Shou! In this world there are things hard to understand, yet Heaven never fails to requite any evil deed! No matter how clever and resourceful people may be, Heaven is even more skillful in retribution! Alas! How can this not make people afraid!
There are also those who falsely accuse and kill others — this is like trading knives and killing one another!

The preceding passage spoke of forcibly seizing others’ wealth, and here it goes on to speak of killing through false accusation; this is because the matter of killing through false accusation always arises from the calamity of coveting wealth and being unable to part with it. And there are roughly seven kinds of wrongful killing.
The first is a judge’s verdict: a judge, having accepted bribes, cruelly and falsely incriminates a prisoner.
The second is leading troops in war: a general indulges his soldiers in massacre and plunder, and falsely claims credit for military merit.

The third is a doctor’s use of medicine: a doctor, out of greed for money, sells counterfeit drugs to people, or prescribes the wrong medicine and kills a patient, yet argues stubbornly and refuses to admit his error.
The fourth is destroying a pregnancy: for the sake of saving expense, one neglects to raise a baby girl and drowns her; or, indulging in lust one causes a pregnancy and then aborts the fetus.
The fifth is wicked officials in the yamen: deceiving their superiors, abusing their authority to act tyrannically, swindling people’s money, and framing others.
The sixth is harming others through geomancy: bribing a geomancer to alter and destroy the feng shui of another’s ancestral grave, in order to frame that person and bring calamity upon him.
The seventh is an incompetent teacher ruining others: an incompetent teacher who does not teach well harms other people’s children, and ruins the whole life of another’s son.

These seven ways of killing through false accusation, though not alike in method, are the same in that they falsely put people to death! Such offenses are not pardoned by Heaven’s law; if they do not bring man-made calamity, they will surely bring Heaven’s punishment. Though it is called killing others, in truth it is suicide!

In the Song dynasty there was a Chan master who, when young, was drunk. While contending with someone over money, he struck the man with all his might, and the man he struck died on the spot. Fearing the punishment, he fled to a distant place. Later, moved by remorse, he left the household life to become a monk and practiced with bitter diligence. In time he comprehended the great matter and saw his nature clearly, becoming a great Chan master. Moreover he ascended the seat and expounded the Dharma, with several hundred students. When he was over seventy, one morning after bathing he ascended the seat and told the assembly: “Do not move, do not speak; watch the old monk settle a case from forty years ago.” When noon came, a soldier suddenly arrived at the monastery, drew his bow, and was about to shoot the master. The old Chan master joined his palms in salutation and said to the soldier: “I have been waiting for you here a long time!” The soldier, astonished, said: “You and I have never met; why then should I want to kill you the moment I see you? I myself do not understand the reason.” The old master said: “A debt must be repaid and the exchange made fairly — please strike; do not hesitate!” He turned to the assembly and said: “After I die, give this layman a meal, and after the meal escort him home. If you have so much as a single word of reproach for him, you will be defying Heaven and betraying the way of the teacher, and you will not be my disciple.” The soldier, hearing these words, was only the more perplexed, and insisted that the master explain. The master said: “Because you have passed through another life and been reborn in another body, you have forgotten; but I am still in this world, and so have not forgotten.” He therefore told the soldier what had happened in the past. And the soldier, who had never learned to read, suddenly intoned in a loud voice this verse: “Grievance repaid with grievance — when will it cease? Life after life entangled — was this by chance? Better with the master to find release, And now on this very spot to the Pure Land advance.” Having recited this, still holding his bow, he passed away standing. The master then came down from the seat, shaved his head, gave him a Dharma name, changed his clothes, and placed him in the burial niche. He himself sat cross-legged, took leave of the assembly, and passed away seated.

One killed a man forty years before, and the debt was repaid forty years after. The claiming of the debt was indeed somewhat late, but repaying the debt is a thing that never changes! Fortunately both were men of great capacity, so that when they met face to face on the road of enmity, what had been a bitter adversary turned instead into a good and karmic affinity! The soldier, by threatening with death the one who owed him a life-debt, caused him through that very circumstance to cultivate and in that very moment to realize the Way. And the master, by waiting for and urging on the creditor who was owed a life by him, thereby untied the knot of enmity between them and in that very moment passed away seated. This is truly a singular and wondrous karmic affinity, rare in a thousand ages! If the master had not truly attained the Way, or if the soldier had not possessed such great capacity, then he surely would not have been willing to give up the claim and not collect it. Then the principle that killing another is no different from suicide becomes very clear indeed! For the seven kinds of wrongful killing enumerated above, people of the world should strictly guard against each as the occasion arises, and never lightly borrow the harsh debt of killing.

Whoever greedily takes wealth that is not rightfully his is like eating meat that has been soaked by the dripping of a leaking roof, or drinking wine that has been steeped with the feathers of the poisonous bird. Such “leaked meat and poisoned wine” are both fatally toxic; not only do they afford no momentary drunkenness or fullness, but the day of death arrives immediately.

This section again sets forth the harm of covetous profit. Because the world’s craving for gain is so strong, Taishang speaks with an earnest and compassionate heart, exhorting again and again and reminding us over and over. As for the offenses of lust, killing, violence, and the like that people commit, these are not easy to commit, and those who commit them are not many. Only in the matter of obtaining wealth is there endless variety, and it is very hard to investigate. Because there is not a day in the world when money is not used, there is not a person in the world who does not take money! Since there is no person who does not take money, yet among the ways people take it few conform to righteousness and many do not — this is a fact that goes without asking.

Then what is righteousness? Righteousness is acting properly and in accord with reason and human feeling. Whenever one takes others’ wealth and they are glad to give it, that is near to human feeling and accords with righteousness. When they are unwilling to give it, that is contrary to human feeling and not righteous. When one takes it and can openly tell others of it, that is reasonable and accords with righteousness; when one takes it and cannot tell others of it, that is unreasonable and not righteous. Whether the wealth taken be much or little — if it is taken contrary to righteousness and can still be used with an easy and contented mind, then one may as well go along with what people’s hearts favor and simply let it be! Yet Taishang admonishes us earnestly about this, knowing that just as there are those in the world who take wealth unrighteously, so there are those who lose wealth unrighteously; for when one person is gratified, another is grieved; or when one person is gratified, ten people, a hundred people, even thousands and tens of thousands of people are grieved!

Know that the Way of Heaven requires repayment: Heaven is utterly impartial, so how could it show special favor to those who take wealth unrighteously? Yet the misfortunes accumulated in the unseen world — the spirit and the gods wish to see these matters dealt with fairly, and therefore will surely deal with them actively. Taishang knows the reason and warns people with upright words, saying: “Do not take.” But people do not listen. So he gently instructs the world, saying: “It cannot be obtained.” But people do not believe. Then he admonishes them with cautionary words: “To gain ill-gotten wealth is inauspicious!” But the world too regards only the present and gives no thought to the future. Therefore it is best to awaken the world, saying: “To gain and not to gain are the same!” In this way, perhaps the world’s greed for wealth may thereby diminish. So he draws the analogy of leaked meat and poisoned wine. Since leaked meat and poisoned wine are both extremely toxic — the instant they touch the mouth one dies — no matter how reckless or foolish a person may be, no one knowingly eats leaked meat and drinks poisoned wine to excess! If one knows that ill-gotten wealth is leaked meat and poisoned wine, then although thousands and tens of thousands of unrighteous riches lie ready to be taken, one will firmly refuse and not accept them! Is this not being the same whether one gains or not? And so if one gains them but does not use them, are they not useless castoffs of the world? And why then should people exhaust their contrivance and make their schemes to seek the useless castoffs of the world?

Yet the fragrance of leaked meat is like the choicest roast, and the sweetness of poisoned wine is no less than ambrosia. When the world sees their fragrance and sweetness, it again conceives a hope and says: “Hm! Perhaps it is not necessarily toxic!” Consequently there are but few who do not eat heartily of leaked meat and drink deeply of poisoned wine! By the time one can neither vomit it up nor swallow it down, the bowels snap and the skin splits, and very soon one dies. Then, too late, one sighs and says: “Why could I not have seen this outcome earlier?” At that point it is already impossible! Whereas a dish of greens, a meal of wheat, coarse wine, and common vegetables — though they do not taste very good in the mouth, yet one eats one’s fill and drinks one’s fill, and patting one’s belly one is serene and content, at ease and at peace. The sorrow and joy between the two are vastly far apart! For the evidence of these things there has been detailed explanation in the foregoing; I will not append it again here.

When the mind gives rise to a good thought, though the good has not yet been done, it already moves the auspicious spirits to follow and protect, hoping that his virtuous conduct will be perfected and showering blessings upon him from many directions. Or when the mind gives rise to an evil thought, though the evil has not yet been done, it already moves the baleful spirits to follow and observe, waiting until his evil is full to send down calamities from many directions.

Here the word “mind” is singled out, precisely to tell the world: the hinge of calamity and fortune lies entirely in the one mind. It is hoped that people will know, at the very source, that they must be cautious! Let us carefully weigh the initial particle “now” and the word “or” — they carry the sense that a thought issues either from good or enters into evil. Therefore it should be read together with the chapter “Rising at the Cock’s Crow” in the Jinxin chapter of Mencius.

The Buddhist sutras say: “The formation of the myriad phenomena of the universe is all manifested from our one mind.” They also say: “Because our mind can follow defiled and pure conditions, it thereby creates the distinctions of the Ten Dharma Realms. Worldly dharmas and transcendent dharmas are never beyond the scope of the Four Noble and Six Ordinary realms. (The Four Noble are the Buddha, the Bodhisattva, the Pratyekabuddha, and the Śrāvaka. The Six Ordinary are gods, humans, asuras, beasts, hungry ghosts, and hell beings.) Such being the Ten Dharma Realms, they originally have no self-nature, but are all created by our one mind! Thus the mind can become a Buddha, the mind can become a sentient being, the mind can become a heaven, and the mind can become a hell.” And what is meant by the mind rising is the very moment our thought first stirs. A single thought, though extremely subtle, can yet move Heaven and Earth and the ghosts and spirits. If a person can give rise to a single good thought, this very good thought is the talisman that destroys hell, the wisdom sword that cuts off all evil, the compassionate ferry that crosses the sea of suffering, the bright lamp that pierces the darkness. If a single evil thought arises, then the evil paths of the three realms — beasts, hungry ghosts, and hell — appear before one, and one sinks into them without end! Therefore the auspicious spirits and the baleful spirits are both drawn by the good and evil thoughts of the person’s mind and arrive immediately, without the least delay.

Master Hanshan of the Ming dynasty said: “The thought must be seen through at its very arising; do not let it grow while the matter has not yet come. If, just as an evil thought arises, one cuts it off with a single stroke, then the root of karmic power is eliminated on the spot, and false thoughts have no place to arise. Therefore the key to transcending the ordinary and entering the holy lies entirely here!”

Formerly, Yuan Zishi bitterly resented a certain Mr. Miao for being ungrateful and betraying his kindness. About four o’clock one morning, carrying a knife, he set out for the Miao household to kill Miao. On the way he passed a nunnery, whose master, Xuanyuan Weng, had risen early to recite the sutras. He saw several hundred ghosts of strange and monstrous shapes following Yuan Zishi, each holding an axe or an sword, advancing fiercely with fierce and vicious looks upon their faces. Before long Yuan Zishi returned; and this time Xuanyuan Weng saw that those following him all wore golden crowns on their heads and jade pendants at their waists, a hundred or more in orderly groups, surrounded by flowers, incense, banners, and canopies, most solemn in appearance, with serene and joyful looks upon their faces. Xuanyuan Weng therefore invited Yuan Zishi into the hall and asked him the reason. Yuan Zishi said: “Miao was ungrateful and betrayed my kindness; I had just gone to kill him. But when I reached the gate of his house, I thought: although Miao has wronged me, his wife and children are innocent! Moreover he still has an old mother at home. If I kill him, it is the same as killing his whole family. My heart could not bear it, so I changed my thought and returned!” Xuanyuan Weng told him what he had just seen, and congratulated him, saying: “What you have done is already known to the gods; you will surely enjoy a high office and rank in the future!” Yuan Zishi, hearing these words, thereafter applied himself vigorously and diligently to doing good. Later, sure enough, he passed the examinations and rose to the office of prime minister.

Laozi said: “Good and evil — how far apart are they after all?” I have reflected on this saying of Laozi again and again. On the whole these two paths, good and evil, differ but little at their start — merely the rightness or wrongness of a thought as it rises in the ordinary course of daily life! If one understands this principle and earnestly cultivates and reflects, then one’s mind-ground will naturally become wholly good; blessings and virtue will consequently increase without cease, and calamity will all withdraw! We have seen how Yuan Zishi, by a single thought of good, could turn calamity into fortune, and how swift it was! Therefore is not the principle — that when the mind gives rise to good or evil, the auspicious and baleful spirits already follow — all the more to be believed?

“Those who have committed evil deeds, if afterward they repent of their own accord, do no evil, and practice all good, then in the long run they will surely gain auspiciousness and felicity — what is meant by turning calamity into fortune.”

If there is someone who has done evil deeds in the past and later repents and reforms, and who must cut off all evil deeds and practice all good deeds, doing so for a long time, then he will surely obtain auspiciousness and felicity — that is to say, turning calamity into fortune!

This section specially brings out the two words “repent” and “reform,” showing people the method of correcting faults and turning to goodness — that is, the very opportunity for turning calamity into fortune! To reform is to correct one’s faults; to repent is to confess with remorse. In this world those who are purely good and wholly without evil are very few, while those who have once done evil are very many! Yet a wicked person can change and become a good person. Therefore Taishang, with earnest and compassionate words, says it again and again, and at the end of the text sets forth the original intent of correcting faults and repentance, aiming precisely to break through the barrier of delusion and make people turn back to the shore! Again, fearing that the world might misapprehend the meaning of “put down the butcher’s knife and become a Buddha on the spot,” and vainly hope that a cup of water could quench the fire of a whole cartload of burning wood, he says: “Do no evil,” in the hope that one will scrape away one’s evil karma completely. He says again: “Practice all good,” in the hope that one will accumulate virtuous conduct to fullness. Doing this, after a long time, one can gradually dissolve the karmic offenses previously committed, so that their calamity can be entirely dispelled; and afterward one’s practice grows fuller day by day, and the newly added blessings arrive of themselves.

Now the foolish who lack wisdom, knowing their own wrongdoing — or moved by a stirring of conscience — wish to rely on monks and Daoists to bow and repent on their behalf, in the hope of wiping away their karmic offenses. Such conduct is like using a cupful of water to quench a burning cartload of fire! Is this not a great confusion and inversion? Moreover, the offenses of the past have barely been repented of, while new offenses are added again, until in the end one still sinks in the sea of suffering. Not only does one lose this body and life, but one also destroys one’s very nature — how deeply pitiful! If a person repents and reforms in this way, does he not greatly betray the earnest admonition of Taishang’s compassionate heart?

Alas! Taishang teaches people the method of correcting faults and repenting; these few words are most urgent and hit the mark with every stroke. As the saying goes, a single pill of divine elixir can turn iron into gold; a single phrase of supreme principle can turn the ordinary into the holy. Therefore the world should vow to practice it, for only thus can one correspond to Taishang’s great compassion for the world! Now I will first explain the method of repentance, and afterward the method of reform. What is called repentance is the important method of correcting the faults of the past so that the future does not repeat the same mistakes, and of producing the good and destroying the evil! Therefore the root of goodness should be nurtured, and all virtuous conduct will grow from it; while the root of evil should be exposed, and all karmic offenses will thereby be destroyed!

First, one must correctly believe in cause and effect. Neither superstitious nor mistakenly conceiving of cause and effect, one believes that doing good unfailingly brings blessing and doing evil unfailingly brings calamity. Even if no actual deed has yet been done, the retribution still exists; for although thoughts arise and cease moment by moment, karmic power never disappears. Faith is the source of entering the Way, and only wisdom enables one to enter; it is the root of all good. With this right faith one overturns the mind of the icchantika who has no root of goodness!

Second, one must repent of sins and evil. This has shame and remorse as its root. By shame, the sin I have committed is not fit for a human being; by remorse, this sin I have committed will surely bring Heaven’s punishment. This is called the white dharma, meaning one overturns the black dharma of shamelessness!

Third, one must stand in fear of impermanence. When a person’s breath stops, life immediately comes to an end; and the consciousness must go to receive retribution according to karmic power, turning endlessly! By awakening to the principle of impermanence, one overturns the mind that does not fear falling into the evil paths.

Fourth, one must confess and reveal one’s sins. One reveals to others the gravity of the karmic offenses one has committed; because the offenses are thus exposed, the seeds of evil karma wither away, just as when one cuts a tree’s root the branches and leaves wither and fall with it — this overturns the mind that conceals karmic offenses!

Fifth, one must cut off the thought that continues to do evil. Thoroughly and resolutely, with vigor and decisiveness, one casts away all evil karma, just as a steel knife cuts through a thing so that a single slash severs it entirely — this overturns the thought that continues to do evil!

Sixth, one must arouse the bodhi mind. Vowing to remove the suffering and distress of all sentient beings, and to bestow happiness upon all sentient beings — with this vast mind one overturns the mind that ranges over all evil karma!

Seventh, one must cultivate merit and virtue to make up for the faults one has committed. Diligently and earnestly one urges oneself to correct the conduct of the three actions — body, speech, and mind — without the slightest slackness. This is called cultivating merit and establishing virtue, and overturns the mind that does not cultivate the three actions and gratuitously gives rise to evil.
Eighth, one must protect the true Dharma. By not drawing near to heterodox teachers of wrong paths who destroy the Buddha’s true Dharma, one overturns the mind that destroys all good deeds!

Ninth, one must contemplate the immeasurable merit, spiritual powers, and wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions. Earnestly praying that the Buddhas, in compassionate pity, will gather and protect me and help me extinguish my karmic offenses — this cooling, wondrous medicine overturns the mind that remembered evil spiritual friends!

Tenth, one must contemplate that the nature of sin is originally empty. Karmic offenses arise from the mind, and must also be extinguished by the mind! Hence it is said: “When the mind is extinguished, sin also perishes.” If one knows that sin and fortune originally have no self-nature, and that the essence of the mind is originally empty and still, then by returning to the source one can attain ultimate perfect purity — this overturns the mind of ignorance, inversion, and attachment!

The sutras say: “The ocean of all karmic hindrances arises from false thoughts. If one wishes to repent, sit upright and contemplate the real mark; all sins are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can melt away.” Therefore we should repent with utmost sincerity and earnestness, like a soiled garment not washed for a hundred years, which in a single day can be washed clean; or like an ancient mirror covered with dust for a thousand years, which in a single moment can be wiped to reveal the brightness it originally possessed. Thus repentance can undo the faults of a thousand lives and ten thousand kalpas, and destroy the karmic offenses of the four grave offenses and the five rebellious deeds. If one can sincerely repent, there is no evil karma that cannot be extinguished, and no good karma that cannot be produced!

Venerable Aniruddha, in a former life, had been a thief. One night he slipped into a temple to steal. Seeing the Buddha-lamp about to gutter out, he drew his arrow and used it to lift the wick; at once the lamp burst into brilliant, dazzling light. Aniruddha was seized with dread, and on the spot renounced evil for good. The evil karma he had wrought gradually dissolved, and the good he practiced gradually was perfected, until at last he attained the fruit of a sage.

Yang Zhonghe of the Song dynasty had served as the judicial assessor of Xuzhou. In the Tiansheng reign he was dispatched by the court to take up the post of judge in Caizhou. Because he had convicted men unjustly, the Northern Dipper memorialized against him, and grave punishment was about to fall. Overwhelmed with remorse and fear, Zhonghe at once resigned his post in Caizhou and vowed to cultivate a hundred good deeds to atone for his fault. Every time he met traveling monks or Daoists, the poor, the widowed, the orphaned, the solitary, or households stricken by death or sickness, he never failed to give alms and relief. Within a few years he had given away his entire estate. Morning and evening he served the incense of the Perfected Lord Zhenwu with all his heart. Moved by his courage in reforming and pitying his straitened circumstances, the Perfected Lord transformed himself into a Daoist and entrusted him with the sacred lots of the Twelve Perfected Ones, so that he might earn a modest living, settle his life, and continue his cultivation. After his death he was received by the Great Emperor of Mount Tai and appointed to the spirit office of Registrar of Records at Maxi, and the court posthumously honored him as the Perfected Man Wuben.

Mr. Mao Qizong of the Ming dynasty said: “The six yao lines of the Qian hexagram in the Book of Changes conclude in auspiciousness. At the outset it speaks of no calamity; later, from self-complacency, come error and regret. Yet because at the end one can repent, one is thereby able to repair one’s faults and move toward the auspicious.”

Again Mr. Chen Liangmo said: “The poverty or wealth, rank or lowliness, long life or short life of a person — even his every sip and morsel, every act and rest — are all fixed by fate and cannot be resisted. Yet the pivot by which fortune and misfortune are turned lies in the individual himself, and ‘fate’ cannot confine him. For the fixed decree is Heaven’s appointment, while response is Heaven’s heart. Heaven takes the benefit of all things as its fundamental purpose; it is utterly sincere and free from the slightest partiality. If a person can from his inmost heart give rise to a single thought of saving others and benefiting things, and at the very outset acts with no ulterior motive, then though it be but an instant and a single small matter, because his inner sincerity reaches its utmost, it naturally ascends to move the heart of Heaven, like an echo answering a sound. This is the certain principle. Fate is the decree of Heaven; once the heart of Heaven is moved, the decree of Heaven turns in accordance with it — how could it possibly be confined? Consider the state’s system of punishment and reward, which surely cannot be altered at will. If a minister is truly able to move his sovereign’s heart with loyalty, then though he be banished or exiled, he may yet be recalled; at the very moment of execution the sovereign may issue a special pardon. In the briefest space, joy and anger change entirely — and what then is unalterable? From this one knows that the heart of Heaven and the decree of Heaven rise and fall together, and that the many deeds of hidden virtue and reward recorded through the ages are indeed clearly credible.”

Therefore the auspicious man, whose speech is good, whose sight is good, whose deeds are good — having three good deeds in a single day, at the end of three years Heaven will surely send him blessing.
